elimination.verdict: That leaves C. Faster onset and longer duration mean the same drink has a bigger effect.

questions.concept: Polypharmacy is the concurrent use of multiple medications, counting prescription, over-the-counter, and herbal products together.

questions.stem: An 80-year-old takes lisinopril, metformin, and furosemide daily, plus ibuprofen, acetaminophen, a herbal sleep supplement, and a stool softener. Which definition does this meet?

options.text: Taking any medication prescribed by more than one provider
options.rationale: Multiple prescribers is a risk factor for duplication, not the definition of polypharmacy.

options.text: Taking three or more prescription medications daily, regardless of any other products
options.rationale: Below the threshold. Polypharmacy begins at five.

options.text: Taking medications that require cutting tablets in half to achieve the ordered dose
options.rationale: A concern within polypharmacy, but not the definition.

options.text: Taking five or more medications at the same time, including over-the-counter drugs and supplements
options.rationale: The definition, and the inclusion of over-the-counter products and supplements is the part patients and nurses most often overlook.

questions.takeaway: Five or more medications at once, counting over-the-counter drugs and supplements. Polypharmacy is the concurrent use of multiple medications, counting prescription, over-the-counter, and herbal products together.
questions.strategy: When an option adds a qualifier that widens the definition correctly, it is often the answer. Here the qualifier is that non-prescription products count.

strategies: Favor qualifiers
Global or umbrella option

steps.detail: The question asks for the definition, not a related risk.
Three is below the threshold.
Describes a contributing factor.
Describes a dosing concern within polypharmacy.

elimination.verdict: That leaves D. Supplements are not regulated the same way as prescriptions, which is why they count.

questions.concept: Polypharmacy is the concurrent use of multiple medications, counting prescription, over-the-counter, and herbal products together.

questions.stem: A nurse visits a family whose 86-year-old relative has recently moved in with them. They ask what they should expect as she ages and what should prompt a call. Which statement by a family member indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "If she becomes confused suddenly, I should call, because that is not normal aging."
options.rationale: Accurate. Sudden confusion is a red flag and delirium is potentially reversible.

options.text: "Her skin will get thinner and drier, and that is expected."
options.rationale: Accurate. Reduced skin resilience and moisture are expected integumentary changes.

options.text: "If she starts leaking urine, that is just part of getting older."
options.rationale: Urinary incontinence is not an expected change of aging. It is common in older adults and it is assessed rather than accepted, because the causes are often treatable.

options.text: "She may need more light to read than she used to."
options.rationale: Accurate. Sensory changes of aging include reduced acuity in lower light.

questions.takeaway: Expected changes are gradual. Incontinence and sudden confusion are not expected at any age.
questions.strategy: The trap is that the wrong statement sounds compassionate. Accepting incontinence as aging is what stops anyone looking for the cause.

strategies: Negative polarity
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Skin, vision, and reaction time are expected.
Incontinence is abnormal at any age.
Sudden confusion is correctly identified as not normal.

elimination.verdict: A is the statement needing correction: incontinence is assessed, not accepted.

questions.stem: An 82-year-old living alone takes eight medications including a morning diuretic and a bedtime sedative. She has fallen twice in six weeks, both times at night. Which observation most warrants further teaching?

options.text: The patient uses a weekly pill organizer filled at the start of each week
options.rationale: An intervention that reduces risk.

options.text: The patient cannot open the bottles and asks a neighbor to do it each week
options.rationale: Physical barriers cause missed doses in patients who understand their regimen perfectly. Ability to open bottles, use pill planners, and measure liquids is part of the assessment.

options.text: The patient reads the label with reading glasses
options.rationale: Using glasses is an adaptation that supports safe administration.

options.text: The patient keeps a written list of medications and brings it to appointments
options.rationale: Supports accuracy and helps with reconciliation.

questions.takeaway: Much of medication safety in older adults is physical rather than cognitive.
questions.strategy: Three of these options are adaptations that reduce risk. Find the one describing a barrier, not a strategy.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The question asks which finding increases risk.
Glasses support safe reading.
An organizer reduces error.
A list supports reconciliation.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B. Dependence on a neighbor to open bottles means doses are missed when the neighbor is away.

questions.scenario: An 82-year-old has been in a rehabilitation unit for three weeks following a hip fracture. Review the functional record.
questions.stem: The nurse reviews the functional record, which tracks ambulation, meals eaten, weight, and assistance with dressing across the admission. Which conclusion does the nurse draw?

options.text: The patient is progressing as expected for her age
options.rationale: Every measure is moving the wrong way. Age does not explain a three-week decline.

options.text: The patient is experiencing functional decline and requires comprehensive assessment
options.rationale: Declining mobility, intake, weight, and self-care together suggest a geriatric syndrome, which involves multiple factors and requires comprehensive assessment.

options.text: The patient should be discharged since rehabilitation has plateaued
options.rationale: This is not a plateau, it is a decline, and discharging without assessment abandons the problem.

options.text: The weight loss is the only finding requiring follow-up
options.rationale: Isolating one measure misses that four are moving together, which is the point of the trend.

questions.takeaway: When several measures decline together, think geriatric syndrome and assess comprehensively.
questions.strategy: Trend items reward reading across rows as well as down columns. One declining measure is a finding; four declining together is a pattern.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: All four measures worsen across three weeks.
Decline is not expected progress.
A decline is not a plateau.
Four measures are moving, not one.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B. Poor intake, weight loss, and reduced mobility feed each other.

questions.stem: A home health nurse teaches an 81-year-old about fall prevention after two falls in the past six weeks. The patient describes the changes she plans to make around the house and to her routine. Which patient statement indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "I will move the rugs out of the hallway."
options.rationale: Accurate. Scatter rugs are an environmental hazard.

options.text: "I will ask about taking my water pill earlier in the day."
options.rationale: Accurate. Diuretic timing drives the night-time toileting when falls happen.

options.text: "I will replace the bulb at the top of the stairs."
options.rationale: Accurate. Adequate lighting, especially at night, is an intervention.

options.text: "I will stay in bed more so I do not risk falling again."
options.rationale: Immobility causes deconditioning, which weakens the strength and balance that prevent the next fall. The answer to fall risk is more safe movement, not less movement.

questions.takeaway: The answer to fall risk is more safe movement, not less.
questions.strategy: Reducing activity feels like the safe choice and it produces the weakness that causes the next fall. Watch for options that reduce risk by reducing life.

strategies: Negative polarity
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Find the statement to correct.
Rugs, diuretic timing, and lighting are all correct.
One statement buys safety with deconditioning.

elimination.verdict: A is the statement needing correction: bed rest is not fall prevention.

questions.stem: An 84-year-old is moving from the home she has lived in for forty years into an assisted living facility. Since arriving three days ago she has been anxious, mildly confused in the evenings, and has asked repeatedly when she is going home. Which nursing action is most appropriate?

options.text: Explain that anxiety after a move is normal and will pass
options.rationale: Dismisses the experience and offers nothing.

options.text: Limit visitors for the first week so the patient can settle
options.rationale: Increases isolation at the moment connection matters most.

options.text: Request a sedative to manage the anxiety until she settles into the new surroundings
options.rationale: Medication for an environmental and emotional problem, and sedatives increase fall risk.

options.text: Maintain the patient's usual routines where possible and include them in decisions
options.rationale: Relocation is a major life stressor involving loss of familiar surroundings, change in routine, loss of control, and separation from relationships. Maintaining routine and including the patient restores some control.

questions.takeaway: Relocation stress is treated with routine, inclusion in decisions, and orientation, not with medication.
questions.strategy: When the cause of distress is a loss of control, look for the option that gives some control back.

strategies: Patient-centered option

steps.detail: The stressor is a move, with anxiety and mild confusion.
Deepens the separation from relationships.
Normalizes without helping.
Adds fall risk and treats the wrong problem.

elimination.verdict: That leaves D. Promote orientation as well.

questions.stem: A nurse is caring for an 84-year-old admitted two days ago with a hip fracture. The daughter reports her mother became confused overnight and does not recognize the room. Which conclusion by the nurse is correct?

options.text: Sudden confusion is a red flag requiring assessment for an underlying cause
options.rationale: Sudden confusion is a red flag. Hospital-acquired delirium is common two to three days after admission, and infection, poor oxygenation, medications, and acute illness are contributing factors.

options.text: Confusion is expected at this age and requires reassurance only
options.rationale: Age is not a diagnosis. Treating a new change as normal aging is the error to avoid.

options.text: The daughter should be asked to stay overnight to reorient her mother
options.rationale: Family presence may help, but it does not investigate why the change happened.

options.text: The confusion indicates the onset of dementia and should be documented as a new baseline
options.rationale: Dementia is progressive and chronic. An overnight change is acute and fits delirium.

questions.takeaway: Expected age-related changes are gradual. Sudden change is a red flag and gets investigated. Delirium is acute, fluctuating, and potentially reversible, with altered consciousness. Dementia is chronic and progressive with clear consciousness.
questions.strategy: When a stem gives you a time frame, use it. Years suggests aging or dementia. Hours or days suggests an acute cause.

strategies: Assessment before intervention

steps.detail: Onset is overnight, on day two of a hospital admission.
Attributes a sudden change to age.
Dementia does not begin overnight.
Comforting, but it skips finding the cause.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A. Think delirium and investigate the cause.

questions.concept: Delirium is acute, fluctuating, and potentially reversible, with altered consciousness. Dementia is chronic and progressive with clear consciousness. Depression develops over weeks with intact consciousness.

questions.stem: A nurse admits an 86-year-old after a fall at home. On assessment she finds thin dry skin, slower reaction time during transfers, and reduced hearing for high-pitched sounds. Her daughter reports her mother became confused overnight. Which findings require further nursing assessment rather than being attributed to normal aging? Select all that apply.

options.text: Sudden confusion
options.rationale: A red flag. Expected changes are gradual.

options.text: Slower reaction time
options.rationale: Listed as a change that may occur with normal aging.

options.text: A new unexplained fall
options.rationale: A red flag, and a fall is always a clinical clue.

options.text: Changes in sensory perception
options.rationale: Listed as a change that may occur with normal aging.

questions.takeaway: Gradual changes are expected with aging. Sudden confusion and a new unexplained fall are not, and both need assessment rather than attribution to age.
questions.strategy: Sort by how fast it appeared. Anything sudden or new is assessed; anything gradual and symmetrical is usually expected.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Two findings are gradual and two are new.
Slower reaction time and sensory change are expected with aging.
Overnight confusion and a fall at home.

elimination.verdict: A and C are selected: both appeared suddenly.

questions.stem: A nurse admits an 81-year-old using the 4 Ms framework. He takes nine medications, scores 22 of 30 on cognitive screening, walks 20 feet with a frame, and states his priority is returning to his woodworking shed. Which element does his stated priority represent?

options.text: Reviewing the patient's medication list for duplication
options.rationale: That is Medication.

options.text: Asking the patient what goals are most important to them for this admission
options.rationale: What Matters is the patient's goals and preferences, and it is placed first in the framework deliberately.

options.text: Screening for delirium, dementia, and depression using a validated cognitive tool
options.rationale: That is Mentation.

options.text: Assessing gait and transfer safety, which determines how much assistance he requires
options.rationale: That is Mobility.

questions.takeaway: The 4 Ms: What Matters, Medication, Mentation, Mobility. What Matters comes first. The 4 Ms framework for age-friendly care: What Matters, Medication, Mentation, and Mobility.
questions.strategy: Each distractor here is one of the other Ms. Match the action to the right M rather than judging which is most important.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The question names one specific M.
Medication.
Mentation.
Mobility.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B. patient-centered care means asking what matters to this person.

questions.concept: The 4 Ms framework for age-friendly care: What Matters, Medication, Mentation, and Mobility.

questions.stem: An 81-year-old is transferred to a restorative care setting after hospitalization for pneumonia. She walked independently before admission and now needs assistance. She is expected to regain her previous level of function. What is the goal of this care?

options.text: Sustaining a need that is not expected to change
options.rationale: That describes continuing care.

options.text: Diagnosing and treating a new illness that has developed during the admission
options.rationale: Secondary care.

options.text: Regaining function lost during the illness so she can return to her previous level
options.rationale: Restorative care aims at recovery, as distinct from continuing care which sustains a need that will not end.

options.text: Preventing illness before it occurs so that hospitalization is avoided altogether
options.rationale: Preventive care.

questions.takeaway: Restorative care aims at recovery. Continuing care sustains. Restorative care aims at regaining function after illness or injury. Continuing care sustains a need that is not expected to end.
questions.strategy: The expected trajectory decides it. Ask whether the goal is regaining something or sustaining someone.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Expected to regain her previous level.
Continuing care sustains.
Treatment and prevention.

elimination.verdict: That leaves C: restorative care aims at recovery, as distinct from continuing care which sustains a need that will not end.

questions.concept: Restorative care aims at regaining function after illness or injury. Continuing care sustains a need that is not expected to end.

questions.stem: During an admission assessment, a caregiver answers every question directed at the older adult and becomes irritated when the nurse asks to speak with the patient alone. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Find a reason to speak with the patient alone and assess her directly
options.rationale: A caregiver who will not permit private contact is itself a warning sign, and the patient cannot disclose in his presence.

options.text: Document the caregiver's involvement and continue the assessment with him present
options.rationale: Records the behavior as attentiveness and loses the only chance to hear from her.

options.text: Ask the caregiver to describe a typical day at home in detail
options.rationale: Gathers useful context and still leaves him controlling every answer.

options.text: Report the caregiver to adult protective services on the basis of this observation
options.rationale: Reasonable suspicion is the threshold for reporting, and answering for a patient alone does not yet meet it.

questions.takeaway: A caregiver who blocks private contact is a red flag. Create the opportunity to assess the patient alone.
questions.strategy: One distractor under-reacts by documenting, one gathers more from the wrong person, one over-reacts. The key gets her alone.

strategies: Assessment before intervention

steps.action: Ask who has not been heard
steps.detail: The patient herself.
Both keep him in control of the account.
Nothing yet meets reasonable suspicion.

elimination.verdict: That leaves speaking with her privately.

questions.scenario: A 79-year-old admitted three days ago for pneumonia is now agitated and inattentive, with symptoms that come and go through the day. She takes eight medications including a nightly sedative. Temperature 38.2 C, and she has not had a bowel movement since admission.
questions.stem: Complete the diagram by selecting from the choices below.

options.text: Assess for reversible causes including infection, oxygenation, and medications
options.rationale: Delirium has contributing causes: infection, fever, poor oxygenation, medications, and acute illness. Finding the cause is the treatment.

options.text: Review the medication list with the provider for contributing agents
options.rationale: Sedatives are a common contributor, and polypharmacy is a risk in older adults.

options.text: Apply wrist restraints to prevent the patient pulling at lines
options.rationale: Restraints worsen delirium and agitation and are a last resort after less restrictive measures.

options.text: Reorient the patient once per shift and otherwise limit interaction
options.rationale: Reduced interaction increases disorientation.

options.text: Request an order for an additional sedative
options.rationale: Adds to the medication burden that may be causing the delirium.

options.text: Delirium
options.rationale: Acute onset, fluctuating course, inattention, and altered consciousness, with fever and medications as contributors.

options.text: Dementia
options.rationale: Progressive and chronic over years, without fluctuation or acute onset.

options.text: Depression
options.rationale: Mood changes, withdrawal, and loss of interest rather than fluctuating inattention.

options.text: An expected change of aging
options.rationale: Age is not a diagnosis, and this is a change from baseline.

options.text: Level of consciousness and attention
options.rationale: The two features that define delirium and track whether it is resolving.

options.text: Temperature and signs of infection
options.rationale: Infection and fever are contributing factors.

options.text: Serum cholesterol
options.rationale: Unrelated to acute delirium.

options.text: Hair and nail growth
options.rationale: Not a monitoring parameter here.

options.text: Deep tendon reflexes
options.rationale: Not what tracks delirium.

questions.takeaway: Delirium is acute, fluctuating, and caused by something. Find the cause rather than sedating the symptom. Delirium is acute, fluctuating, and potentially reversible, with altered consciousness.
questions.strategy: Two options in the action pool make the problem worse while looking like management. Sedation and restraint both increase delirium.

strategies: Assessment before intervention

steps.detail: Acute onset with fluctuation and inattention is delirium.
Both worsen delirium.
Reduced orientation increases confusion.

elimination.verdict: Actions A and B, condition A, parameters A and B.

questions.concept: Delirium is acute, fluctuating, and potentially reversible, with altered consciousness. Dementia is chronic and progressive with clear consciousness. Depression develops over weeks with intact consciousness.

questions.scenario: A 77-year-old lives with an adult grandson who manages her finances. Over four months she has lost 9 kg, her antihypertensive was last filled in March, and she has been brought to the emergency department twice with dehydration. She has a pressure injury on her sacrum and says she is often alone all day.
questions.stem: Which findings support a concern for neglect or financial exploitation? Select all that apply.

options.text: Unintentional weight loss of 9 kg over four months
options.rationale: Unmet nutritional need is a core indicator of neglect.

options.text: A prescription last filled four months ago
options.rationale: Withheld medication is neglect, and it raises the question of where the money went.

options.text: Repeated presentations with dehydration
options.rationale: A recurring unmet basic need rather than an isolated event.

options.text: A sacral pressure injury
options.rationale: Suggests prolonged immobility without repositioning or attention.

options.text: The grandson managing her finances
options.rationale: Managing money for a relative is common and lawful. It becomes a concern only when her needs go unmet because of it.

options.text: Being alone during the working day
options.rationale: Many older adults are alone during the day. Alone is not the same as neglected.

options.text: Living with an adult family member
options.rationale: A living arrangement rather than a finding.

questions.takeaway: Neglect shows as unmet basic needs over time. A family member handling money is not itself exploitation.
questions.strategy: Two distractors describe an arrangement rather than a finding. Ask what has actually gone unmet.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Weight, medication, hydration, and skin are findings.
Managing money and living together are arrangements.
Being alone by day is common and not itself neglect.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, and D are selected.

questions.stem: Highlight the findings that contribute to this patient's risk of falling.
questions.takeaway: Falls are multifactorial: previous falls, medications, toileting, vision, and the environment.
questions.strategy: Two findings in this note are protective rather than hazardous. Read each for whether it raises or lowers the chance of a fall. Two findings reduce rather than create risk.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Four findings raise risk.
Grab bars and family contact.
Medication, toileting, and environment interact at night.

elimination.verdict: Highlight s1, s2, s3, and s4.

questions.nursesNote: 1100: Home visit. Patient is 84, lives alone in a two-story house. Daughter visits weekends. Since the last visit six weeks ago the patient has fallen twice, once on the stairs and once at night going to the bathroom. Reports getting up three to four times nightly to void. Takes a nightly sedative, a morning diuretic, an antihypertensive, two over-the-counter analgesics, a herbal sleep supplement and a stool softener. Reports cutting one tablet in half because the dose seemed high. Wears bifocals. Scatter rugs throughout the hallway. Burned-out bulb at the top of the stairs. Grab bars present in the bathroom. Weight down 4 kg since the last visit. VS: T 36.6 C; HR 76; BP lying 142/84, standing 118/68.

segments.text: Two falls in the past six weeks
segments.rationale: A previous fall is the strongest predictor of another, because whatever caused the first is usually still there.

segments.text: Nightly sedative and a morning diuretic
segments.rationale: The two specified medication classes for fall risk. One slows reflexes and clouds judgment, the other drops pressure on standing.

segments.text: Getting up three to four times nightly to void
segments.rationale: Night-time toileting in poor light is when falls happen, and the diuretic timing is driving it.

segments.text: Scatter rugs and a burned-out bulb at the top of the stairs
segments.rationale: Correct environmental hazards, and the location of the bulb makes it the worst possible placement.

segments.text: Grab bars present in the bathroom
segments.rationale: A safety measure already in place, so it reduces risk rather than creating it.

segments.text: Daughter visits at weekends
segments.rationale: Social contact and support. It does not itself create fall risk.

questions.caseTitle: Older adult with recurrent falls at home

questions.stem: Complete the sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.takeaway: A fall is a clinical clue. Ask why the patient fell.
questions.strategy: Every contributor in this note can be changed. Options that relocate her or restrict her fluids treat the fall as a fixed fact.

strategies: Assessment before intervention

steps.detail: Five contributors present at once.
Decides before assessing.
Risks dehydration and misses the timing.

elimination.verdict: Blank 1 is A and blank 2 is A.

questions.sentence: The patient's situation is best described as [[1]], and the nurse's first action is to [[2]].

options.text: multifactorial fall risk
options.rationale: Previous falls, two fall-risk medication classes, nocturia, bifocals, and environmental hazards all present together.

options.text: a single environmental hazard
options.rationale: The rugs and the bulb matter and they are one contributor among several.

options.text: an expected consequence of aging
options.rationale: Age is not a diagnosis, and every contributor here is modifiable.

options.text: a neurological emergency
options.rationale: Nothing in the note describes acute neurological change.

options.text: assess gait, balance, vision, toileting, and the home environment
options.rationale: A fall is a clinical clue. The assessment looks for the modifiable reasons behind it rather than treating the fall as the whole event.

options.text: recommend she move to assisted living
options.rationale: A placement decision before anyone has established what is causing the falls.

options.text: advise her to stop drinking fluids after noon
options.rationale: Risks dehydration, which causes dizziness and falls, and it does not address the diuretic timing.

questions.caseTitle: Older adult with recurrent falls at home

questions.stem: For each proposed action, determine whether it is INDICATED or NOT INDICATED for this patient.
questions.takeaway: The answer to fall risk is more safe movement, not less movement.
questions.strategy: Two actions here reduce her risk by reducing her life. Both create deconditioning or overstep scope. One proposed action reduces falls by reducing movement. Consider what that costs.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Rugs, lighting, medications, and toileting.
Outside nursing scope and irrelevant to falls.
Deconditioning worsens the underlying problem.

elimination.verdict: Four actions are indicated and two are not.

rows.text: Secure or remove the scatter rugs
rows.rationale: An effective intervention, and the hallway is where she walks at night.

rows.text: Replace the bulb at the top of the stairs
rows.rationale: Adequate lighting especially at night is specified, and the top of a staircase is the worst place for darkness.

rows.text: Review the medication list with the provider, including the over-the-counter products
rows.rationale: She takes seven products including a sedative and a diuretic, and polypharmacy counts non-prescription items.

rows.text: Advise her to stop taking the stool softener without discussing it
rows.rationale: Discontinuing a medication is outside nursing scope and it addresses nothing in her fall risk.

rows.text: Discuss moving the diuretic to the morning and earlier if possible
rows.rationale: Diuretic timing drives the nocturia that has her walking at night.

rows.text: Recommend she remain in bed at night and use a bedpan
rows.rationale: Immobility causes deconditioning, which weakens the strength and balance that prevent the next fall.

questions.caseTitle: Older adult with recurrent falls at home
questions.concept: CUS escalates a concern with graded language: I am Concerned, I am Uncomfortable, this is a Safety issue. SBAR reports; CUS escalates when reporting has failed.

questions.stem: For each finding at the follow-up visit, determine whether it reflects IMPROVEMENT, NO CHANGE, or DECLINE compared with the first visit, or whether it is a NEW FINDING not previously assessed.
questions.takeaway: A plan can be working on most measures while one continues to worsen and another appears for the first time.
questions.strategy: Four rows improved and it would be easy to stop reading. The two that matter clinically are the ones that did not. One finding has worsened and one has no baseline. Both matter more than the four that improved.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Five measures were recorded at the first visit.
Weight is still falling.
Acuity was never assessed.

elimination.verdict: Four improved, one declined, one new finding.

questions.baseline: First visit: two falls in six weeks, voiding three to four times nightly, scatter rugs present, standing BP 118/68 from lying 142/84, weight down 4 kg.

rows.text: No falls in the past six weeks
rows.rationale: Down from two.

rows.text: Voiding once nightly
rows.rationale: The diuretic was moved to the morning.

rows.text: Rugs removed and stair bulb replaced
rows.rationale: Both specified hazards addressed.

rows.text: Standing BP 128/76 from lying 138/82
rows.rationale: The orthostatic drop has narrowed from 24 points to 10 after the medication review.

rows.text: Weight down a further 2 kg
rows.rationale: Continued unintended weight loss, and it was already falling at the first visit. Nutrition is a fall risk factor through weakness and vitamin D and calcium status.

rows.text: Reports her vision has become blurred in the past week
rows.rationale: Her bifocals were noted at the first visit but acuity was never assessed, so there is no baseline. New blurred vision requires assessment in its own right.

questions.caseTitle: Older adult with recurrent falls at home

questions.stem: Complete the sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.takeaway: Two fall-risk medication classes acting at night, producing the trip she takes in the dark.
questions.strategy: Several contributors are real. Rank by what can change this week and what was present at the moment she fell.

strategies: Priority key word

steps.detail: At night, going to the bathroom.
The diuretic, taken in the morning but acting through the evening.
The staircase and the weekend support cannot change this week.

elimination.verdict: Blank 1 is A and blank 2 is A.

questions.sentence: Of the contributors identified, the one the nurse can address soonest with the greatest effect is [[1]], and the reason is [[2]].

options.text: the timing of the diuretic and the nightly sedative
options.rationale: Both are fall-risk medication classes and both act at night, which is when she fell.

options.text: the two-story layout of the house
options.rationale: A structural feature that cannot be changed quickly.

options.text: the weekend-only family support
options.rationale: A support gap rather than a direct cause of the falls.

options.text: they produce the night-time toileting in poor light where the falls happened
options.rationale: The diuretic drives the nocturia and the sedative slows her reflexes when she gets up.

options.text: medication changes require no discussion with the provider
options.rationale: Adjusting or stopping a medication sits with the prescriber.

options.text: her age is the main contributor
options.rationale: Age is not a diagnosis and is not modifiable.

questions.caseTitle: Older adult with recurrent falls at home

questions.stem: The provider agrees to review the regimen. Which 2 nursing actions are appropriate?
questions.takeaway: Report everything she takes, including what she changed herself. Then address the timing that puts her in the dark.
questions.strategy: Exactly two are requested. Three wrong options act outside scope, risk dehydration, or reduce her movement.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The complete list and the self-adjustment.
Stopping a product is the prescriber's.
Both trade one risk for another.

elimination.verdict: A and B are selected.

options.text: Report the full list, including the over-the-counter and herbal products, and the self-adjusted dose
options.rationale: Polypharmacy counts everything she takes, and cutting a tablet in half is a change nobody knows about.

options.text: Ask about moving the diuretic earlier in the day and reassess the night-time voiding
options.rationale: Addresses the cause rather than managing the consequence.

options.text: Advise her to stop the herbal supplement today
options.rationale: Discontinuing a product is outside nursing scope and the interaction has not been assessed.

options.text: Advise her to restrict fluids after noon
options.rationale: Risks dehydration, which causes dizziness and falls.

options.text: Recommend she use a bedpan overnight to avoid walking
options.rationale: Immobility causes the deconditioning that produces the next fall.

options.text: Document that she is non-adherent for cutting her tablet
options.rationale: Labels a decision instead of reporting it, and discards the reason she gave.

questions.caseTitle: Older adult with recurrent falls at home

chapters.title: Concepts of Care for LGBTQ+ Patients

questions.stem: A clinic finds that several LGBTQ+ patients have not returned after an initial visit, and two describe feeling judged by staff. The nurse manager reviews the evidence on why this population experiences worse health outcomes than the general population. Which factor is a contributor?

options.text: Lack of affirmation in care, which deters people from using services
options.rationale: Occurs alongside bias and discrimination during care and heterocentric policies. Care avoided is care not received.

options.text: A reluctance among providers to prescribe medication
options.rationale: Not a contributing factor.

options.text: Lower rates of health insurance in all LGBTQ+ populations
options.rationale: Not one of the drivers.

options.text: A biological predisposition to chronic disease
options.rationale: Not a cause. The disparities are driven by how care is delivered and experienced.

questions.takeaway: The disparities come from bias, heterocentric policies, and lack of affirmation, not from anything intrinsic to patients.
questions.strategy: When a stem asks about a health disparity, look for a system or care-delivery cause rather than a patient-level one.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The question asks for a contributor.
Locates the cause in the patient rather than the system.
Not a contributing factor.
Not a contributing factor.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A. Avoidance of care is itself an outcome of non-affirming environments.

questions.stem: A teenager arrives at a clinic and the intake form asks for mother's name and father's name. The receptionist reacts visibly when the teenager explains they have two mothers. Which understanding does this illustrate?

options.text: Front desk staff are not part of the care team
options.rationale: The opposite. Their interaction shaped the patient's experience of the whole visit.

options.text: Documentation requirements must take priority over patient comfort
options.rationale: The form could be written differently without losing any information.

options.text: The teenager should have completed the form differently
options.rationale: Places responsibility on the patient for a form that did not fit their family.

options.text: Harm often happens before the clinical encounter begins
options.rationale: A heterocentric form combined with a visible reaction exposed the patient in a waiting room, before any clinician was involved.

questions.takeaway: The form and the front desk are part of the care. Harm can happen before a nurse is involved.
questions.strategy: When a stem describes a non-clinical interaction, ask what it reveals about the system rather than about the individuals.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The events occur at intake, before any clinical encounter.
The form can be revised without losing data.
Reception staff shape the patient experience.
Blames the patient for the form.

elimination.verdict: That leaves D. Use forms that ask for parent or guardian names, and take information without visible reaction.

questions.stem: A nurse feels uncomfortable caring for a transgender patient and asks to be reassigned. The unit is short-staffed and no colleague is free to swap. Which action is most appropriate?

options.text: Ask a colleague to take the assignment instead
options.rationale: Avoidance, and it leaves the patient with whichever nurse is available rather than with competent care.

options.text: Avoid discussing anything related to gender during the encounter
options.rationale: Omits relevant assessment and models discomfort.

options.text: Reflect on the personal biases and assumptions behind the discomfort, and seek education
options.rationale: Self-reflection is a domain: examine assumptions, cultivate accountability, and commit to self-awareness and growth, alongside educating yourself.

options.text: Ask the patient to explain their identity so the nurse can learn
options.rationale: Places the burden of education on the patient during their own care.

questions.takeaway: Self-reflection first, then education. Not avoidance, and not asking the patient to teach you.
questions.strategy: Discomfort in a nurse is answered by self-examination and learning. Options that transfer the work to the patient or a colleague are wrong.

strategies: Patient-centered option

steps.detail: The nurse's discomfort is the finding.
Avoids rather than addresses.
Makes the patient the teacher.
Omits assessment.

elimination.verdict: That leaves C, which pairs self-reflection with ongoing education.

questions.stem: A nurse prepares to care for a patient scheduled for gender-affirming surgery and reviews the range of procedures that fall under that heading, recognizing that transitioning is individualized and no patient has all of them. Which procedures are included in the range of gender-affirming surgeries? Select all that apply.

options.text: Masculinizing chest reconstruction, also called top surgery
options.rationale: Masculinizing chest reconstruction sits within the range of gender-affirming surgeries, and no patient has all of them since transitioning is individualized.

options.text: Coronary artery bypass grafting
options.rationale: A cardiac procedure unrelated to gender-affirming care.

options.text: Cholecystectomy
options.rationale: Gallbladder surgery, unrelated to gender-affirming care.

options.text: Genital surgical procedures, also called bottom surgery
options.rationale: Genital surgical procedures are one option in the range, and many transgender patients never have them.

options.text: Appendectomy
options.rationale: An abdominal procedure unrelated to gender-affirming care.

options.text: Gynecologic surgery
options.rationale: Gynecologic surgery belongs to the range, and a patient who has had it may still require screening based on remaining anatomy.

questions.takeaway: The range spans gynecologic, chest, genital, and facial procedures. Not every patient has any of them. Gender-affirming care is recognized as medically necessary rather than cosmetic. Transitioning is individualized and no patient has every procedure in the range.
questions.strategy: One clearly unrelated option in a select-all is a gift. Take it out and evaluate the rest against the correct list.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The question asks which procedures fall in the correct range.
A cardiac procedure, unrelated to gender affirmation.

elimination.verdict: A, D and F are selected.

questions.concept: Gender-affirming care is recognized as medically necessary rather than cosmetic. Transitioning is individualized and no patient has every procedure in the range.

questions.stem: Before discharge, a 31-year-old transgender man reviews his ongoing health screening with the nurse. He takes testosterone, has had chest reconstruction, and retains a cervix. Which patient statement indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "Since I take testosterone, I do not need cervical screening any more."
options.rationale: Screening follows the anatomy that is present, not the gender marker or the hormone regimen. Testosterone does not remove the organ or the risk.

options.text: "My chest surgery is relevant to how you plan my care after this procedure."
options.rationale: Accurate. Surgical history affects positioning and assessment.

options.text: "Not everyone who is transgender has the same surgeries."
options.rationale: Accurate. Transitioning is individualized and no patient has every procedure in the range.

options.text: "I still need cervical screening because I have a cervix."
options.rationale: Accurate. Anatomy determines screening.

questions.takeaway: Screen the anatomy that is present. Hormone therapy does not remove an organ or its risk.
questions.strategy: This matters most because the screening gap causes real harm.

strategies: Negative polarity
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Find the incorrect belief.
A cervix present means cervical screening.
Testosterone changes neither the organ nor the risk.

elimination.verdict: A is the statement needing correction: hormones do not replace screening.

questions.stem: A nursing student uses the terms sex, gender identity, gender expression, and sexual orientation as though they mean the same thing. Which statement reflects correct understanding of these four concepts?

options.text: Sex assigned at birth, gender identity, gender expression, and sexual orientation vary independently
options.rationale: Sex assigned at birth is what was recorded from anatomy. Gender identity is who the person knows themselves to be. Gender expression is how they present it. Sexual orientation is who they are drawn to.

options.text: Knowing a patient's gender identity tells the nurse their sexual orientation
options.rationale: All four concepts vary independently. Knowing one tells you nothing about the other three.

options.text: Gender expression and gender identity are the same thing
options.rationale: Identity is internal; expression is outward presentation. They can differ.

options.text: Sexual orientation is determined by sex assigned at birth
options.rationale: No such relationship exists.

questions.takeaway: Four separate concepts. Knowing one tells you nothing about the other three. Four distinct concepts: sex assigned at birth, gender identity, gender expression, and sexual orientation. None predicts another.
questions.strategy: Any option that infers one of the four from another is wrong by definition. That single rule answers most items on this topic.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
Global or umbrella option

steps.detail: The question tests the relationship between the four concepts.
Infers orientation from identity.
Collapses internal identity into outward expression.
Infers orientation from anatomy at birth.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A. They vary independently.

questions.concept: Four distinct concepts: sex assigned at birth, gender identity, gender expression, and sexual orientation. None predicts another.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old arrives for a scheduled colonoscopy. The chart lists a legal name he does not use and a gender marker that does not match how he presents. He has not returned for two previous appointments. Which action is appropriate?

options.text: Avoid using any name and address the patient as sir or ma'am
options.rationale: Gendered honorifics carry the same risk as the wrong name, with less information behind them.

options.text: Use the patient's preferred name and pronouns, and document both
options.rationale: Practicing affirming language and communication means using preferred names and pronouns. Both can be recorded so the whole team uses them.

options.text: Use the legal name in all interactions to avoid documentation errors
options.rationale: Prioritizes the record over the person and is not required for accurate documentation.

options.text: Ask the patient which name to use only when family is not present
options.rationale: Treats the name as something to conceal, which undermines the affirmation.

questions.takeaway: Use preferred names and pronouns, and document them so the team does too.
questions.strategy: Options that hide a patient's identity to avoid awkwardness are wrong. The affirming answer is the open one.

strategies: Patient-centered option

steps.detail: A mismatch between legal name and used name.
Puts the record ahead of the patient.
Makes the name conditional on who is watching.
Substitutes a gendered guess.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B. Documenting both keeps the record accurate and the care affirming.

questions.stem: A midwifery unit reviews why same-sex and transgender parents report poorer birthing experiences than other families using the same service. Staff examine the paperwork, the language used, and the care provided after birth. Which factors contribute to poor birthing experiences among LGBTQ+ parents? Select all that apply.

options.text: Bias or discrimination during care
options.rationale: Bias during care shapes whether a parent is treated as a parent, and it is a documented driver of poorer birthing outcomes.

options.text: Universal access to affirming postpartum care
options.rationale: Access is inconsistent, which is part of why outcomes are poorer.

options.text: Invalidation as parents
options.rationale: Being treated as though you are not the parent undermines the relationship at the moment it is forming.

options.text: Shorter average labor duration
options.rationale: Not among the contributors to poorer reported experiences.

options.text: Consistently shorter postpartum stays
options.rationale: Length of stay is not among the contributors to poorer reported experiences.

options.text: Birth trauma
options.rationale: Birth trauma is more likely when a parent feels unsafe or unheard, so the experience and the outcome are connected.

questions.takeaway: Poor birthing experiences and outcomes are driven by bias, policy, invalidation, and gaps in affirming care.
questions.strategy: Look for the option that describes the solution rather than the problem. It is the reversal, and it is the one to reject.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The question asks for contributing factors.
Describes access that, when absent, is itself a contributor.

elimination.verdict: A, C and F are selected.

questions.stem: A nurse in a sexual health clinic takes a history from a 23-year-old who identifies as non-binary, uses they and them, and declines to state a gender on the form. The nurse needs the history to be clinically useful. Which approach is correct?

options.text: Base the history on the sex recorded at birth in the chart
options.rationale: The chart records a marker rather than the anatomy present or the behavior that determines risk.

options.text: Base the history on the patient's gender identity
options.rationale: Identity does not predict anatomy or behavior, and assuming it produces the wrong screening.

options.text: Ask about anatomy and behavior using the patient's own words for their body
options.rationale: Screening and risk follow the anatomy present and what the patient actually does. Their words for their body keep the history accurate and the encounter safe.

options.text: Omit the sexual history unless the patient raises it
options.rationale: Omission is how screening gaps occur in this population. The history is taken as it would be for anyone.

questions.takeaway: Take the history from anatomy and behavior, in the patient's own words. Identity and chart markers predict neither.
questions.strategy: Two wrong options substitute a label for an assessment. Ask what is present and what the patient does.

strategies: Patient-centered option

steps.detail: Anatomy present and behavior.
A chart marker and an identity, neither of which predicts anatomy.
Omission creates the screening gap.

elimination.verdict: That leaves C: anatomy and behavior, in the patient's own words.

questions.stem: A school nurse notices that four LGBTQ+ students have made appointments in six weeks reporting difficulty sleeping, and two have lost weight. One discloses he has thought about not being here. Which statement explains this pattern?

options.text: Mental health screening should be deferred until the patient raises it
options.rationale: Deferring screening perpetuates the overlooked-needs pattern.

options.text: Mental health is a particular concern among LGBTQ+ young people
options.rationale: It is a reason affirming care matters.

options.text: Mental health outcomes are equivalent to the general population
options.rationale: LGBTQ+ patients experience worse health outcomes overall.

options.text: Mental health concerns are unrelated to experiences of discrimination
options.rationale: Bias and discrimination during care are drivers of poorer outcomes.

questions.takeaway: Mental health is a particular concern among LGBTQ+ young people, and affirming care is protective.
questions.strategy: Options claiming equivalence between a marginalized group and the general population usually contradict the disparity data.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The question asks for an accurate statement.
Discrimination is a driver.
Contradicts the disparity findings.
Waiting for the patient perpetuates overlooked needs.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B: specified specifically, and it is a reason affirming care matters.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old three months into hormone therapy under specialist supervision asks the nurse what benefit to expect beyond physical changes. Which statement is accurate?

options.text: These medications reduce gender dysphoria, depression, anxiety, and suicidality
options.rationale: A specified benefit, and they are safe for both youth and adults with provider supervision and appropriate management.

options.text: These medications are available over the counter
options.rationale: They are prescription medications requiring provider supervision.

options.text: They are recommended only for adults
options.rationale: Described as safe for both youth and adults with appropriate supervision.

options.text: The effects are immediate
options.rationale: Effects may take an extended period and some are not fully realized quickly.

questions.takeaway: HRT significantly reduces negative psychological outcomes and is safe with provider supervision.
questions.strategy: Timing and access distractors are common in medication items. Check whether the option adds a restriction the source does not.

strategies: Eliminate absolutes

steps.detail: The question asks for an accurate statement about HRT.
Effects are not immediate.
These are prescription medications.
Only for adults adds a restriction that is not accurate.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A: a specified benefit, and they are safe for both youth and adults with provider supervision and appropriate management.

questions.stem: A patient admitted to a surgical unit has a legal name on the wristband that he does not use. He tells the night nurse his correct name, and by the following afternoon three different staff have addressed him by the legal name. Which action is most appropriate?

options.text: Ask him to tell each staff member himself as they arrive
options.rationale: Places the burden of correction on the patient every time someone new enters the room.

options.text: Use the legal name for safety and the correct name socially
options.rationale: Two-name practice guarantees the error continues and signals his name is not the real one.

options.text: Record his correct name and pronouns where all staff will see them
options.rationale: Recording it is what stops the error recurring with each new person, rather than leaving him to correct everyone individually.

options.text: Change the legal name in the record
options.rationale: The legal name is needed for identification and billing. Both are recorded rather than one replacing the other.

questions.takeaway: Record both names, use the correct one, and put it where every staff member will see it.
questions.strategy: The distinction is between fixing the system and fixing each encounter. Options that make the patient repeat himself are the ones to cut.

strategies: Patient-centered option

steps.detail: Three staff, same error, one day.
He has already told them once.
One entrenches the error, one deletes needed information.

elimination.verdict: That leaves C: record it where staff will see it.

questions.stem: A patient in the intensive care unit has a same-sex partner of 14 years who is not a legal spouse and is not listed as next of kin. Unit policy restricts visiting to immediate family. The patient is intubated and cannot speak. Which action is most appropriate?
questions.takeaway: The patient defines who counts as family. Legal status is not the test.
questions.strategy: Watch for options that apply an extra requirement to this patient that would not be applied to anyone else.

strategies: Patient-centered option

steps.detail: Fourteen years, and the person who knows his wishes.
Applies the rule without examining it.
Both add conditions others would not face.

elimination.verdict: That leaves D: advocate for his chosen family.

options.text: Apply the policy and restrict the partner to the waiting area
options.rationale: Applies a rule without considering whether it serves this patient, and it excludes the person closest to him.

options.text: Allow access only when a legal relative is also present
options.rationale: Makes his partner's presence conditional on a relative who may not exist or may not be close to him.

options.text: Ask the partner to provide documentation of the relationship
options.rationale: Imposes a proof requirement not applied to opposite-sex partners.

options.text: Advocate for the partner's access as the patient's chosen family
options.rationale: Family is defined by the patient rather than by legal status, and a partner of 14 years is the person who knows his wishes.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman tells the nurse at a well-woman visit that she has been with the same female partner for 22 years and has never needed cervical screening because she has never been with a man. Her last smear was 19 years ago. Which response is accurate?

options.text: She may stop screening given her sexual history
options.rationale: A common and harmful assumption. Lower average risk is not the same as no risk.

options.text: She should be screened only if she develops symptoms
options.rationale: Screening detects disease before symptoms appear, which is the point of it.

options.text: She needs screening only if she has had male partners previously
options.rationale: Makes the interval depend on partner history rather than on anatomy.

options.text: She still requires cervical screening on the routine schedule
options.rationale: Human papillomavirus transmits between female partners, and screening follows the anatomy present rather than the sex of a patient's partners.

questions.takeaway: Screen the anatomy that is present. A patient's partners do not determine which organs she has.
questions.strategy: Assumptions about who is at risk cause missed screening in this population. Ask what anatomy is present, not who the patient sleeps with.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A cervix is present.
Both make screening depend on partner history.
Screening precedes symptoms.

elimination.verdict: That leaves D: routine screening continues.

questions.concept: CUS escalates a concern with graded language: I am Concerned, I am Uncomfortable, this is a Safety issue. SBAR reports; CUS escalates when reporting has failed.

questions.stem: A nurse educator runs a session on caring for LGBTQ+ patients. Which statement by a staff nurse indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "If I use the wrong pronoun, I should correct it, apologize briefly, and move on."
options.rationale: Accurate, and it keeps the focus on the patient rather than the nurse's discomfort.

options.text: "If I use the wrong pronoun, saying nothing is better than drawing attention to it."
options.rationale: Silence leaves the error uncorrected and communicates that it did not matter. Correct it, apologize briefly, and move on.

options.text: "Gender-affirming care is medically necessary rather than cosmetic."
options.rationale: Accurate, and calling it optional misrepresents it.

options.text: "I should ask for a patient's name and pronouns and record them for all staff."
options.rationale: Accurate. Recording it is what stops the error recurring.

questions.takeaway: Correct the error, apologize briefly, and move on. Silence is not neutrality.
questions.strategy: The wrong statement is motivated by not wanting to embarrass the patient. It embarrasses them more, because the error stands.

strategies: Negative polarity
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Find the mistaken approach.
Accurate, and it keeps the focus on the patient rather than the nurse's discomfort.
Accurate.
Accurate, and calling it optional misrepresents it.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B: silence leaves the error uncorrected and communicates that it did not matter.

questions.stem: A nurse reflects on her practice after a patient tells her he has avoided health care for years because of how he was treated. She wants to identify what she and her unit can change. Which nursing actions support an affirming environment for LGBTQ+ patients? Select all that apply.

options.text: Use the patient's preferred name and pronouns
options.rationale: Part of practicing affirming language and communication.

options.text: Participate in ongoing training about LGBTQ+ health issues
options.rationale: Educate yourself is one of the five specified domains.

options.text: Ask the patient to educate the staff about their identity
options.rationale: Places the burden of education on the patient during their own care.

options.text: Reflect on personal biases and assumptions
options.rationale: Self-reflection, including accountability and commitment to growth.

options.text: Use intake forms that do not assume a heterosexual two-parent family
options.rationale: Addresses heterocentric policies, a driver of poor experiences.

options.text: Record the patient's legal name only, to keep documentation consistent
options.rationale: Preferred name and pronouns are used and documented alongside the legal name.

questions.takeaway: Educate yourself, self-reflect, use affirming language, and fix the systems patients meet.
questions.strategy: Two wrong options here shift work onto the patient or prioritize the record over the person. Both patterns recur.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The question asks which actions support affirmation.
Makes the patient responsible for staff education.
Puts documentation consistency ahead of the patient.

elimination.verdict: A, B, D, and E remain, covering education, self-reflection, language, and systems.

questions.stem: A nurse works with a 74-year-old lesbian patient admitted for a hip fracture. Her partner of 41 years is not listed as next of kin, and she declines to say why. She has refused two doses of analgesia. Which concern should the nurse assess?

options.text: Lower rates of chronic conditions than the general older population
options.rationale: Reversed. Higher rates of chronic conditions and poorer overall health are.

options.text: Struggles with isolation and loneliness
options.rationale: Occurs alongside historical discrimination, lifetime exposure to stigma and violence, higher rates of chronic conditions, and overlooked reproductive and sexual health needs.

options.text: Greater likelihood of having adult children as caregivers
options.rationale: Not a specified finding, and family estrangement is part of why isolation is significant.

options.text: Higher rates of participation in senior services
options.rationale: Lack of affirmation discourages people from using services.

questions.takeaway: Lifetime stigma, isolation, higher chronic disease burden, and overlooked sexual health needs.
questions.strategy: When two options state opposite directions of the same variable, one is likely the answer. Decide which direction the evidence reports.

strategies: Opposite pair, look closely

steps.detail: The question asks for a characteristic finding.
States the direction backwards.
Not a contributing factor, and estrangement contributes to isolation.
Non-affirming environments reduce service use.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B: occurs alongside historical discrimination, lifetime exposure to stigma and violence, higher rates of chronic conditions, and overlooked reproductive and sexual health needs.

questions.scenario: A hospital is reviewing why LGBTQ+ patients report poorer experiences on its inpatient units than in its outpatient clinics.
questions.stem: Which factors contribute to poorer inpatient experiences? Select all that apply.

options.text: Shared rooms assigned by the gender marker in the record
options.rationale: Placement by marker rather than identity exposes patients and is a frequent source of distress.

options.text: Visiting rules that define family by legal relationship
options.rationale: Excludes chosen family and partners who are not legal spouses.

options.text: Repeated handovers between staff who have not been told the name and pronouns
options.rationale: Each new shift repeats the error, and the patient carries the correction.

options.text: Outpatient clinics scheduling longer appointments
options.rationale: Describes the clinics rather than a factor worsening the inpatient experience.

options.text: Gowns and toiletries supplied in one standard set
options.rationale: Applies to every patient equally and is not a contributor.

options.text: Inpatient stays being longer than a clinic visit
options.rationale: Length alone does not produce a poorer experience; what happens during it does.

options.text: Staff asking the patient's name at each medication round
options.rationale: Identity verification before a dose is required safety practice.

questions.takeaway: Inpatient systems repeat the encounter many times a day. Room assignment, visiting rules, and handover are where harm accumulates.
questions.strategy: Ask what the inpatient setting does repeatedly that a clinic does once.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Room placement, visiting, and handover.
One describes the clinic, one describes length alone.
Standard supplies and identity checks apply to everyone.

elimination.verdict: A, B, and C are selected.

questions.scenario: A 16-year-old with a diagnosis of gender dysphoria attends clinic with a parent. The patient has recently started hormone therapy under specialist supervision and reports low mood and social isolation at school. The parent asks whether treatment can simply be stopped until the patient is older.
questions.stem: Complete the diagram by selecting from the choices below.

options.text: Explain that gender-affirming care is medically necessary and supported by strong evidence
options.rationale: Described as medically necessary and potentially life-saving care, and hormone therapy significantly reduces dysphoria, depression, anxiety, and suicidality.

options.text: Assess mood, isolation, and safety, and involve mental health services
options.rationale: Mental health is a particular concern among LGBTQ+ young people, and gender-affirming care spans mental health, medical, and social services.

options.text: Agree that treatment should pause until adulthood
options.rationale: Hormone therapy is described as safe for both youth and adults with provider supervision, and disruption is a contributor to poor outcomes.

options.text: Advise the patient to conceal their identity at school to reduce conflict
options.rationale: Concealment is not affirmation and increases isolation.

options.text: Refer the family to a provider who does not offer gender-affirming care
options.rationale: Removes access to care that is described as medically necessary.

options.text: A patient receiving gender-affirming care with mental health needs requiring assessment
options.rationale: Combines the medical picture with the mental health concern in LGBTQ+ young people.

options.text: An adverse reaction to hormone therapy requiring discontinuation
options.rationale: Nothing in the scenario describes an adverse physical reaction.

options.text: A patient whose treatment should be deferred pending maturity
options.rationale: Contradicts the evidence described for youth with appropriate supervision.

options.text: A routine adolescent visit requiring no additional follow-up
options.rationale: Low mood and isolation require assessment.

options.text: Mood, and screening for suicidality
options.rationale: Correct as outcomes that hormone therapy improves and as a particular concern in this population.

options.text: Social support and experiences of isolation
options.rationale: Isolation and loneliness are, and school is where this patient's difficulty is occurring.

options.text: Serum sodium
options.rationale: Not a monitoring priority described here.

options.text: Bone mineral density weekly
options.rationale: Not a parameter here identifies, and weekly monitoring is not plausible.

options.text: Daily weight
options.rationale: Not relevant to the concerns described.

questions.takeaway: Gender-affirming care is medically necessary and reduces dysphoria, depression, anxiety, and suicidality. Disruption is a harm. Gender-affirming care is recognized as medically necessary rather than cosmetic. Transitioning is individualized and no patient has every procedure in the range.
questions.strategy: The parent's question is sincere and the answer is still no. Options that pause, conceal, or redirect care all appear reasonable and all cause the harms it names.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Ongoing affirming care plus a specified mental health concern.
Disruption in hormone therapy is a contributor to poor outcomes.
Both reduce affirmation and access.

elimination.verdict: Actions A and B, condition A, parameters A and B.

questions.concept: Gender-affirming care is recognized as medically necessary rather than cosmetic. Transitioning is individualized and no patient has every procedure in the range.

questions.stem: Highlight the findings that require nursing action.
questions.takeaway: Harm often happens before the clinical encounter: the form, the name on the chart, the pronoun at the bedside.
questions.strategy: Two findings here are his medical history and inform your assessment. The rest are things the service is doing to him. Two findings are his medical history rather than problems requiring action.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Two findings are his care; four are the system's.
Anatomy determines screening.
It excludes before anyone speaks.

elimination.verdict: Highlight s1, s2, s3, and s4.

questions.nursesNote: 1100: Patient is 31, admitted for elective surgery. Transgender man. Chart lists a legal name the patient does not use; he asks to be called Sam. Two staff members have used incorrect pronouns during this admission. Takes testosterone under specialist supervision and had masculinizing chest reconstruction two years ago. Has not had genital surgery and retains a cervix; no record of cervical screening. Intake form offers fields for mother's name and father's name only.

segments.text: Chart lists a legal name the patient does not use
segments.rationale: Using a name a patient does not use, repeatedly and in front of others, is a harm that occurs before any clinical care begins.

segments.text: Two staff members have used incorrect pronouns during this admission
segments.rationale: Requires correction and an apology, and repeated misgendering drives avoidance of health care.

segments.text: Patient has not had a cervical screening despite retaining a cervix
segments.rationale: Screening follows anatomy rather than gender marker, and this is a genuine gap in preventive care.

segments.text: Intake form offers only mother's name and father's name
segments.rationale: A policy written around one family structure, which excludes the patient before anyone speaks.

segments.text: Takes testosterone under specialist supervision
segments.rationale: Appropriate prescribed care. It informs what screening is needed and is not a problem.

questions.stem: A 56-year-old newly diagnosed with hypertension discusses his ongoing care with the nurse. He asks how the teaching he is receiving now differs from the screening that found the problem. Which patient statement indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "Learning to manage my blood pressure now counts as primary prevention."
options.rationale: Primary prevention acts before a condition exists. He already has hypertension, so teaching aimed at preventing its complications is tertiary prevention.

options.text: "Cardiac rehabilitation after a heart attack would be tertiary prevention."
options.rationale: Accurate. Tertiary limits damage and restores function in established disease.

options.text: "My blood pressure screening was secondary prevention because it found something already there."
options.rationale: Accurate. Secondary prevention detects a condition early.

options.text: "Quitting smoking before any lung disease develops is primary prevention."
options.rationale: Accurate. Primary prevention prevents onset.

questions.takeaway: Primary prevents onset. Secondary detects early. Tertiary limits damage in established disease.
questions.strategy: Two statements describe teaching. They sit at different levels, and the deciding question is whether the disease already exists.

strategies: Negative polarity
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: He already has hypertension.
Teaching about an existing condition is tertiary.
Screening, cessation, and rehabilitation are correctly placed.

elimination.verdict: A is the statement needing correction: that teaching is tertiary, not primary.

questions.stem: A nurse counsels a 62-year-old man with a family history of myocardial infarction. He smokes fifteen cigarettes daily, has not exercised in years, eats mostly processed food, and his cholesterol is elevated. She plans teaching around what he can actually change. Which cardiovascular risk factors should the nurse target for teaching? Select all that apply.

options.text: Cigarette smoking
options.rationale: Modifiable and the highest-yield target.

options.text: Sedentary lifestyle
options.rationale: Modifiable through activity.

options.text: Family history of early myocardial infarction
options.rationale: Non-modifiable. Useful for risk assessment, not for intervention.

options.text: Untreated hypertension
options.rationale: Modifiable through medication and lifestyle.

options.text: Age 62
options.rationale: Age cannot be changed, so it is a non-modifiable risk factor. It still matters for screening decisions.

options.text: Diet high in saturated fat
options.rationale: Modifiable through nutrition teaching.

questions.takeaway: Assess all risk factors and intervene on the modifiable ones.
questions.strategy: Sort into modifiable and non-modifiable first. Age, sex, ethnicity, and family history are never the teaching target.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Polarity is positive. This is a select all that apply, so there is no single best answer. Judge each option separately.
Non-modifiable.
Non-modifiable.

elimination.verdict: Keep A, B, D, F. In a SATA, judge each option as its own true or false statement rather than picking a single best answer.

questions.stem: A nurse runs two sessions. The first helps patients increase physical activity and improve nutrition to raise their general wellbeing, with no particular disease in mind. The second teaches patients with a family history of colorectal cancer about screening. Which statement describes these?

options.text: Both are illness prevention
options.rationale: The first has no particular disease in mind.

options.text: The first is tertiary prevention and the second is primary

options.text: Both are health promotion
options.rationale: The second targets a specified disease, which makes it prevention.

options.text: The first is health promotion and the second is illness prevention
options.rationale: Health promotion raises overall wellbeing; illness prevention targets a specific condition.

questions.takeaway: Health promotion raises overall wellbeing. Illness prevention targets a specific condition.
questions.strategy: Ask whether a particular disease is specified. If it is, you are in prevention. Both sessions are worthwhile. The distinction is whether a specific condition is being targeted.

The two sessions differ.

questions.stem: A patient with terminal cancer receiving hospice care tells the nurse he has made peace with his diagnosis, is spending his remaining time with family, and feels more at ease than he has in years. Which statement explains this?

options.text: Wellness is possible in the presence of illness
options.rationale: Wellness is a state of balance and fulfillment rather than the absence of disease.

options.text: Wellness is the same as remission of disease

options.text: Wellness refers only to physical functioning

questions.takeaway: Health and illness are not opposites. A person can be seriously ill and still be moving toward wellness.

questions.stem: A nurse assesses two patients with the same diagnosis whose management of it differs greatly. Which variables influence health? Select all that apply.

options.text: Genetics and age
options.rationale: Both are named variables and both are non-modifiable.

options.text: Lifestyle and environment
options.rationale: Two of the named variables, and the ones nursing intervention can most often reach.

options.text: Culture and socioeconomic status
options.rationale: Culture shapes what health means to a person; socioeconomic status shapes what is available to them.

options.text: Access to health care
options.rationale: The last of the named variables. A plan the patient cannot reach does not work.

options.text: The severity of the diagnosis itself
options.rationale: The stem states both patients share the diagnosis, so it cannot explain the difference between them.

questions.stem: A patient with well-controlled multiple sclerosis tells the nurse she considers herself healthy because she teaches full time, travels, and is writing a book. Which model of health does her statement reflect?

options.text: Clinical model
options.rationale: The clinical model defines health as the absence of disease. By that definition she would not be healthy.

options.text: Adaptive model
options.rationale: The adaptive model defines health as flexible adjustment to change, which is not the emphasis in her statement.

options.text: Role performance model
options.rationale: Close, but role performance stops at fulfilling expected roles. She is describing something larger than her job.

options.text: Eudaimonistic model
options.rationale: This model defines health as the fullest realization of a person's potential, which is what she is describing.

questions.takeaway: The clinical model is the narrowest definition of health and the eudaimonistic is the broadest.

questions.stem: A patient is admitted with an exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. He asks when he will be back to normal, and the nurse explains how his condition differs from the pneumonia he had two years ago. Which statement about chronic illness is accurate?

options.rationale: Many chronic conditions have exacerbations and remissions rather than steady decline.

options.rationale: The defining feature of chronic illness is that it does not resolve and reshapes identity and daily life, which is what separates it from his pneumonia.
