questions.stem: A patient who smokes tells the nurse he knows smoking causes lung cancer but does not believe it will happen to him, and he has never tried to quit. His father died of a heart attack at 61. Which component of the Health Belief Model does his statement illustrate?

options.text: Perceived barriers
options.rationale: What stands in the way, such as cost, time, fear, or health literacy. He has not specified an obstacle.

options.text: Perceived susceptibility
options.rationale: Whether he believes the risk applies to him. He knows smoking causes cancer and does not believe it will happen to him, and that gap is perceived susceptibility.

options.text: Perceived benefits
options.rationale: Whether he believes quitting would help, which he has not commented on.

options.text: Perceived severity
options.rationale: How serious he believes the consequence would be. He is not disputing that lung cancer is serious.

questions.takeaway: Perceived is the word doing all the work. It is not whether a risk is real, it is whether the patient believes it applies to them. The Health Belief Model explains why people do or do not act on health advice through four beliefs: perceived susceptibility, perceived severity, perceived benefits, and perceived barriers.
questions.strategy: All four options begin with perceived. Decide which belief the patient's own words are about before comparing them.

strategies: Priority key word

steps.detail: He accepts the general risk and rejects that it applies to him.
He does not dispute the seriousness.
He has not commented on whether quitting would help.
He names no obstacle.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B: the gap between knowing a risk and believing it applies to you is perceived susceptibility.

questions.concept: The Health Belief Model explains why people do or do not act on health advice through four beliefs: perceived susceptibility, perceived severity, perceived benefits, and perceived barriers.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old with crushing chest pain and diaphoresis tells his wife it is indigestion and refuses to go to hospital. He has had no previous cardiac events. Which concept explains his response?

options.text: Dependent patient role
options.rationale: This stage begins after accepting treatment and the authority of the provider.

options.text: Symptom experience
options.rationale: The first stage, where the person perceives something is wrong and interprets it, often in a way that minimizes the threat.

options.text: Medical care contact
options.rationale: He has not contacted care. That is what he is avoiding.

questions.takeaway: Symptom experience includes interpretation, and misinterpretation is why patients delay. Illness behavior is how people monitor, interpret, and respond to their own symptoms, influenced by culture, family, education, and past experience.

questions.stem: A nurse on a busy medical unit has worked six extra shifts this month, eats at the workstation, has stopped going to her running club, and reports sleeping poorly. She says she will rest once the staffing improves. Which 2 responses are appropriate?
questions.takeaway: A nurse's own health practices affect her capacity to deliver care. Change starts with one realistic step rather than waiting for conditions to improve.
questions.strategy: Two wrong options defer and two escalate. The workable answer names the link to practice and finds one change she can actually make.

strategies: Patient-centered option

steps.detail: Rest once staffing improves, which she does not control.
Both defer or normalize an accumulating pattern.
One prescribes, one turns health into a performance issue.

elimination.verdict: A and B are selected.

options.text: Point out that her own health practices affect her capacity to care for others
options.rationale: Nurses model and depend on the same health behaviors they teach. Sustained neglect of sleep, nutrition, and activity reduces clinical performance before it feels like illness.

options.text: Help her identify one change she could realistically make this week
options.rationale: A small achievable change is what behavior change requires. Waiting for conditions to improve is not a plan.

options.text: Agree that rest can wait until the staffing situation resolves
options.rationale: Ties her health to a condition she does not control and may not change.

options.text: Advise her to reduce her hours immediately
options.rationale: Prescribes a solution she has not chosen and may not be able to afford.

options.text: Reassure her that fatigue is normal in nursing and passes
options.rationale: Normalizes a pattern that is accumulating rather than resolving.

options.text: Document a performance concern based on her reported fatigue
options.rationale: Converts a health conversation into a disciplinary one and ends the disclosure.

questions.stem: A nurse plans a health promotion program for a community with a high rate of childhood obesity. She is choosing between screening at schools, treating children already diagnosed, and working with schools on physical activity and food provision. Which activity is the best example of primary prevention?

options.text: Referral of children with elevated blood glucose to endocrinology
options.rationale: Referral after an abnormal result is part of secondary prevention.

options.text: A nutrition and physical activity curriculum for all students
options.rationale: Delivered to everyone before disease exists, aimed at preventing it. That is primary prevention.

options.text: BMI screening at the school health office
options.rationale: Screening detects a problem that may already exist, which is secondary prevention.

options.text: A weight management clinic for children already diagnosed
options.rationale: Treating an existing condition to limit its effects is tertiary.

Referral after an abnormal result is part of secondary prevention.

Treating an existing condition to limit its effects is tertiary.

questions.stem: A nurse counsels a 58-year-old who says he wants to stop smoking after 35 years. He describes what he believes is standing in his way and what he thinks would need to change. Which patient statement indicates a need for further teaching?

Treat each option as true or false

questions.stem: A 46-year-old is five days after emergency surgery that left him with a colostomy. He turns his head away during every pouch change and has not looked at the stoma. The stoma is pink and the skin around it is intact. Which nursing response is appropriate?

options.text: Acknowledge that illness changes how people see themselves and let him set the pace
options.rationale: Illness affects self-concept and body image, and a patient who cannot yet look at a stoma is having a recognized response rather than refusing care.

options.rationale: She gathered assessment data the first nurse did not, and gave him a chance to raise something. The numbers are the same; the assessment is not.

options.text: Nothing clinically, since the measurements are the same
options.rationale: Treats vital signs as the only data available during an encounter.

options.text: More accurate readings than the first nurse obtained
options.rationale: The readings are stated as identical. Accuracy is not the difference.

questions.takeaway: A routine task is also an assessment opportunity. What you gather alongside the numbers is part of the data.
questions.strategy: The stem rules out accuracy by stating the readings match. Ask what else changed hands.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The readings are identical.
Accuracy is explicitly not the difference.
Both claim nothing was gained.

questions.stem: A nurse and a colleague discuss how they maintain the therapeutic relationship with patients and families. Which statement by the colleague indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "Sitting down with a patient who is crying is a real nursing intervention."
options.rationale: Accurate. Presence is being physically and emotionally available.

options.text: "Advocating for a family member to stay overnight can be appropriate."
options.rationale: Accurate. Advocacy explores what the request means rather than applying the rule reflexively.

options.text: "If a patient asks for my personal number after discharge, refusing would seem cold."
options.rationale: Declining warmly and explaining the professional boundary is the appropriate response. Personal contact creates an obligation inside a professional relationship.

options.text: "Sharing my own family's illness at length moves the focus onto me."
options.rationale: Accurate. Self-disclosure at length shifts the focus from the patient.

questions.takeaway: Caring is warm and bounded. Declining warmly and explaining why maintains both.
questions.strategy: The wrong statement treats a boundary as unkindness. The test is whose needs the action serves.

strategies: Negative polarity
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Find the mistaken belief.
Personal contact serves the relationship, not the care.
Presence, advocacy, and self-disclosure are correctly described.

elimination.verdict: A is the statement needing correction: declining warmly is not coldness.

questions.stem: A nurse sits with a patient who has just been told her treatment has not worked. The patient falls silent, then says she does not know what to tell her children. Which nurse responses open the conversation rather than closing it? Select all that apply.

options.text: Remain silent and stay present while she gathers herself
options.rationale: Silence gives her room to continue, and presence is being physically and emotionally available.

options.text: Tell me what worries you most about that conversation
options.rationale: An open invitation that follows her rather than directing her.

options.text: It sounds as though telling them feels harder than the news itself
options.rationale: Names the feeling, which is what therapeutic communication does.

options.text: Children are more resilient than we give them credit for
options.rationale: False reassurance, and it closes the subject she has just opened.

options.text: You should tell them as soon as possible
options.rationale: Giving advice, which replaces her judgment with the nurse's.

questions.takeaway: Therapeutic communication opens the conversation rather than closing it, and it names feelings. Presence is being physically and emotionally available to a patient, and sitting down is what signals you are not about to leave.
questions.strategy: Reassurance and advice both feel helpful and both end the exchange. That is why they are the standard wrong answers.

strategies: Patient-centered option

steps.detail: A specific fear about her children.
It dismisses the fear.
It replaces her judgment.

elimination.verdict: A, B, and C are selected.

questions.concept: Presence is being physically and emotionally available to a patient, and sitting down is what signals you are not about to leave. Therapeutic communication opens the conversation rather than closing it, and it names feelings. False reassurance and advice are the two standard blocks.

questions.stem: A patient in the last hours of life is unresponsive and breathing irregularly. His wife has been sitting silently at the bedside and asks the nurse whether he can still hear her. What is the nurse's best response?

options.text: "You can talk to him if it makes you feel better."
options.rationale: Dismissive, implying it benefits only her rather than reaching him.

options.text: "Hearing is often preserved, so talking to him may still reach him."
options.rationale: We speak to unresponsive patients as though they can hear, and saying so supports the family as well.

options.text: "He cannot hear you at this stage."
options.rationale: Inaccurate, and it removes a source of comfort and connection at the point she needs it most.

options.text: "Let me ask the provider about that for you."
options.rationale: Deflects a question the nurse can answer herself.

questions.takeaway: Speak to an unresponsive patient as though he can hear, and tell the family they can too.
questions.strategy: Answers that reduce a family's connection at end of life are rarely correct.

strategies: Favor qualifiers
Priority key word

steps.detail: Whether he can still hear her.
Inaccurate and it closes the connection.
Deflects a question the nurse can answer.
Frames it as her comfort rather than reaching him.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B: hearing is often preserved, so encourage her to talk to him.

questions.stem: A nursing student discusses caring with her instructor after a shift in which she felt she had been kind but rushed. She describes what she believes caring in nursing involves. Which student statement indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "Caring can be developed rather than being something you either have or do not."
options.rationale: Accurate, which is why Caritas Coaching exists.

options.text: "Caring is about warmth, so it is separate from whether I am technically competent."
options.rationale: Competence sits inside the definition of caring: intentional concern for another's wellbeing through compassion, respect, presence, empathy, and competence. A kind nurse who is not safe is not delivering caring as it is professionally defined.

options.text: "Two nurses can take the same accurate vital signs and deliver different care."
options.rationale: Accurate, and it is the central claim.

options.text: "Patients identify attentiveness and listening as the behaviors most indicative of caring."
options.rationale: Accurate. That is what patient feedback consistently reports.

questions.takeaway: Caring is compassion, respect, presence, empathy, and competence. Competence is part of the definition.
questions.strategy: The element students leave out is competence. Any statement separating caring from clinical skill is the one to correct.

strategies: Negative polarity
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Competence is one of them.
One statement places competence outside caring.
All three are accurate.

elimination.verdict: A is the statement needing correction: competence is part of caring, not separate from it.

questions.stem: A patient's A1C is 9.1% and he has been taking metformin twice daily for six months. The nurse wants to use Caritas Coaching in the conversation. Which response reflects that approach?

options.text: "Let me go over why metformin matters for your blood sugar."
options.rationale: Instruction. It delivers the nurse's knowledge rather than drawing out his experience, and he has been taking it for six months already.

options.text: "I will write out a schedule so you do not forget the evening dose."
options.rationale: Solves the problem for him with a solution she chose, before knowing whether forgetting is the issue.

options.text: "What gets in the way of taking it at the second time of day?"
options.rationale: Caritas Coaching partners with the patient to surface his own barriers and solutions, rather than supplying the nurse's. The question assumes he has reasons worth hearing.

options.text: "Your A1C is 9.1%, which tells us the diabetes is not controlled."
options.rationale: Reports a result. Accurate, and it gives him information rather than inviting him into the problem.

questions.takeaway: Caritas Coaching partners rather than instructs. The nurse draws out the patient's own barriers and strengths instead of supplying answers.
questions.strategy: Three options are competent nursing: teaching, problem-solving, and reporting a result. Only one hands the problem back to the patient to define.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Coaching hands that to the patient.
It supplies the nurse's knowledge.
It chooses a solution before the barrier is known.

elimination.verdict: That leaves C: the patient defines the barrier.

questions.concept: The Caritas Processes are Watson's guiding principles for relationship-centered care. They describe how you are with a patient rather than what you do to them. Caritas Coaching partners with patients instead of instructing them, helping them find their own strengths and solutions. Not did you take your medicine, but what challenges are you having with it.

questions.stem: A 51-year-old has just been told her cancer has metastasized. When the nurse enters, she is sitting with the untouched lunch tray, crying quietly. She has declined her analgesia. Which action best demonstrates presence?

options.text: Sit with her quietly and remain available
options.rationale: Presence is being with rather than doing for. Silence gives her time and signals that she is not alone.

options.text: Leave the room to give her privacy and return in an hour
options.rationale: Leaving reads as abandonment at the moment connection matters most.

options.text: Explain the treatment options her provider mentioned
options.rationale: Information she cannot absorb right now. High distress blocks the ability to take in explanations.

options.text: Tell her that many patients do well with further treatment
options.rationale: False reassurance, which shuts down expression of feeling.

questions.takeaway: Presence is an intervention. Sitting quietly is doing something, not doing nothing. Presence is being physically and emotionally available to a patient, and sitting down is what signals you are not about to leave.
questions.strategy: When a patient is overwhelmed, the correct answer is usually the one that stays and says least.

strategies: Negative polarity
Priority key word

steps.detail: Key word: best. More than one option may be true, so you are ranking them.
Leaving reads as abandonment at the moment connection matters most.
Information she cannot absorb right now.
False reassurance, which shuts down expression of feeling.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A. Presence is being with rather than doing for.

questions.concept: Presence is being physically and emotionally available to a patient, and sitting down is what signals you are not about to leave.

questions.stem: A nurse and a colleague discuss why Caritas Coaching often works when repeated teaching has not. Which statement explains the difference?

options.text: The patient identifies the barrier, so the solution fits him
options.rationale: Teaching assumes the problem is missing knowledge. Coaching assumes the patient knows something the nurse does not, and builds the plan from there.

options.text: It transfers responsibility for the outcome to the patient
options.rationale: Coaching shares the work rather than handing it over. The nurse stays engaged in the plan.

options.text: It delivers the same information in simpler language
options.rationale: Plain language helps and it is still the nurse supplying the content. Coaching changes who defines the problem.

options.text: It repeats the teaching until the patient retains it
options.rationale: Repetition addresses memory. If the barrier is cost, transport, or side effects, repeating will not touch it.

questions.takeaway: Teaching supplies knowledge. Coaching assumes the patient holds information the nurse needs and builds the plan from it.
questions.strategy: Ask who defines the problem. If the nurse still does, it is teaching however it is delivered.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Coaching hands that to the patient.
It supplies the nurse's knowledge.
It chooses a solution before the barrier is known.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A: the patient defines the barrier.

questions.stem: A nursing student assumes caring means being kind to patients. Her instructor explains that the professional definition includes an element students often leave out. Which response is accurate?

options.text: Meeting patients' physical needs efficiently and without unnecessary delay
options.rationale: Task completion without the relational content is what caring is contrasted against.

options.text: A personality trait some nurses have and others do not
options.rationale: caring is treated as professional practice that can be developed.

options.text: Intentional concern for another's wellbeing through compassion, respect, presence, empathy, and competence
options.rationale: Competence sits inside the definition, which is why caring is not separable from clinical skill.

options.text: A warm and friendly manner with patients and their families throughout
options.rationale: Manner is part of it and the definition is broader and includes competence.

questions.takeaway: Caring is deliberately looking after someone's wellbeing, and competence is part of the definition. Presence is being physically and emotionally available to a patient, and sitting down is what signals you are not about to leave.
questions.strategy: The element students drop is competence. A kind nurse who is not safe is not delivering caring as it is professionally defined. One element of the definition is easy to leave out. Look for the option that includes it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Five elements including competence.
Manner alone is too narrow.
A trait, and task completion.

elimination.verdict: That leaves C: competence sits inside the definition, which is why caring is not separable from clinical skill.

questions.stem: Highlight the moments in this shift where the nurse can apply caring principles.
questions.takeaway: Caring should be present during every skill, and most of it uses time you were already spending.

questions.nursesNote: 0700: Patient is 62, admitted overnight after being told her cancer has metastasized. Tearful and quiet. During the shift the nurse will take her vital signs, administer her medications, assist her to bathe following an episode of incontinence, and change a wound dressing. The nurse is also rostered to restock the supply cupboard and complete next month's staffing roster. The patient's daughter asks to stay overnight at the bedside, which the unit does not usually allow.

segments.text: Taking her vital signs on admission
segments.rationale: Introduce yourself and explain what you are doing. Every nursing skill is also a caring interaction.

segments.text: Administering her medications
segments.rationale: Teach while administering and answer questions, using time already committed.

segments.text: Assisting her to bathe after an episode of incontinence
segments.rationale: Protect privacy and promote dignity, which is where the caring content of this task sits.

segments.text: Changing her wound dressing
segments.rationale: Control pain first and explain each step, which reduces the fear during the procedure.

segments.text: Restocking the supply cupboard
segments.rationale: Necessary work with no patient interaction.

segments.text: Completing the unit's staffing roster
segments.rationale: Administrative work unrelated to patient care.

questions.stem: The patient begins crying and does not respond to questions. The nurse has three other patients and a medication round due. Which 2 actions best demonstrate presence?
questions.takeaway: Presence is being physically and emotionally available. Sitting down changes how long she believes you will stay. Presence is being physically and emotionally available to a patient, and sitting down is what signals you are not about to leave.
questions.strategy: Exactly two are requested. Three wrong options are kind actions that all involve leaving or redirecting. Several unselected options are kind and involve leaving.

strategies: Patient-centered option

steps.detail: She is crying and not answering.
It closes the conversation.
Deferring and handing on both remove you.

elimination.verdict: A and B are selected.

options.text: Sit down with her and remain available without filling the silence
options.rationale: Being physically and emotionally available. Sitting signals you are not about to leave.

options.text: Acknowledge what she has been told and let her lead what comes next
options.rationale: Follows her rather than directing her, and it opens the conversation rather than closing it.

options.text: Reassure her that treatments have improved a great deal
options.rationale: False reassurance, and it closes a conversation she has just opened.

options.text: Explain that you will return after the medication round
options.rationale: Defers the moment she is in now, and the moment will have passed.

options.text: Offer to call the chaplain and step out
options.rationale: Chaplaincy may help later, and offering it now hands her on rather than staying.

options.text: Ask a series of questions to determine what is upsetting her
options.rationale: She has just been told her cancer has spread. Questions direct the exchange rather than following her.

questions.stem: For each nursing action, determine whether it MAINTAINS the therapeutic relationship or CROSSES a boundary.
questions.takeaway: Caring is warm and bounded. Declining warmly and explaining why maintains both.
questions.strategy: Two crossings here come from genuine warmth. The test is whose needs the action serves.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Three actions serve the patient.
At length moves the focus.
Personal contact and gifts both create them.

rows.text: Advocating for the daughter to stay overnight and explaining the request to the team

rows.text: Giving the patient her personal phone number to stay in touch after discharge

questions.strategy: Two wrong routes here: follow the rule without thinking, or ignore it entirely. Advocacy is neither.

The rule has not been examined against this situation.
Advocacy happens with the team, not around it.

elimination.verdict: Blank 1 is A and blank 2 is A.

questions.sentence: When the daughter asks to stay overnight, the nurse should [[1]], because [[2]].

options.text: explore what staying would mean for the family and advocate with the team
options.rationale: Advocacy examines the request rather than applying the rule reflexively, and the patient is stable.

options.text: apply the unit policy and decline the request
options.rationale: Applies a rule without considering whether it serves this patient and family.

options.text: allow her to stay without informing anyone
options.rationale: Bypasses the team rather than advocating within it.

options.text: caring includes advocating for what the patient and family need

questions.stem: During the shift the nurse performs vital signs, a medication round, a bed bath after incontinence, and a dressing change. Which 2 actions apply caring principles without requiring additional time?
questions.takeaway: Every nursing skill is also a caring interaction, and most of it uses time you were already spending.

Returning later and handing over.
Neither is caring.

options.rationale: Uses time already committed to the task, and it is specified directly.

options.text: Return after the shift to sit with her for an hour

options.rationale: Hands the relationship to someone else.

options.text: Explain everything at the end of the shift once the tasks are done

questions.takeaway: Not everything that stays the same has failed. Tearfulness after this news is expected rather than unresolved.
questions.strategy: The unchanged row is the one to leave alone. Treating an expected emotional response as an unmet outcome is its own error. One unchanged finding is an expected response rather than an unmet outcome.

chapters.title: Caring for Patients with Chronic Illness

questions.stem: Before discharge, a 68-year-old newly diagnosed with heart failure talks through his plans with the nurse. He describes what he expects over the coming months and how he plans to manage at home. Which patient statement indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "Most of managing this happens at home, in between my clinic appointments."
options.rationale: Accurate, which is why self-management support matters.

options.text: "Giving up my allotment has affected me as much as the symptoms themselves have."
options.rationale: Accurate. Chronic illness affects roles and self-perception, not only the body.

options.text: "Once my swelling and breathlessness settle, I will be back to how I was before."
options.rationale: Chronic illness is managed rather than cured. Symptoms can improve while the condition and its effects on roles and daily life continue.

options.text: "I will weigh myself every morning and report any sudden gain to the clinic."
options.rationale: Accurate, and weight gain is an early marker of fluid retention.

questions.takeaway: Disease is the clinical process. Illness is how the person lives it, and chronic illness is managed rather than cured.
questions.strategy: The wrong statement expects resolution. Chronic means the condition persists even when the symptoms do not.

strategies: Negative polarity
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Find the mistaken expectation.
Back to how I was assumes resolution.
Monitoring, self-management, and role loss are all accurate.

elimination.verdict: A is the statement needing correction: chronic illness is managed, not resolved.

questions.stem: A practice nurse is planning the year's work for patients with long-term conditions and wants to focus on preventing complications rather than responding to them. She reviews which activities fall within the nursing role. Which nursing actions support health promotion and prevention for patients with chronic illness? Select all that apply.

options.text: Screening for diseases
options.rationale: Screening finds disease before symptoms appear, which is when intervention changes the trajectory rather than managing damage.

options.text: Treating each acute episode as it presents
options.rationale: Episodic treatment is the approach chronic care redesign moves away from.

options.text: Promoting adherence
options.rationale: Adherence determines whether a plan has any effect, and promoting it means finding the barrier rather than repeating the instruction.

options.text: Discouraging patients from asking questions about their condition
options.rationale: Undermines self-management, which depends on the patient understanding their condition.

options.text: Limiting patient questions to scheduled appointments
options.rationale: Restricting questions undermines the self-management being built.

options.text: Encouraging appropriate screening and prevention efforts
options.rationale: Encouraging screening extends the nurse's role beyond the individual visit into prevention at a population level.

questions.takeaway: Screening, education, adherence, and self-management education. Self-management support builds the patient's capability, because the patient manages the condition between visits where no nurse is present.
questions.strategy: A distractor that reduces the patient's understanding is always wrong where self-management is the goal.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The question asks which actions support prevention.
Reduces the understanding self-management requires.

elimination.verdict: A, C and F are selected.

questions.concept: Self-management support builds the patient's capability, because the patient manages the condition between visits where no nurse is present. CUS escalates a concern with graded language: I am Concerned, I am Uncomfortable, this is a Safety issue. SBAR reports; CUS escalates when reporting has failed.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old with rheumatoid arthritis has stopped attending her book group, declines invitations, and tells the nurse there is no point planning anything. She rates her pain 4 of 10 on stable medication. Which psychosocial effects should the nurse assess for?

options.text: Depression, social isolation, and loneliness
options.rationale: The specified psychosocial effects of chronic illness, and all three are consistent with the withdrawal described.

options.text: Anxiety, mania, and psychosis
options.rationale: Mania and psychosis are not psychosocial effects of chronic illness.

options.text: Grief, denial, and bargaining
options.rationale: Stages of adjustment rather than the psychosocial effects.

options.text: Delirium, dementia, and depression
options.rationale: Delirium and dementia are cognitive conditions rather than psychosocial effects of chronic illness.

questions.takeaway: Depression, social isolation, and loneliness, with age-specific developmental needs.
questions.strategy: Two distractors are real frameworks from a different area. Match the set to the framework in question.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The question asks for the psychosocial needs.
Delirium and dementia are cognitive conditions rather than psychosocial effects of chronic illness.
Mania and psychosis are not psychosocial effects of chronic illness.
Stages of adjustment rather than the psychosocial effects.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A: the psychosocial effects of chronic illness, and all three are consistent with the withdrawal described.

questions.scenario: A 77-year-old with heart failure, arthritis, and type 2 diabetes attends clinic monthly. The family attributes recent changes to getting older.
questions.stem: The nurse reviews three months of records showing weight, reported fatigue, ankle swelling, and walking distance. The family attributes the changes to getting older. Which conclusion does the nurse draw?

options.text: The changes are consistent with normal aging in a patient of this age
options.rationale: Age-related changes can mask signs of chronic illness, which is exactly why this explanation is rejected.

options.text: The pattern suggests worsening heart failure and requires assessment and provider notification
options.rationale: Rising weight, increasing fatigue, new ankle swelling, and falling exercise tolerance together indicate fluid retention.

options.text: The weight gain reflects improved nutritional intake
options.rationale: Weight gain with edema and reduced tolerance is fluid, not nutrition.

options.text: The reduced walking distance is explained by arthritis alone
options.rationale: Arthritis does not explain the weight gain or the edema. Attributing everything to one condition is the multimorbidity trap.

questions.takeaway: Overlapping conditions mask each other. Read the measures together rather than assigning each to a diagnosis. Multimorbidity is managing two or more concurrent chronic conditions, and it is the normal case in older adults rather than the exception.
questions.strategy: In multimorbidity, the temptation is to explain each finding with a different existing condition. Ask instead what single process explains all of them.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Weight, fatigue, edema, and tolerance all move together across three months.
Age does not explain a three-month progressive change.
Weight with edema is fluid.
Arthritis explains one row, not four.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B. Fluid retention explains every row at once.

questions.concept: Multimorbidity is managing two or more concurrent chronic conditions, and it is the normal case in older adults rather than the exception.

questions.stem: A nurse manager reviewing her medical unit notes that nearly every older patient is treated for more than one long-term condition at once. Which implication follows for how care is organized?

options.text: The most recently diagnosed condition should take priority over the others
options.rationale: Recency is not clinical priority.

options.text: Chronic conditions should be addressed only after acute problems resolve
options.rationale: They interact, and deferring them worsens the acute picture.

options.text: Each condition should be managed by a separate specialist team independently
options.rationale: Produces conflicting plans and duplicated appointments.

options.text: Care is planned around the person rather than a single disease pathway
options.rationale: Multimorbidity is the normal case in older adults, and single-disease pathways conflict when several apply at once.

questions.takeaway: Multimorbidity is the normal case in older adults, which is why care is organized around the person. Multimorbidity is managing two or more concurrent chronic conditions, and it is the normal case in older adults rather than the exception.
questions.strategy: Options treating conditions as separable are the pattern here. They interact, which is the whole point.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Most patients have several conditions at once.
Separate teams produce conflicting plans.
Recency and sequencing are not priority.

elimination.verdict: That leaves D: multimorbidity is the normal case in older adults, and single-disease pathways conflict when several apply at once.

questions.concept: Multimorbidity is managing two or more concurrent chronic conditions, and it is the normal case in older adults rather than the exception.

questions.scenario: A 59-year-old with type 2 diabetes and hypertension has missed two clinic appointments, reports taking medications only when he remembers, smokes 15 cigarettes daily, and says he does not understand what his blood pressure readings mean. He lives alone and works two jobs.
questions.stem: Complete the diagram by selecting from the choices below.

options.text: Assess adherence, symptom management, tobacco use, and lifestyle
options.rationale: The specified assessment priorities for patients with chronic illness.

options.text: Provide self-management education, including what his readings mean and how to respond
options.rationale: Self-management education builds the capability he uses between visits, which is where chronic illness is lived.

options.text: Arrange daily home nursing visits indefinitely
options.rationale: Creates dependence rather than capability, and does not address understanding.

options.text: Tell him non-adherence will lead to complications and document the warning
options.rationale: Warning is not education, and blame does not build self-management.

options.text: Ask his family to take over his medications
options.rationale: He lives alone, and removing him from his own care is not indicated.

options.text: A patient with chronic disease requiring self-management support and health promotion
options.rationale: Combines the adherence, tobacco, and health literacy findings with the model's self-management focus.

options.text: A patient in acute hypertensive crisis
options.rationale: Nothing in the scenario describes acute decompensation.

options.text: A patient requiring immediate hospitalization
options.rationale: No acute indication is present.

options.text: A patient who has declined all treatment
options.rationale: He is taking medications inconsistently, which is not refusal.

options.text: Blood pressure and glycemic control over time
options.rationale: The measures that show whether self-management is improving.

options.text: Understanding, checked through teach-back
options.rationale: He states he does not understand his readings, so confirmed understanding is the parameter that matters.

options.text: Serum amylase
options.rationale: Not relevant to these conditions.

options.text: Daily temperature
options.rationale: Not a monitoring priority here.

options.text: Visual acuity weekly
options.rationale: Eye examinations are important in diabetes but not as a weekly monitoring parameter.

questions.takeaway: Chronic illness care builds capability. Assess adherence and lifestyle, then teach for self-management. Self-management support builds the patient's capability, because the patient manages the condition between visits where no nurse is present. It confirms understanding rather than confirming that teaching was delivered.
questions.strategy: Two action options treat the patient as the problem rather than the partner. Warning and taking over both fail for the same reason.

strategies: Patient-centered option

steps.detail: Inconsistent adherence plus low health literacy in chronic disease.
Creates dependence instead of capability.
Neither builds self-management.

elimination.verdict: Actions A and B, condition A, parameters A and B.

questions.concept: Self-management support builds the patient's capability, because the patient manages the condition between visits where no nurse is present. Teach-back asks the patient to explain the plan in their own words. It confirms understanding rather than confirming that teaching was delivered.

questions.stem: A 59-year-old with type 2 diabetes tells the nurse his glucose readings range from 180 to 320 mg/dL and he does not know what to do about any of them, so he has stopped checking. He takes metformin when he remembers. Which nursing action best supports self-management?

options.text: Set a fixed schedule of checks and record them for review at his next visit
options.rationale: Reinstates the monitoring without restoring its purpose, which is why he stopped.

options.text: Teach him to interpret his own readings and what to do at each range
options.rationale: He stopped checking because the numbers meant nothing to him. Self-management support gives data a decision attached to it.

options.text: Arrange for a family member to prompt his metformin each day
options.rationale: Addresses the missed doses and moves responsibility away from him.

options.text: Simplify the regimen to once-daily dosing with the provider
options.rationale: May help adherence and does nothing about readings he cannot act on.

questions.takeaway: Self-management support means the patient can interpret his own data and act on it, not just collect it.
questions.strategy: Three options are reasonable diabetes interventions. Ask which one addresses the reason he stopped.

strategies: Patient-centered option

steps.detail: He does not know what to do with the numbers.
More data, same problem.
One shifts responsibility, one changes dosing.

elimination.verdict: That leaves teaching him to interpret and respond.

questions.concept: Self-management support builds the patient's capability, because the patient manages the condition between visits where no nurse is present.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old with multiple sclerosis tells the nurse she has stopped attending the book club she has belonged to for years because she is embarrassed by her tremor, and that she no longer feels like the person her friends knew. Her tremor is unchanged on her current treatment. Which concept does this best illustrate?

options.text: Comorbidity
options.rationale: Refers to an additional condition alongside a primary one.

options.text: Chronic disease
options.rationale: Chronic disease is the medical focus: the clinical process in the body, diagnosed and lasting a year or longer.

options.text: Chronic illness
options.rationale: Chronic illness is the personal focus, meaning the emotional and social experience. Withdrawing from a social group because of how the condition feels is illness, not disease.

options.text: Multimorbidity
options.rationale: Multimorbidity is managing two or more concurrent chronic conditions.

questions.takeaway: Disease is the clinical process. Illness is how the person lives it.
questions.strategy: When a stem describes what a condition does to someone's life rather than to their body, the answer is illness.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The finding is social withdrawal driven by embarrassment.
Disease is the biological process.
Only one condition is described.
No second condition is mentioned.

elimination.verdict: That leaves C. The tremor is disease; the empty chair at the book club is illness.

questions.concept: CUS escalates a concern with graded language: I am Concerned, I am Uncomfortable, this is a Safety issue. SBAR reports; CUS escalates when reporting has failed.

questions.stem: A community nurse assesses a family caregiver during a home visit. She is 68, has cared for her husband with dementia for two years, lives with him, and manages his personal care alone. Which factors place a family caregiver at risk for poor health? Select all that apply.

options.text: Providing care for more than one year
options.rationale: Caregiving past a year moves the demand from a temporary effort to a sustained one, and the health effects accumulate with duration.

options.text: Having respite care available weekly
options.rationale: Respite reduces caregiver strain rather than raising risk.

options.text: Caring for someone with Alzheimer disease or dementia
options.rationale: Dementia care carries constant supervision and behavioral demands, which is why it is singled out from other caregiving.

options.text: Sharing the caregiving role with three siblings
options.rationale: Shared caregiving reduces the burden carried by any one person.

options.text: Living within walking distance of a clinic
options.rationale: Proximity to services eases caregiving rather than raising risk.

options.text: Providing care for a family member with significant needs
options.rationale: Significant needs mean the physical and time demands are high, which limits the caregiver's own sleep, activity, and health care.

questions.takeaway: Five caregiver risk factors, and they stack. Consider the caregiver in the care plan.
questions.strategy: One option in this set describes support rather than burden. That is the exclusion.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The question asks which factors create risk.
Respite relieves burden rather than adding to it.

elimination.verdict: A, C and F are selected.

questions.stem: A community health nurse notices that several patients with asthma live in the same poorly maintained housing complex and that local air quality data show elevated pollutant levels. She considers what falls within her professional role beyond treating each patient. Which action reflects the nurse's role in relation to public policy and chronic disease?

options.text: Recognizing environmental factors that influence health and using reputable information sources
options.rationale: Occurs alongside awareness of policies affecting chronic disease prevention, providing health education, and encouraging screening and prevention.

options.text: Limiting practice to individual patient care only, since policy sits outside nursing
options.rationale: Excludes prevention and population-level awareness.

options.text: Avoiding any discussion of health policy with patients under all circumstances at all
options.rationale: Health education about prevention and screening is explicitly part of the role.

options.text: Endorsing specific political candidates to patients who ask about health policy
options.rationale: Outside the professional role and not what policy awareness means.

questions.takeaway: Know the policies, recognize environmental influences, use reputable sources, teach, and encourage screening.
questions.strategy: Policy items reward the option describing professional awareness and education rather than advocacy for a position.

strategies: Eliminate absolutes

steps.detail: The question asks about the nurse's role.
All circumstances is absolute and contradicts health education.
Outside the professional role.
Only excludes prevention work.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A: occurs alongside awareness of policies affecting chronic disease prevention, providing health education, and encouraging screening and prevention.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old with COPD is discharged after his third admission this year. His saturation is 90% on room air, he will use home oxygen at 2 L, and he cannot coordinate his inhaler. Which nursing action best reflects chronic care?

options.text: Coordinate with the patient, family, caregivers, and the health care team
options.rationale: Care often includes patients, families, caregivers, and a team spanning physical, occupational, and speech therapy and specialty physicians.

options.text: Schedule a follow-up appointment and end nursing involvement at the point of discharge
options.rationale: Ends coordination at the moment self-management begins.

options.text: Refer the patient to a single specialist for ongoing management of everything
options.rationale: Narrows care to one discipline.

options.text: Provide written discharge instructions to the patient before he leaves the unit
options.rationale: Necessary but insufficient. Chronic illness care extends past the individual and past a single handout.

questions.takeaway: Chronic illness care is a team effort that includes the family and caregivers.
questions.strategy: Key word best. All four options are things someone might do; the answer is the one that matches the model of care.

strategies: Priority key word

steps.detail: Discharge planning for a chronic condition.
A handout alone does not coordinate care.
Narrows to one discipline.
Withdraws coordination too early.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A: care often includes patients, families, caregivers, and a team spanning physical, occupational, and speech therapy and specialty physicians.

questions.stem: A nurse visits a 67-year-old who has cared for her husband with dementia at home for two years. She describes how she is managing and what she plans to do about her own health. Which caregiver statement indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "Caring for someone with dementia is harder than most people realize."
options.rationale: Accurate. Dementia care carries constant supervision and behavioral demands.

options.text: "As long as I am coping, my own appointments can wait."
options.rationale: Caregiving past a year, being 65 or older, dementia care, living with the care recipient, and high needs are risk factors for the caregiver's own health. Deferring her own care is how that risk becomes illness.

options.text: "Living with him means there is no point in the day when I am able to stop."
options.rationale: Accurate, and it is a risk factor.

options.text: "I should ask about respite before I reach the point of not coping."
options.rationale: Accurate. Respite arranged early is more useful than respite arranged in crisis.

questions.takeaway: Caregiver risk factors compound. Deferring your own health care is how sustained caregiving becomes illness.
questions.strategy: The wrong statement is the one every caregiver says. Coping is not the same as being well.

strategies: Negative polarity
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Find the mistaken belief.
Duration, age, dementia, living together, high needs.
Coping now does not protect health later.

elimination.verdict: A is the statement needing correction: her own care does not wait for things to settle.

questions.stem: A nurse admits a 61-year-old with a blood pressure of 176/98 who smokes 20 cigarettes daily, has missed four clinic appointments, and whose A1C is 9.4%. Which assessment is most important for planning his care?

options.text: Surgical history and anesthesia tolerance
options.rationale: Perioperative concerns rather than chronic illness assessment.

options.text: Immunization status and travel history, since both affect long-term risk
options.rationale: Relevant elsewhere, not the priorities.

options.text: Range of motion, reflexes, and gait only, since function drives chronic outcomes
options.rationale: A physical subset that omits the behavioral and lifestyle areas specified.

options.text: Adherence, symptom management, tobacco use, alcohol consumption, and lifestyle
options.rationale: The specified assessment priorities for patients with chronic illness.

questions.takeaway: Adherence, symptoms, tobacco, alcohol, and lifestyle.
questions.strategy: The list mixes clinical and behavioral areas. An option containing only physical findings is too narrow.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The question asks for the assessment priorities.
Only narrows to physical findings.
Not the correct set.
Perioperative rather than chronic.

elimination.verdict: That leaves D: the assessment priorities for patients with chronic illness.

questions.stem: A clinic wants patients with long-term conditions to arrive at appointments already knowing their numbers and what changed since last time. Which component of the Chronic Care Model does this describe?

options.text: Acute care triage
options.rationale: Sorts by urgency of presentation rather than organizing long-term care.

options.text: Infection surveillance
options.rationale: Belongs to infection control.

options.text: Clinical information systems
options.rationale: Shared, accessible data is what lets both the patient and the team see the trend rather than a single visit.

options.text: Emergency preparedness
options.rationale: An organizational function rather than a component of the model.

questions.takeaway: Six components: community, health system, self-management support, delivery system design, decision support, clinical information systems.
questions.strategy: Match the activity to the component that enables it. Data that follows the patient between visits is the information system.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Knowing the numbers and the change over time.
Triage and surveillance belong elsewhere.
An organizational function.

elimination.verdict: That leaves C: clinical information systems.

questions.concept: The Chronic Care Model organizes long-term condition care through community resources, the health system, self-management support, delivery system design, decision support, and clinical information systems. Self-management support builds the patient's capability, because the patient manages the condition between visits where no nurse is present.

questions.stem: Two patients were diagnosed with rheumatoid arthritis in the same year. One works full time with pain rated 2 of 10 on stable medication. The other has left work and rates her pain 7 of 10. Which statement explains this difference?

options.text: The same condition produces different limitation and different meaning in different people
options.rationale: Chronic illness is the lived response, which varies with work, support, coping, and what the person values, even at identical disease severity.

options.text: The second patient's disease has progressed further than the first
options.rationale: Possible and unstated. Assuming severity explains the gap is exactly what individualized assessment is meant to test.

options.text: The second patient has a lower pain threshold than the first
options.rationale: Reframes a difference in function as a personal deficiency.

options.text: The first patient has adapted more successfully to her diagnosis
options.rationale: Describes the outcome rather than explaining it, and implies the second has failed at something.

questions.takeaway: Disease is the process; illness is the response. The same disease produces different lives.
questions.strategy: Three distractors locate the difference in the patient. Ask whether the stem gives any evidence for that.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Same diagnosis, same year, different function.
Not stated anywhere.
Both explain the gap as a personal shortfall.

elimination.verdict: That leaves variation in effect and meaning between individuals.

questions.scenario: A 62-year-old with COPD has been admitted three times this year. He uses home oxygen, has stopped attending his choir, and tells the nurse he no longer plans anything in case he cannot manage it on the day.
questions.stem: Which nursing conclusions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: The withdrawal from choir is a psychosocial effect requiring assessment
options.rationale: Social isolation and loneliness are psychosocial effects of chronic illness, not an incidental detail.

options.text: Repeated admissions suggest the between-visit management needs review
options.rationale: Most chronic illness management happens at home. Three admissions in a year points to what is failing there.

options.text: He should be screened for depression
options.rationale: Depression is a recognized effect of chronic illness and his statement suggests loss of anticipated future.

options.text: The withdrawal is an expected response requiring no action
options.rationale: Common is not the same as acceptable. It is assessed.

options.text: His oxygen should be increased to allow more activity
options.rationale: A prescribing decision, and nothing indicates his current flow is inadequate.

options.text: He is not adhering to his treatment plan
options.rationale: Nothing in the situation supports that conclusion, and it assigns blame instead of assessing.

questions.takeaway: Chronic illness reaches beyond the disease. Withdrawal and loss of future planning are findings that need assessing.
questions.strategy: Two distractors normalize the withdrawal or blame him. Assess before concluding either.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Choir, planning, and three admissions.
Common does not mean it needs no action.
One prescribes, one blames.

elimination.verdict: A, B, and C are selected.

questions.stem: A 79-year-old with heart failure and arthritis attends clinic reporting fatigue that has worsened over six weeks. Her weight is up 3 kg since her last visit and she has stopped walking to the corner shop. Her daughter says this is just getting older. Which nursing response is most appropriate?

options.text: Weigh her daily and review the pattern at her next scheduled visit
options.rationale: A reasonable heart failure intervention applied at the wrong moment. The change is already present.

options.text: Reinforce the importance of daily weights and sodium restriction
options.rationale: Correct teaching that treats the situation as an adherence problem rather than a clinical change.

options.text: Discuss an activity plan to rebuild the walking she has stopped
options.rationale: Addresses the symptom as deconditioning when it may be the presenting sign of decompensation.

options.text: Assess for medication effects and changes in her chronic conditions
options.rationale: Weight gain of 3 kg with worsening fatigue and reduced activity is a heart failure picture, and it needs assessing rather than attributing.

questions.takeaway: Fatigue with weight gain and reduced exercise tolerance in heart failure is decompensation until assessed.
questions.strategy: Three options are genuine heart failure care delivered at the wrong point. Assessment comes before intervention.

strategies: Assessment before intervention

steps.detail: 3 kg up, six weeks of worsening fatigue.
The change has already happened.

steps.action: Cut the teaching and activity options
steps.detail: Both intervene before assessing.

elimination.verdict: That leaves assessing for medication effects and disease change.

questions.stem: A patient newly diagnosed with type 2 diabetes tells the nurse that his father had it too, so there was nothing he could have done. He works twelve-hour shifts, eats mostly takeaway food, and has not exercised in years. Which factors are described as contributing to chronic disease?

options.text: Infectious exposure in early childhood that predisposes the person to later disease
options.rationale: Not one of the categories.

options.text: Genetic, environmental, and lifestyle factors including tobacco, alcohol, and nutrition
options.rationale: The three specified categories, and genetics interacts with the others rather than acting alone.

options.text: Lifestyle factors only, since behavior is what the patient is able to change
options.rationale: Excludes genetics and environment.

options.text: Genetic factors only, since family history determines who develops the condition
options.rationale: Genetics is one of three specified categories.

questions.takeaway: Genetic, environmental, and lifestyle factors, interacting rather than acting separately.
questions.strategy: Options containing only are almost always wrong when a condition is multifactorial.

strategies: Eliminate absolutes
Global or umbrella option

steps.detail: The question asks what contributes to chronic disease.
Only excludes two categories.
Only excludes two categories.
Not among the factors.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B: the three specified categories, and genetics interacts with the others rather than acting alone.

questions.stem: A clinic is redesigning how it cares for patients with long-term conditions, having found that most problems arise between visits rather than during them. The team reviews the framework built around planned rather than reactive chronic care. Which are components of the Chronic Care Model? Select all that apply.

options.text: Community
options.rationale: Community resources extend care beyond the clinic, which matters because chronic illness is lived mostly outside health care settings.

options.text: Self-management support
options.rationale: Self-management support builds the patient's capability, since they manage the condition between visits and that is where most of it happens.

options.text: Acute rehabilitation
options.rationale: A care setting rather than a component of the chronic care framework.

options.text: Delivery system design
options.rationale: Delivery system design determines how visits, follow-up, and team roles are arranged so chronic care is planned rather than reactive.

options.text: Emergency department throughput
options.rationale: A measure of acute service flow rather than a component of chronic care.

options.text: Emergency preparedness
options.rationale: An organizational function rather than a component of chronic care.

questions.takeaway: Community, self-management support, health system, delivery system design, decision support, clinical information systems. The Chronic Care Model organizes long-term condition care through community resources, the health system, self-management support, delivery system design, decision support, and clinical information systems. Self-management support builds the patient's capability, because the patient manages the condition between visits where no nurse is present.
questions.strategy: Five of the six are offered. Recognize the one that is the outlier rather than trying to rank importance.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The question asks which options belong to the model.
Not among the six components.

elimination.verdict: A, B and D are selected.

questions.concept: The Chronic Care Model organizes long-term condition care through community resources, the health system, self-management support, delivery system design, decision support, and clinical information systems. Self-management support builds the patient's capability, because the patient manages the condition between visits where no nurse is present.

questions.stem: Highlight the findings that require the nurse's attention at this visit.
questions.takeaway: Age-related changes can mask signs of chronic illness. Assess new symptoms rather than attributing them.
questions.strategy: The family's explanation is deliberately included. It tells you what to teach, and it is not itself a finding. One finding is the family's interpretation rather than a clinical finding.

A teaching cue rather than a clinical finding.

questions.nursesNote: 1130: Patient is 77, attends clinic with heart failure, type 2 diabetes and arthritis, all diagnosed eight years ago. Over the past three weeks his weight is up 3 kg and he reports new ankle swelling. Walks 90 meters before stopping, down from 300 meters. Has stopped attending the allotment he has tended for 20 years. States he takes his medication only when he remembers. Family attributes the changes to getting older. VS: T 36.8 C; HR 96; RR 20; BP 138/84; SpO2 93% on room air.

segments.text: Weight up 3 kg with new ankle swelling over three weeks
segments.rationale: Fluid retention, and the combination with reduced exercise tolerance points at worsening heart failure.

segments.text: Walks 90 meters before stopping, down from 300 meters
segments.rationale: A measurable fall in exercise tolerance over the same period.

segments.text: Has stopped attending the allotment he has tended for 20 years
segments.rationale: Chronic illness affects roles and self-perception, and social withdrawal is a psychosocial need.

segments.text: Takes medication only when he remembers
segments.rationale: Adherence is an assessment priority, and it may explain the deterioration.

segments.text: Diagnosed with heart failure and type 2 diabetes eight years ago
segments.rationale: Background history rather than a finding requiring attention now.

segments.text: Family attributes the changes to getting older
segments.rationale: Their explanation, and it is a cue about understanding rather than a clinical finding.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence by selecting from the choices below.

questions.stem: The nurse plans this visit. Which 2 actions address what is driving his deterioration?
questions.takeaway: Find the modifiable cause and report the trend. Accepting the change as aging is the error.

rows.text: Weight up 3 kg with new ankle swelling

rows.rationale: A measurable physiological limit and a change in what he can do with his day.

questions.stem: A nurse plans care for an 83-year-old admitted with pneumonia who also has arthritis, lives with her daughter, and is anxious about losing her independence. The nurse sets goals with the patient and her daughter rather than for them. Which statement describes gerontological nursing assessment?

options.text: It focuses on physiological findings, since psychosocial issues are outside nursing scope
options.rationale: Assessment takes into account the interrelation between physical and psychosocial aspects of aging.

options.text: It addresses goals established with the older adult, family, and team
options.rationale: Mutually established is the operative phrase, and the assessment is tailored to the older person.

options.text: It measures disease severity as the primary outcome of the whole assessment
options.rationale: The effects of disease and disability on current functional status are what matter.

options.text: It uses the same approach and parameters as for younger adults without adjustment
options.rationale: Techniques and parameters are adapted to accommodate normal changes associated with aging.

questions.takeaway: Goals are mutually established with the older adult, the family, and the team, and assessment is tailored to the person.
questions.strategy: the answer usually includes the patient and family as partners rather than as recipients.

questions.stem: A 79-year-old who lives alone is discharged after a stroke with mild left-sided weakness. She needs help with dressing and stairs but is expected to improve over several weeks. Which type of care setting best matches her needs?

options.text: Continuing care in a residential facility
options.rationale: Continuing care supports needs not expected to change. Hers is expected to improve.

options.text: Hospice care
options.rationale: For a life-limiting illness with comfort as the goal.

options.text: Restorative care with rehabilitation services
options.rationale: Function has been lost and is expected to return. Restorative care exists to recover it.

options.text: Acute care on a medical unit
options.rationale: She is medically stable. Acute care manages an active episode of illness.

questions.takeaway: Match the setting to the trajectory. Function expected to return means restorative care.
questions.strategy: Ask whether the need is expected to change. Improving means restorative; permanent means continuing.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Expected to improve over weeks.
She is medically stable.
Both assume the need will not improve.

elimination.verdict: That leaves C: restorative care.

questions.concept: Restorative care aims at regaining function after illness or injury. Continuing care sustains a need that is not expected to end. CUS escalates a concern with graded language: I am Concerned, I am Uncomfortable, this is a Safety issue. SBAR reports; CUS escalates when reporting has failed.

questions.scenario: The nurse reviews assessment findings for three older adults on the unit.
questions.stem: For each finding, click to specify whether it is consistent with delirium, dementia, or depression. Each finding may support more than one condition.

rows.text: Acute onset over hours to days
rows.rationale: Only delirium develops acutely. Dementia is progressive over years and depression develops over weeks to months.

rows.text: Impaired memory
rows.rationale: All three affect memory, which is why memory alone never distinguishes them.

rows.text: Symptoms that fluctuate through the day
rows.rationale: Fluctuation is the signature of delirium.

rows.text: Withdrawal and loss of interest in usual activities
rows.rationale: The specified presentation of depression in older adults.

rows.text: Altered level of consciousness
rows.rationale: Consciousness is clear in dementia and in depression.

rows.text: Gradual decline in the ability to manage finances and medications
rows.rationale: Progressive loss of instrumental activities is the dementia pattern.

rows.text: Potentially reversible when the underlying cause is treated
rows.rationale: Delirium resolves when the cause is corrected and depression responds to treatment. Dementia does not reverse.

questions.constraint: Each column must have at least one response selected.
questions.takeaway: Onset and consciousness separate the three Ds. Memory does not. Delirium is acute, fluctuating, and potentially reversible, with altered consciousness. Dementia is chronic and progressive with clear consciousness. Depression develops over weeks with intact consciousness.
questions.strategy: The row that catches people is impaired memory, because it belongs to all three. Look for the rows that belong to only one. Each column must have at least one response selected, and one finding belongs to all three.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Acute onset, fluctuation, and altered consciousness are delirium alone.
Memory impairment appears in all three.
Two of the three can improve with treatment.

elimination.verdict: Delirium claims four rows, dementia two, depression two, with overlap on memory and reversibility.

questions.concept: Delirium is acute, fluctuating, and potentially reversible, with altered consciousness. Dementia is chronic and progressive with clear consciousness. Depression develops over weeks with intact consciousness.

questions.stem: A nursing student tells her instructor she finds older adults depressing to care for because they remind her of her own aging. Which response by the instructor is most appropriate?

options.text: "Nurses must examine their own attitudes toward aging, and that is a priority."
options.rationale: Attitudes come from personal experiences, education, employment experiences, and the attitudes of coworkers and institutions, so they can be examined and changed.

options.text: "You should request assignments on a different unit until you feel ready."
options.rationale: Avoidance, and it leaves the attitude unexamined.

options.text: "Focus on the tasks in front of you and try not to think about it during the shift."
options.rationale: Suppression rather than reflection, and it models the avoidance being cautioned against.

options.text: "Most nurses feel that way at first and it passes with more experience."
options.rationale: Normalizes without addressing, and experience alone does not change an unexamined attitude.

questions.takeaway: Forming positive attitudes toward older adults and gaining specialized knowledge about aging are priorities for all nurses.

Eliminate options that deny patient feelings

questions.stem: An 83-year-old admitted two days ago becomes acutely confused during the evening shift. She was oriented on admission. Place the nurse's actions in the correct order, from FIRST to LAST.

options.text: Assess the patient, including vital signs, oxygen saturation, and level of consciousness
options.rationale: You establish what is happening before deciding what it means. Poor oxygenation and infection are contributors.

options.text: Review the medication record for recently administered or newly started agents
options.rationale: Medications are a specified contributing factor and are among the fastest reversible causes to identify.

options.text: Notify the health care provider of the change from baseline and the assessment findings
options.rationale: The provider needs the findings in order to prescribe investigation or treatment.

options.text: Implement safety measures using the least restrictive interventions available
options.rationale: Safety is managed while the cause is being investigated, and restraints are a last resort.

options.text: Document the change, the assessment, the notification, and the interventions
options.rationale: The record closes the sequence so the next nurse knows what changed and what was done.

questions.takeaway: Assess, look for reversible causes, notify, keep her safe with the least restrictive measure, document.
questions.strategy: Sudden confusion items are answered by remembering that delirium has a cause. The sequence is find it, report it, then manage safety. Safety matters throughout, but consider which action must come FIRST when the cause is unknown.

steps.detail: Assessment precedes every other action.
Documentation closes the sequence.
Medications, then notification, then safety measures.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, D, E.

Eliminate options that deny patient feelings

questions.stem: Four older adults are on the unit: one confused after surgery who can be reoriented, one with advanced dementia who believes she must collect her children from school, one who enjoys describing his years working on the railway, and one frightened before a procedure. Match each nursing approach with the technique it BEST demonstrates. Each term is used only once.

items.text: A nurse gently restates the day, the location, and who she is for a patient with post-operative confusion
items.rationale: Restates time, place, and person, and it fits acute, reversible confusion where the patient can be reoriented.

items.text: A nurse responds to the feeling behind a statement rather than correcting a patient with advanced dementia who believes she must collect her children
items.rationale: Acknowledges the emotion rather than the fact, and it fits chronic irreversible confusion where reorientation causes distress.

items.rationale: Uses recall of past events to support identity and self-worth.

Decide whether the confusion is reversible before choosing between them.

Advanced dementia calls for validation.
Recall of the past is reminiscence; physical contact is touch.

questions.stem: An older adult admitted three days ago for pneumonia is now inattentive, with symptoms that fluctuate through the day and periods of altered consciousness. Which condition does the nurse suspect?

options.text: Dementia
options.rationale: Generalized impairment of intellectual functioning that interferes with social and occupational functioning, and it develops over years.

options.text: Depression
options.rationale: Presents with mood changes, withdrawal, and loss of interest.

options.text: An expected change of aging
options.rationale: Age is not a diagnosis and this is a change from baseline.

options.text: Delirium
options.rationale: An acute confusional state. Acute onset, fluctuation, inattention, and altered consciousness together.

Dementia is chronic and progressive.
