questions.concept: Delirium is acute, fluctuating, and potentially reversible, with altered consciousness. Dementia is chronic and progressive with clear consciousness. Depression develops over weeks with intact consciousness.

questions.scenario: An 86-year-old is admitted for observation after a fall at home. The nurse completes a head-to-toe assessment.
questions.stem: For each finding, indicate whether it is an EXPECTED change of aging or a finding that REQUIRES further assessment.

rows.text: Skin has lost resilience and moisture
rows.rationale: A specified integumentary change of aging.

rows.text: Reduced bowel sounds on auscultation
rows.rationale: Peristalsis slows with age, producing reduced sounds. Absent sounds would be a different matter.

rows.text: New urinary incontinence
rows.rationale: Incontinence is abnormal and typically embarrassing, and it is more common in women but occurs in men too. Common is not the same as expected.

rows.text: Slower voluntary reflexes and less ability to respond to multiple stimuli
rows.rationale: A specified neurological change.

rows.text: Confusion beginning this morning
rows.rationale: Sudden confusion is a red flag, and delirium is a risk in acute care.

rows.text: Increased anteroposterior diameter of the thorax
rows.rationale: A specified change alongside decreased respiratory muscle strength.

questions.takeaway: Expected changes are gradual. Sudden change is investigated, and incontinence is abnormal at any age.
questions.strategy: Read each row for the words new or sudden. Those move a finding out of the expected column regardless of what it describes.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Gradual changes are expected.
Frequently dismissed as aging and specified as abnormal.
Onset this morning is acute.

elimination.verdict: Four rows expected, two require assessment.

questions.stem: A nurse assesses an 80-year-old who managed independently until this admission and now needs help with bathing, dressing, and walking 20 feet. She has also lost weight during the admission. Which statement about functional status is accurate?

options.text: Functional status is best measured once the acute illness has resolved
options.rationale: Sensible-sounding and it loses the baseline comparison that makes the change visible.

options.text: Weight loss during admission explains a decline of this kind
options.rationale: One plausible contributor treated as the whole explanation.

options.text: A decline in function usually signals illness rather than aging itself
options.rationale: Age alone does not take away bathing and walking over one admission. A functional change of this speed points to something treatable.

options.text: Function typically declines during hospitalization and returns after discharge
options.rationale: Hospital-associated decline is real and frequently does not reverse on its own, which is why it is assessed rather than waited out.

questions.takeaway: Rapid functional decline in an older adult is a symptom, not aging. Look for the cause.
questions.strategy: Each distractor contains something true. Ask which one would have you wait rather than assess.

strategies: Eliminate absolutes

steps.detail: Independent until this admission.
Both defer assessment.
Weight loss is a contributor, not the explanation.

elimination.verdict: That leaves decline as a signal of illness.

questions.stem: An 85-year-old with advanced dementia becomes distressed each afternoon, saying she must leave to collect her children from school. Staff have repeatedly corrected her and told her the children are adults, and her agitation has increased each time. Which approach is appropriate?

options.text: Leave her alone until the episode passes, so she is not further distressed
options.rationale: Abandons a distressed patient.

options.text: Acknowledge the feeling behind the statement and redirect gently
options.rationale: Validation is used where the patient cannot be reoriented. You respond to the emotion rather than correcting the fact.

options.text: Reorient her to the date and explain her children are adults
options.rationale: Reality orientation suits a patient who can be reoriented, and repeated correction has already increased her distress.

options.text: Agree that she should go and offer to walk her to the door
options.rationale: Deception, and it sets up a further distressing moment when she cannot leave.

questions.takeaway: Reality orientation for a patient who can be reoriented. Validation where she cannot.
questions.strategy: The stem tells you correction has already failed, which is what selects validation over orientation. One option would be correct for a different patient. Read what has already been tried.

strategies: Patient-centered option

steps.detail: Repeated correction increased agitation.
Orientation has already failed.
Deception and abandonment.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B: validation is used where the patient cannot be reoriented.

questions.stem: The nurse admits an 86-year-old from home following a fall. She assesses the skin, cognition, continence, senses, and mobility, and speaks with the daughter about recent changes. Highlight the findings that require further nursing assessment.

segments.text: Patient is alert and oriented to person, place, and time.
segments.rationale: A normal baseline, and it is the reference point against which any later change is measured.

segments.text: Skin is thin and dry with reduced elasticity.
segments.rationale: An expected integumentary change of aging.

segments.text: Reports new difficulty controlling urine over the past two weeks.
segments.rationale: Urinary incontinence is abnormal at any age. It is common in older adults and it is not expected.

segments.text: Skin has lost resilience and moisture since her last visit two years ago.
segments.rationale: Her deck names loss of skin resilience and moisture as an expected integumentary change of aging.

questions.stem: A nurse tells a colleague there is no point teaching an 88-year-old about her new warfarin dose because she will not retain it. The patient scores 28 of 30 on cognitive screening and manages her own finances. Which attitude does the nurse's statement reflect?

options.text: Reality orientation
options.rationale: A communication technique that restates time, place, and person.

options.text: Reminiscence
options.rationale: A technique using recall of past events.

options.text: Functional decline
options.rationale: A measurable change in the ability to perform daily activities.

options.text: Ageism
options.rationale: Discrimination against people due to increasing age, and it is banned by current laws. Here it removes a patient's right to education based on age alone.

questions.takeaway: Ageism is discrimination by age, and nurses must first assess their own attitudes toward older adults and toward their own aging. Ageism is assuming capability, preference, or prognosis from a person's age rather than assessing the individual.
questions.strategy: Statements that withhold care, teaching, or choice on the basis of age alone are ageism, however practical they sound.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Teaching is withheld because of age, not because of any assessed barrier.

questions.stem: Harm data is reviewed for older adults admitted to a medical unit over the past year, looking at what happened to them during hospitalization rather than what brought them in. Which adverse events are associated with hospitalization in this population? Select all that apply.

options.text: Delirium

options.text: Improved functional independence

options.text: Malnutrition

options.text: Faster wound healing than in younger adults
options.rationale: Healing is slower in older adults, not faster.

options.text: Increased appetite during admission
options.rationale: Appetite typically falls during hospitalization rather than rising.

questions.stem: An 87-year-old repeatedly asks the nurse to repeat questions and answers inconsistently. The television is on and two staff are talking in the doorway. She wears hearing aids that are at home. Which action is most appropriate?

options.rationale: Shouting distorts, and the television can simply be turned off.

options.rationale: Attributes a sensory problem to cognition, which is a consequential error in an older adult.

options.text: Reduce the background noise, face her directly, and speak clearly without shouting
options.rationale: Correct adaptations for hearing impairment. Shouting distorts speech rather than clarifying it.

options.text: Ask her family to answer on her behalf so the assessment can be completed
options.rationale: Bypasses a patient who can communicate with adaptation.

questions.takeaway: Reduce noise, face the patient, do not shout. Sensory change is not confusion. A tort is a civil wrong. Quasi-intentional torts cause harm through the nature of the act. Unintentional torts arise where the person knew or should have known the care was substandard.

questions.stem: A family asks the nurse about their 88-year-old relative's sudden confusion, which began overnight three days after hip surgery. The family asks what is happening and what should be done. Which family statement indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "Her confusion started overnight, so her dementia must be getting worse."
options.rationale: Dementia is chronic and progressive over years. A change occurring overnight is delirium until proven otherwise, and delirium has a cause that is often reversible.

options.text: "An infection can show up as confusion before she runs a fever."
options.rationale: Accurate. In older adults the classic signs are often absent.

options.text: "The pain medication she started yesterday could be part of what is happening."
options.rationale: Accurate. Medications are a contributor to delirium.

options.text: "Tying her hands down would probably make her more agitated than she is now."
options.rationale: Accurate. Restraints worsen delirium and agitation and are a last resort.

questions.takeaway: Sudden confusion is delirium until proven otherwise. Dementia develops over years.
questions.strategy: Onset is the discriminator. Anything that appears overnight cannot be a chronic progressive process.

strategies: Negative polarity
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Overnight rules out dementia.
Infection and medication are both specified.
Restraints worsen the condition.

elimination.verdict: A is the statement needing correction: overnight onset means delirium, not dementia.

She has received two doses of an opioid analgesic in the past six hours.

options.text: Progression of dementia
options.rationale: Dementia is chronic and progressive over years. She was oriented three days ago.

questions.nursesNote: 0330: Patient admitted three days ago following surgical repair of a fractured hip. Alert and oriented to person, place, and time on admission. Night staff report she has been pulling at her intravenous line since 0100 and has dislodged it once. Currently unsure of the month and believes she is at home. Daughter telephoned and confirms this is new. Received an opioid analgesic at 0130 and at 2230. Urine in the catheter bag is dark and cloudy. Has passed no bowel motion since admission. VS: T 37.9 C; HR 104; RR 22; BP 104/62; SpO2 91% on room air.

segments.text: Confusion about the month and her location, new since 0100
segments.rationale: Sudden confusion is a red flag, and hospital-acquired delirium is common two to three days after admission.

segments.text: Temperature 37.9 C with dark cloudy urine
segments.rationale: Infection is a contributor to delirium, and in an older adult it may present as confusion without a high fever.

segments.text: SpO2 91% on room air
segments.rationale: Poor oxygenation is a contributor to delirium and is a finding in its own right.

segments.text: Two doses of opioid analgesic in the past six hours
segments.rationale: Medications are a contributor, and opioids are among the commonest.

segments.text: Age 84
segments.rationale: Age is not a diagnosis, and a change from baseline is clinically significant regardless of age.

segments.text: Reduced skin elasticity noted on admission
segments.rationale: An expected integumentary change of aging, documented before the current change.

questions.strategy: Exactly two are requested. Two wrong options rank one source above another, and ranking is not how these work.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: An alert patient speaking for himself.
Preparation, not substitute.
Sources answer different questions.

elimination.verdict: A and B are selected.

options.text: The patient is the primary source of data
options.rationale: He is alert and able to answer, so his own account takes precedence.

options.text: The record is reviewed beforehand as preparation rather than as a substitute
options.rationale: It tells you what to ask about; it does not replace asking.

options.text: The wife's account should replace his where they differ
options.rationale: Family provide supplementary information. Where an alert patient differs, his account is the primary source.

options.text: The provider's note is the definitive source for nursing assessment
options.rationale: It informs the picture and is not the nurse's assessment.

options.text: Physical examination findings are less reliable than the patient's report
options.rationale: The two answer different questions, and neither ranks above the other.

options.text: Observation of behavior is not a formal data source
options.rationale: Observation of patient behavior is specified directly.

questions.stem: A nurse admits a patient to a medical unit at 1400. He is alert, has no acute distress, and is expected to stay several days. Which type of assessment does she perform now?

options.text: A comprehensive assessment covering all systems and the health history
options.rationale: An admission to an inpatient unit calls for the full picture, which becomes the baseline every later change is measured against.

options.text: No assessment until the provider has seen him
options.rationale: Nursing assessment does not wait on the medical one.

options.text: An emergency assessment of airway, breathing, and circulation
options.rationale: Reserved for a patient who is unstable. He is in no acute distress.

options.text: A problem-focused assessment of the presenting complaint only
options.rationale: Used when a specific problem arises, not to establish a baseline.

questions.takeaway: Admission calls for a comprehensive assessment. It is the baseline that makes later change visible.
questions.strategy: Match the assessment type to the moment: admission is comprehensive, a new symptom is focused, instability is emergency.

strategies: Assessment before intervention

steps.detail: Admission, stable, multi-day stay.
One is for a new problem, one for instability.
Nursing assessment is independent.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A: a comprehensive admission assessment.

questions.stem: A nurse has completed an abdominal assessment on a patient admitted with nausea and must enter her findings in the record. She wants the entry to be usable by whoever cares for him next. Which entry best records an assessment finding?

options.text: Patient denies any abdominal complaints when asked during the assessment
options.rationale: Records subjective data only and omits the examination.

options.text: Abdomen appears fine on inspection with no obvious abnormality noted
options.rationale: Vague and interpretive.

options.text: Abdomen soft, non-distended, bowel sounds present in all four quadrants
options.rationale: Objective, specific, and observable.

options.text: Abdominal assessment within normal limits
options.rationale: Within normal limits without detail is not specific enough to be useful or defensible.

questions.takeaway: Document what you found, not the conclusion you drew from it.
questions.strategy: Within normal limits and appears fine are both too vague to defend.

strategies: Priority key word

steps.detail: Polarity is positive. Key word: best. More than one option may be true, so you are ranking them.
Vague and interpretive.
Within normal limits without detail is not specific enough to be useful or defensible.
Records subjective data only and omits the examination.

elimination.verdict: That leaves C. Objective, specific, and observable.

questions.stem: A nurse notes a patient has not eaten for two days, has lost 4 pounds, and has an albumin of 2.8 g/dL. She concludes he has inadequate nutritional intake. Which action has she performed?

options.text: Made an inference from clustered cues
options.rationale: She has moved from individual findings to a conclusion about what they mean together.

options.text: Established a nursing diagnosis
options.rationale: An inference precedes the diagnosis and has not yet been formally stated as one.

options.text: Validated the data against a second source
options.rationale: Validation would mean confirming the findings, not drawing a conclusion from them.

options.text: Recognized cues without interpreting them
options.rationale: She has interpreted them, which is the step beyond recognition.

questions.takeaway: Data becomes cues, cues cluster into a pattern, the pattern produces an inference, and validation comes before you commit to it.
questions.strategy: Find where the stem stops. Drawing a conclusion is inference; confirming it is validation.

strategies: Eliminate absolutes
Negative polarity

steps.detail: No priority key word, so look for the single accurate option.
She has interpreted them, which is the step beyond recognition.
Validation would mean confirming the findings, not drawing a conclusion from them.

questions.stem: A nurse is preparing for an admission interview before entering the room. Which actions belong to the preinteraction phase? Select all that apply.

options.text: Review the record and any previous discharge summary
options.rationale: Preparation, so the interview builds on what is already known rather than repeating it.

options.text: Check whether an interpreter will be needed
options.rationale: Arranged before the encounter rather than discovered during it.

options.text: Identify what she most needs to learn from this patient
options.rationale: Focuses a limited amount of time on what matters for this admission.

options.text: Ask the patient what brought him in today
options.rationale: The opening of the orientation phase, once she is with him.

options.text: Summarize what was discussed and confirm accuracy
options.rationale: Termination phase.

options.text: Explore the history of the presenting problem
options.rationale: Working phase.

questions.takeaway: Preinteraction happens before the encounter: review, arrange, and decide what you need.
questions.strategy: Sort by whether the nurse is with the patient yet. Three of these happen before she enters.

strategies: Assessment before intervention

steps.detail: Preinteraction happens outside the room.
That opens the orientation phase.
Termination and working.

questions.stem: A nurse completes an admission assessment on a 54-year-old with abdominal pain. She records the pain rating he gives her, his temperature, his blood pressure, and his statement that the pain worsens after eating. Which finding is subjective data?

options.text: The untouched meal tray at the bedside
options.rationale: Observed by the nurse, so objective.

options.text: His temperature measured with a tympanic thermometer
options.rationale: Measured by the nurse, so objective.

options.text: His blood pressure taken with an appropriately sized cuff
options.rationale: Measured, so objective.

options.text: The pain rating the patient gives her
options.rationale: A pain rating is the patient's own report of his experience. Attaching a number does not make it observable by anyone else.

questions.takeaway: Subjective data is what the patient reports. A number attached to a symptom does not make it objective.
questions.strategy: Ask who produced the finding. If only the patient can know it, it is subjective however it is scored.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Only the patient can rate his own pain.
Both were measured by the nurse.
The tray was observed.

elimination.verdict: That leaves D: his own pain rating.

questions.stem: A nurse begins an admission interview with a 55-year-old admitted with abdominal pain rated 8 of 10. She needs to understand the pain fully before the provider arrives. Which question type should she use first?

options.text: "You are here for your breathing, correct?"
options.rationale: Leading, and it supplies the answer inside the question.

options.text: "Do you have chest pain?"
options.rationale: Closed, and it presumes which problem matters.

options.text: "Your chart says you have heart failure."
options.rationale: A statement rather than a question, and it starts from the record rather than the patient.

options.text: "What brought you to the hospital today?"
options.rationale: An open question that lets the patient describe the problem in their own terms, which returns cues you did not know to ask about.

questions.takeaway: Open the interview with a question the patient answers in their own words.
questions.strategy: Start open and narrow down. Closed questions clarify a detail once the picture exists.

strategies: Patient-centered option

steps.detail: The opening question of an interview.
Closed and presumptive.
Leading.
Starts from the chart, not the patient.

elimination.verdict: That leaves D: an open question that lets the patient describe the problem in their own terms, which returns cues you did not know to ask about.

questions.stem: A nurse educator explains why assessment carries weight in the nursing process, using a patient whose saturation of 88% was missed on admission and found six hours later. Which statements about assessment are accurate? Select all that apply.

options.text: It is the systematic collection of patient data
options.rationale: The stated purpose of the step.

options.text: It forms the foundation for every later step in the nursing process
options.rationale: Diagnosis, planning, implementation, and evaluation all rest on it, which is why an error here propagates.

options.text: It is ongoing rather than a single event at admission
options.rationale: The process loops, and evaluation data becomes new assessment data.

options.text: It is completed once and does not change during the admission
options.rationale: Contradicts the ongoing nature of the step and the looping structure of the process.

options.text: It draws on the record, the interview, examination, and observation of behavior
options.rationale: The specified sources.

questions.takeaway: Assessment is systematic, ongoing, and the foundation every later step rests on. The nursing process has five steps in order: assessment, diagnosis, planning, implementation, evaluation. Each depends on the one before it.
questions.strategy: Any option describing assessment as a one-time event contradicts the looping structure of the nursing process.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Purpose and principles of assessment.
Assessment is ongoing, not completed once.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, and E are selected.

questions.concept: The nursing process has five steps in order: assessment, diagnosis, planning, implementation, evaluation. Each depends on the one before it.

options.text: Review of systems covering all body systems
options.rationale: Collects subjective data broadly when the situation needs depth in one area.

options.text: Problem-focused assessment of the respiratory and cardiac systems
options.rationale: An acute change calls for a focused assessment of the systems involved.

options.text: Complete health history including family history
options.rationale: Not relevant to the immediate problem.

options.text: Comprehensive head-to-toe assessment covering every body system in turn
options.rationale: Too slow for an acute change and delays intervention.

questions.takeaway: Comprehensive on admission when things are stable, problem-focused when something changes.
questions.strategy: Acute change in the stem always points to a focused assessment.

strategies: Eliminate absolutes

Too slow for an acute change and delays intervention.
Not relevant to the immediate problem.
Collects subjective data broadly when the situation needs depth in one area.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B. An acute change calls for a focused assessment of the systems involved.

questions.stem: A nurse is nearing the end of an admission interview. options.text: Working
options.rationale: Where the data is gathered.

options.text: Termination

options.rationale: Before meeting the patient, reviewing available data.

options.text: Orientation

steps.detail: Polarity is positive. No priority key word, so look for the single accurate option.
Introductions, purpose, and setting expectations.
Before meeting the patient, reviewing available data.
Where the data is gathered.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B. Summarizing, checking for anything missed, and telling the patient what happens next.

questions.stem: A nurse precepts a student who has assessed a patient with abdominal pain, recording his pain rating, vital signs, and an untouched meal tray. The student describes how she sorted the findings. Which student statement indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "The record is preparation; the patient is the primary source."
options.rationale: Accurate. The record tells you what to ask about rather than replacing asking.

options.text: "An untouched meal tray is data; poor appetite is a conclusion about it."
options.rationale: Accurate, and checking the conclusion prevents an error entering the record.

options.text: A pain rating is objective data because a number is attached
options.rationale: A rating scale records the patient's perception. Only the patient can supply it, which makes it subjective regardless of the number.

options.text: "Observation of behavior counts as a formal source of assessment data."
options.rationale: Accurate. It is one of the sources alongside the record, interview, and examination.

questions.takeaway: A number attached to a perception is still subjective. Only the patient can supply it.
questions.strategy: The rating scale is the most reliable trap in assessment items, because a number looks measured.

strategies: Negative polarity
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Only the patient can rate their own pain.

questions.stem: A nurse is documenting her admission assessment and must separate what she observed and measured from what the patient reported. She reviews her notes before entering them in the record. Which findings are objective data? Select all that apply.

options.text: Temperature 38.4 degrees Celsius
options.rationale: A measured value anyone can verify with the same instrument, which is what makes it objective.

options.text: Patient reports nausea
options.rationale: What the patient tells you. Subjective.

options.text: Wound edges approximated with no drainage
options.rationale: An observation you made.

options.text: Patient states he slept poorly
options.rationale: The patient's own report of how he slept, and only he can supply it, so it is subjective.

options.text: Crackles auscultated in the left lower lobe
options.rationale: An examination finding.

options.text: Grimacing during position changes
options.rationale: An observed behavior, which is objective even though it suggests a subjective experience.

questions.takeaway: Behavior you observe is objective. What the behavior means to the patient is subjective.
questions.strategy: Ask whether you could record it without the patient speaking.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Polarity is positive. This is a select all that apply, so there is no single best answer. Judge each option separately.
What the patient tells you.
Subjective.

elimination.verdict: Keep A, C, E, F. In a SATA, judge each option as its own true or false statement rather than picking a single best answer.

questions.stem: An 82-year-old is brought in for confusion that began yesterday. Her temperature is 37.0 C, her pulse is 96, and she reports urinary frequency and burning. Her daughter states she was fully oriented last week. What should the nurse recognize?

options.text: A temperature of 37.0 C makes an infectious cause unlikely
options.rationale: Would hold in a younger adult. In an older adult a normal temperature does not exclude infection.

options.text: Infection in an older adult may present as confusion before a fever appears
options.rationale: The febrile response blunts with age, so confusion with urinary symptoms is often the presenting sign of infection.

options.text: The urinary symptoms should be treated before the confusion is investigated
options.rationale: Splits one presentation into two problems when they are most likely the same problem.

options.text: Confusion of one day's onset needs a cognitive screen before anything else
options.rationale: Screening measures the deficit without looking for its cause.

questions.takeaway: Older adults mount a blunted febrile response. Confusion can be the first sign of infection.
questions.strategy: One distractor applies a rule that is true in younger adults. Ask what age changes about presentation.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 82, new confusion, urinary symptoms.
Does not exclude infection here.
One separates one problem, one measures instead of investigating.

elimination.verdict: That leaves infection presenting as confusion.

questions.stem: A nurse documents that a patient has a poor appetite after seeing two untouched meal trays. Before recording this as a finding she speaks with him and learns he has been fasting for a procedure. Which step has she performed?

options.text: Evaluated an outcome against what was written in the plan of care
options.rationale: No outcome had been set.

options.text: Completed a focused nutritional assessment
options.rationale: A focused assessment would examine intake, weight, and swallowing in a structured way.

options.text: Delegated data collection to assistive personnel for this patient
options.rationale: Nothing was delegated.

options.text: Validated an inference against the patient's own account
options.rationale: Two untouched trays are data. Poor appetite is an interpretation, and checking it prevents an error entering the record.

questions.takeaway: Data is what you observe. An inference is what you conclude, and inferences are checked before they enter the record.
questions.strategy: An untouched tray has several explanations. Recording the conclusion rather than the observation is how an error becomes permanent. Two untouched trays is a fact. Poor appetite is a conclusion about it.

strategies: Assessment before intervention

steps.detail: Untouched trays versus poor appetite.
No structured nutritional assessment described.
No outcome and no delegation.

elimination.verdict: That leaves D: two untouched trays are data.

questions.stem: A patient tells the nurse he has been having headaches for about a month and is worried about them. The nurse wants to understand the pattern, the severity, and what he thinks is causing them before narrowing to specific details. Which question best opens the interview about this new symptom?

options.text: Are you having any pain in your abdomen today, yes or no?
options.rationale: Closed. It invites a yes or no and closes the topic.

options.text: Tell me what has been bothering you most.
options.rationale: Open-ended. It lets the patient lead and introduce what matters to them.

options.text: You are not having chest pain, are you?
options.rationale: Leading. It signals the answer you expect.

options.text: Why did you wait so long to come in?
options.rationale: A why question, which reads as accusation and produces defensiveness.

questions.takeaway: Open the interview broad and let the patient set the direction, then narrow with focused questions.
questions.strategy: Eliminate closed, leading, and why questions first. That usually leaves one option.

Leading.
Closed.

questions.stem: A nurse conducts an admission interview with a patient who is anxious and gives short answers. She wants the interview to produce a usable picture rather than a list of yes and no responses. Which techniques support this? Select all that apply.

options.text: Open the interview with a question he answers in his own words
options.rationale: Open questions return cues you did not know to ask about.

options.text: Sit at his eye level rather than standing over him
options.rationale: Nonverbal communication affects how much a patient discloses.

options.text: Use silence to give him room to continue
options.rationale: Silence invites him to add to what he has said rather than closing the exchange.

options.text: Ask a rapid series of closed questions to cover everything
options.rationale: Produces short answers and misses what he might have volunteered.

options.text: Close by summarizing and asking whether there is anything else
options.rationale: Confirms understanding and gives a final opening.

questions.takeaway: Open first, narrow later, and close by confirming what you heard.
questions.strategy: The wrong option is efficient and produces exactly the short answers the stem is describing as the problem.

strategies: Patient-centered option

steps.detail: Anxiety and short answers.
Closed questions produce short answers.

questions.stem: A 47-year-old two days after abdominal surgery tells the nurse he is fine and needs nothing. As she repositions him he grimaces, tenses, and guards his abdomen with both hands. His last analgesia was six hours ago. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Name the guarding and grimacing to him and ask about the pain directly
options.rationale: Observed behavior is assessment data. Raising it opens the discrepancy without overriding his report or accepting it uncritically.

options.text: Administer the analgesia that is due, since the guarding is clear enough
options.rationale: Treats on observation alone and skips the assessment that would establish what he is experiencing.

options.text: Document that he denies pain and note the guarding separately
options.rationale: Records both and reconciles neither, leaving the next nurse the same contradiction.

options.text: Reposition him and reassess his comfort in thirty minutes
options.rationale: A reasonable comfort measure that defers the assessment of a contradiction already visible.

questions.takeaway: When the report and the observation disagree, raise it. Do not silently pick one.
questions.strategy: Two options act on the observation, one on the report. The key resolves the discrepancy with him.

strategies: Assessment before intervention

steps.detail: He says fine, his body says otherwise.
Acts without assessing.
Both leave the contradiction standing.

elimination.verdict: That leaves naming the observation and asking directly.

questions.stem: A patient denies chest pain, but the nurse notes he is diaphoretic, guarding his left arm, and has declined to walk to the bathroom. His statement and her observations do not agree. Which action is correct?

options.text: Record that the patient denies chest pain and move on
options.rationale: Records one half of the data and discards the half that contradicts it.

options.text: Document that the patient is an unreliable historian
options.rationale: Judges the patient rather than investigating the discrepancy.

options.text: Validate the discrepancy by exploring both the report and the observations further
options.rationale: Conflicting subjective and objective data are not resolved by choosing one. Validation asks what would explain both, and patients commonly describe cardiac pain in other words.

options.text: Treat the observations as correct and the patient's report as inaccurate
options.rationale: Substitutes the nurse's interpretation for the patient's account without exploring either.

questions.takeaway: When subjective and objective data disagree, validate rather than choose. The discrepancy is the finding.
questions.strategy: Every wrong option resolves the conflict by discarding one side. Look for the option that keeps both and investigates.

strategies: Assessment before intervention

steps.detail: His words and his behavior disagree.
Each discards one side.
Labels the patient instead of exploring.

elimination.verdict: That leaves C: validate both.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old on telemetry after a myocardial infarction has been in normal sinus rhythm all shift. The monitor now shows a new irregular rhythm. He is sitting up in bed and has not called out. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Assess the patient, including pulse, blood pressure, and level of consciousness
options.rationale: Treat the patient rather than the monitor. Assessment comes before you act or report.

options.text: Document the rhythm change in the record
options.rationale: Documentation follows assessment.

options.text: Prepare to administer an antiarrhythmic according to the standing protocol
options.rationale: No order exists and the patient's status is unknown.

options.text: Call the provider immediately to report the change in rhythm
options.rationale: You will be asked how the patient looks, and you do not yet know.

questions.takeaway: Assess before you intervene, and assess before you report. The monitor is data, not the patient.
questions.strategy: When one option gathers data and the others act on it, gather first unless the patient is in arrest.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence by selecting from the choices below.

The skin is intact.

options.rationale: Non-blanching redness over a bony prominence with intact skin, in a patient who has not moved since surgery.

options.text: an allergic reaction to the dressing adhesive

questions.stem: For each identified problem, determine whether it is a NURSING DIAGNOSIS, a COLLABORATIVE PROBLEM, or a MEDICAL DIAGNOSIS.
questions.takeaway: Nurses treat responses, not diseases. Collaborative problems need both, and the nursing part is monitoring. A nursing diagnosis classifies the patient's response to illness and is what registered nurses treat independently. A collaborative problem requires both medical and nursing intervention, with the nursing part being monitoring to prevent a complication a physician would treat.
questions.strategy: Ask who would treat it if it happened. If the answer is a physician but the watching is yours, it is collaborative.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Only one names a pathological process.
Two describe watching for a complication.
Pain, mobility, and skin integrity.

elimination.verdict: Three nursing diagnoses, two collaborative problems, one medical diagnosis.

rows.text: Acute pain related to the surgical incision
rows.rationale: A response to illness that registered nurses treat independently through positioning, timing, and non-pharmacological measures alongside prescribed analgesia.

rows.text: Impaired physical mobility
rows.rationale: A response the nurse addresses directly.

rows.text: Monitoring for postoperative hemorrhage
rows.rationale: Requires both medical and nursing interventions, focused on monitoring and preventing a complication a physician would treat.

rows.text: Impaired skin integrity
rows.rationale: A response nurses treat independently.

rows.text: Postoperative ileus
rows.rationale: Identifies a disease process, which is what physicians and advanced practice nurses treat.

rows.text: Monitoring for wound dehiscence

questions.nursesNote: 0900: Patient is 74, admitted six days ago with an ischemic stroke. Right-sided weakness. Requires two assistants to transfer and cannot stand unsupported. segments.text: Requires two assistants to transfer and cannot stand unsupported
segments.rationale: Consistent with the stroke and the reason he is in hospital. It is the problem being treated rather than a new finding.

segments.text: Cannot manage buttons or shoelaces with the affected hand

segments.text: Wife asks when he will walk again

questions.takeaway: Nurses treat responses, not diseases. Collaborative problems need both, and the nursing part is monitoring. A nursing diagnosis classifies the patient's response to illness and is what registered nurses treat independently. A collaborative problem requires both medical and nursing intervention, with the nursing part being monitoring to prevent a complication a physician would treat.
questions.strategy: Ask who would treat it if it happened. If the answer is a physician but the watching is yours, it is collaborative.

questions.stem: A 78-year-old is medically stable two days after surgery with a blood pressure of 124/76, a pulse of 78, and pain of 2 of 10. He tells the nurse he is terrified of dying alone and has not slept for two nights. Which action reflects correct priority setting?

options.text: Address the fear now, since an emergent psychological need can outrank a non-emergent physical one
options.rationale: Maslow orders needs, and an urgent higher-level need can take precedence when nothing physiological is threatened.

options.text: Request a sedative order so he can sleep through the night before surgery
options.rationale: Treats the symptom and avoids the fear producing it.

options.text: Defer the concern until physiological needs are fully addressed
options.rationale: The exam trap. Do not classify only physiological needs as high priority.

options.text: Refer him to the chaplain and continue with routine care
options.rationale: A reasonable referral used here to hand off the conversation rather than have it.

questions.takeaway: Maslow is a guide, not a rigid sequence. Safety is the level most often skipped and psychological needs can be emergent. Maslow's hierarchy ranks needs from physiological, through safety, love and belonging, and esteem, to self-actualization.
questions.strategy: Any option that defers all psychosocial concerns until physical needs are complete is testing this trap.

strategies: Priority key word

steps.detail: Polarity is positive. Key word: priority. More than one option may be true, so you are ranking them.

questions.stem: During a care plan audit that found outcomes written in several different styles, a new graduate explains to her manager how she decides whether an outcome is well written. Which statement by the new graduate indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "The outcome describes what the patient will achieve, not what I will do."
options.rationale: Accurate. An action by the nurse is an intervention rather than an outcome.

options.text: "Physiological problems are not automatically the highest priority."
options.rationale: Accurate, and that assumption is explicitly cautioned against.

options.text: "As long as an outcome is specific and has a date, it is well written."
options.rationale: SMART outcomes are specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, and time-bound. An outcome can meet three criteria and still fail on achievable, which is the one students skip.

options.text: "Priorities are set with the patient, not for the patient."
options.rationale: Accurate, and a barrier the patient names is more useful than a priority you assigned.

questions.takeaway: Specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, time-bound. Achievable and relevant are the two most often skipped.

questions.stem: A nurse writes a discharge plan for a patient with heart failure without discussing it with him. segments.text: Heart rate 118 from 88 at rest

questions.stem: A patient has not met the outcome of ambulating 50 feet with a walker by day three. He walked 15 feet once and rates his pain 7 of 10 on movement. Which actions does the nurse take? Select all that apply.

options.text: Reassess the patient for new or overlooked data
options.rationale: And the reported pain is exactly the kind of data that may have been missed.

options.rationale: Correct.

questions.stem: An outcome stated the patient would maintain a urine output above 30 mL/hr. Over the past six hours his output has been 45, 38, 32, 28, 22, and 18 mL. Which conclusion does the nurse record?

options.rationale: Counting hours ignores which three, and the three that failed are the most recent.

The outcome was measurable.

questions.stem: An outcome states that a patient will demonstrate correct use of a metered-dose inhaler before discharge. He tells the nurse he has used inhalers for years and knows how. Which evaluative measure does this outcome require?

questions.stem: A patient's outcome stated he would tolerate a full diet by day four. By day two he is eating normally with no nausea and has asked when he can go home. Which action does the nurse take?

Both wait for a date that has already been beaten.
Closing is not deleting.

options.text: Remove the nutrition problem from the record entirely
options.rationale: The record keeps what happened. The outcome is closed rather than deleted.

questions.concept: A nursing diagnosis classifies the patient's response to illness and is what registered nurses treat independently. Nurses treat responses, not diseases.

questions.stem: A nurse evaluates an outcome stating the patient will report pain of 3 or less within 60 minutes of analgesia. He reports 5 of 10 at 60 minutes but says it is much better than before. Which conclusion does she record?

options.text: Unable to evaluate, since pain is subjective
options.rationale: Self-reported pain is the accepted measure and the outcome was written around it.

options.text: Partially met, with the current score recorded
options.rationale: He has improved without reaching the stated target, which is exactly what partially met records.

options.text: Met, since he reports improvement
options.rationale: Improvement is not the criterion. The outcome named a number.

options.text: Not met, and the analgesia should be discontinued
options.rationale: Discards the progress and removes what produced it.

questions.takeaway: Partially met records real progress that fell short of the target. Met and not met would both lose it.
questions.strategy: Compare the result against the written criterion, not against how the patient feels about it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Three or less within 60 minutes.
Improvement is not the stated criterion.
One discards progress, one dismisses the measure.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B: partially met.

questions.concept: Teach-back asks the patient to explain the plan in their own words. It confirms understanding rather than confirming that teaching was delivered.

questions.stem: A patient with asthma has just finished a nebulizer treatment. His respiratory rate has fallen from 26 to 20 and his saturation has risen from 91% to 96%. Which source best tells the nurse whether his breathing feels easier?

options.text: The respiratory therapist's impression
options.rationale: A secondhand judgment about a subjective experience.

options.text: The oxygen saturation reading
options.rationale: Objective and useful, and it does not measure how breathing feels.

options.text: The respiratory rate
options.rationale: Objective data that may not track with the patient's experience.

options.text: The patient's own report
options.rationale: The patient knows best whether breathing is easier. Self-report is the measure for that experience.

questions.takeaway: Person-centered evaluation includes asking the patient whether what mattered to them improved.
questions.strategy: When the outcome is about an experience, the patient is the instrument.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Polarity is positive. No priority key word, so look for the single accurate option.
A secondhand judgment about a subjective experience.
Objective and useful, and it does not measure how breathing feels.
Objective data that may not track with the patient's experience.

elimination.verdict: That leaves D. The patient knows best whether breathing is easier.

questions.stem: A nursing student assumes evaluation happens once at the end of a shift. Her preceptor points out that she has been evaluating all morning without naming it. Which statement is accurate?

options.text: Evaluation is performed by the provider rather than by the nurse
options.rationale: It belongs to the nurse.

options.text: Evaluation occurs only at discharge, when the plan of care is closed
options.rationale: Outcomes fall due throughout an admission.

options.text: It occurs whenever an outcome falls due and feeds back into assessment
options.rationale: Evaluation data becomes new assessment data and the process begins its next loop immediately.

options.text: Evaluation is the final step and ends the process
options.rationale: The process loops rather than ending.

questions.takeaway: Evaluation data becomes new assessment data, and the nursing process begins its next loop immediately. Each depends on the one before it.
questions.strategy: Options describing evaluation as an endpoint are wrong. The loop is the point.

strategies: Eliminate absolutes
Global or umbrella option

steps.detail: Outcomes fall due throughout.
Only is absolute.
The process loops, and it is the nurse's.

elimination.verdict: That leaves C: evaluation data becomes new assessment data and the process begins its next loop immediately.

questions.concept: The nursing process has five steps in order: assessment, diagnosis, planning, implementation, evaluation. Each depends on the one before it.

questions.stem: A nurse manager audits evaluation documentation across the unit. Staff describe how they judge whether an outcome has been achieved. Which statement by a staff nurse indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "Partially met records progress that not met would discard."
options.rationale: Accurate, and it makes the next intervention specific rather than repeating everything.

options.text: "A met outcome comes off the plan along with its interventions."
options.rationale: Accurate. Leaving it in place produces unnecessary continued care.

options.text: "If an outcome is unmet, I reassess before changing the interventions."
options.rationale: Accurate. Reassessment and reconsidering the diagnosis come before adjusting the plan.

options.text: "If the interventions were all delivered and documented, the outcome was met."
options.rationale: Delivering care is not the same as achieving an outcome. Evaluation compares the result against the expected outcome and asks what data supports that conclusion.

questions.takeaway: Teaching completed is not learning demonstrated, and interventions delivered is not an outcome met.
questions.strategy: The wrong statement measures the nurse's activity. Evaluation measures the patient.

strategies: Negative polarity
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Delivery versus achievement.
Partially met, revision, and reassessment are correct.
Process is not outcome.

elimination.verdict: A is the statement needing correction: delivering care does not establish the outcome.

questions.stem: A patient rates his pain 3 of 10 thirty minutes after receiving oxycodone 5 mg. He is lying still watching television and is not grimacing. The nurse thinks he looks comfortable enough to be at 1. What should she document?

options.text: Pain rating unreliable
options.rationale: There is no basis for calling it unreliable and it dismisses the patient.

options.text: Pain rated 3 out of 10 by patient report
options.rationale: Pain is what the patient says it is. Self-report is the measure.

options.text: Patient appears comfortable, denies pain
options.rationale: He did not deny pain. He reported a 3.

options.text: Pain rated 1 out of 10 based on nursing assessment
options.rationale: Substituting your judgment for the patient's report falsifies the record.

questions.takeaway: For pain, breathing, nausea, and grief, patient self-report is the only accurate measure there is.
questions.strategy: Any option that replaces the patient's number with the nurse's impression is wrong.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Polarity is positive. No priority key word, so look for the single accurate option.
There is no basis for calling it unreliable and it dismisses the patient.
Substituting your judgment for the patient's report falsifies the record.
He did not deny pain.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B. Pain is what the patient says it is.

questions.stem: A nurse completes an evaluation on a patient three days after surgery and must decide what to do with the plan of care, rather than simply recording whether the goal was reached. Which questions does evaluation ask? Select all that apply.

options.text: Was the goal met, partially met, or not met?
options.rationale: The three-way judgment, and partially met is the option students most often skip.

options.text: What data supports that conclusion?
options.rationale: Correct. A conclusion without supporting data cannot be defended or handed over.

options.text: Does the plan of care need to be revised?
options.rationale: And it is what turns evaluation into the next loop of the process.

options.text: Is the patient's progress comparable to other patients on the unit?
options.rationale: Evaluation compares the patient against their own expected outcomes, not against other patients.

options.text: Did the interventions get documented on time?
options.rationale: Documentation timing is a process measure. Evaluation measures the patient's progress toward the expected outcomes.

questions.takeaway: Evaluation asks whether the goal was met, what data supports that, and whether the plan needs revising.
questions.strategy: Evaluation measures the patient against their own expected outcomes. Options comparing them to others or to paperwork are wrong.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The questions evaluation asks, not the record of whether it happened.
Comparison is against the patient's own expected outcomes.
Documentation timing is a process measure, not patient progress.

elimination.verdict: A, B, and C are selected, which are the three questions specified at this step.

questions.stem: A patient recovering from hip replacement has met the outcome of ambulating independently with a walker, achieved two days ahead of the target date. The plan of care still lists assisted ambulation twice daily. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Wait until discharge to close the outcome, so the record stays consistent
options.rationale: Delays freeing the plan and leaves stale interventions in place.

options.text: Continue the intervention unchanged for the rest of the admission
options.rationale: Continuing care that is no longer needed wastes time and the patient's energy.

options.text: Confirm with the patient, then discontinue that part of the plan and document it
options.rationale: Confirm, discontinue, and document so other nurses do not keep delivering finished care.

options.text: Remove the diagnosis from the record entirely, since it has been resolved
options.rationale: The record shows the history of care. You discontinue the plan, not the history.

questions.takeaway: Met means confirm, then continue or discontinue, and document the discontinuation.
questions.strategy: Look for the option that tells the rest of the team. Undocumented discontinuation is invisible.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Polarity is positive. No priority key word, so look for the single accurate option.
The record shows the history of care.
Continuing care that is no longer needed wastes time and the patient's energy.
Delays freeing the plan and leaves stale interventions in place.

elimination.verdict: That leaves C. Confirm, discontinue, and document so other nurses do not keep delivering finished care.

questions.stem: A nurse evaluates whether a patient met the outcome 'ambulate 50 feet with a walker twice daily by day three.' He walked 30 feet once on day two and 50 feet twice on day three. Which factor determines her conclusion?

options.text: Whether the patient was motivated to participate in the plan of care
options.rationale: Relevant and it comes after checking the outcome itself.

options.text: Whether the outcome was realistic and correctly written
options.rationale: An outcome that was never achievable reads as failed care when it was failed planning.

options.text: Whether other nurses followed the plan as it was originally written
options.rationale: Worth knowing later and not the first check.

options.text: Whether the interventions were documented
options.rationale: Documentation does not explain why the outcome was missed.

questions.takeaway: Run SMART on the outcome before blaming the plan. SMART outcomes are Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, and Time-bound. Measurable and time-bound are what make evaluation possible later.
questions.strategy: When an outcome fails, suspect the outcome before you suspect the care.

strategies: Negative polarity
Priority key word

steps.detail: Key word: first. More than one option may be true, so you are ranking them.
Documentation does not explain why the outcome was missed.
Worth knowing later and not the first check.
Relevant and it comes after checking the outcome itself.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B. An outcome that was never achievable reads as failed care when it was failed planning.

questions.concept: SMART outcomes are Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, and Time-bound. Measurable and time-bound are what make evaluation possible later.

questions.stem: A patient's outcome for pain control has not been met after three days. His pain remains 7 of 10 and he tells the nurse he is afraid of becoming addicted to the oxycodone. Which action does she take?

options.text: Ask the provider to change to a non-opioid analgesic
options.rationale: May be reasonable eventually and it does not address the fear driving the refusal.

options.text: Revise the plan to address the fear, then reassess the pain outcome
options.rationale: The new data reveals a different problem. Address the cause before repeating the intervention.

options.text: Continue the current plan and re-evaluate in another three days
options.rationale: Ignores the reason the outcome was missed.

options.text: Document that the patient is noncompliant with pain management
options.rationale: A label that hides a treatable fear.

questions.takeaway: When an outcome is missed, look for the new data before you repeat the intervention.
questions.strategy: An unmet outcome with a newly discovered cause means revise the plan, not repeat it.

strategies: Negative polarity

steps.detail: No priority key word, so look for the single accurate option.
A label that hides a treatable fear.
Ignores the reason the outcome was missed.
May be reasonable eventually and it does not address the fear driving the refusal.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B. The new data reveals a different problem.

questions.stem: A nurse must evaluate four outcomes: pain control at 3 of 10, saturation above 92%, an independent dressing change, and understanding of a new medication. Which evaluative measures fit these outcomes? Select all that apply.

options.text: Ask the patient to rate his pain against the stated target
options.rationale: Pain is subjective and the patient is the source, compared against the number in the outcome.

options.text: Observe a return demonstration of the dressing change
options.rationale: The only way to evaluate a psychomotor skill.

options.text: Measure the oxygen saturation
options.rationale: A measurable physiological outcome.

options.text: Ask the patient to explain the medication in his own words
options.rationale: Teach-back evaluates understanding rather than confirming delivery.

options.text: Document that all four outcomes were addressed during the shift
options.rationale: Records that the work occurred, not whether any outcome was met.

questions.takeaway: Match the method to the outcome: report for subjective, demonstration for skills, measurement for physiological, teach-back for understanding. Teach-back asks the patient to explain the plan in their own words. It confirms understanding rather than confirming that teaching was delivered.
questions.strategy: The wrong option measures the nurse's activity. Evaluation measures the patient.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Four outcomes, four appropriate methods.
Documenting delivery is not evaluation.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, and D are selected.

questions.concept: Teach-back asks the patient to explain the plan in their own words. It confirms understanding rather than confirming that teaching was delivered.

questions.stem: A nurse inspects a sacral pressure injury during morning care, finding non-blanching redness, and concludes it is improving. Which statement explains why this conclusion is premature?

options.text: One observation cannot establish a trend, and non-blanching redness is not resolving
options.rationale: Evaluation compares against the outcome over time. A single look at a stage 1 injury that still does not blanch shows no healing.

options.text: Wound evaluation requires measurement rather than inspection alone
options.rationale: Measurement adds precision and the flaw here is drawing a conclusion from one point in time.

options.text: Redness is expected after repositioning and should be reassessed in an hour
options.rationale: Blanchable redness would be. Non-blanching redness is the defining feature of a stage 1 injury.

options.text: Wound evaluation belongs to the wound care specialist
options.rationale: Nurses assess and evaluate skin. Referral supplements that rather than replacing it.

questions.takeaway: Non-blanching redness is the injury, not a normal pressure response. One observation is not a trend.
questions.strategy: One distractor is technically reasonable and misses the real flaw. One confuses blanching with non-blanching.

strategies: Eliminate absolutes

steps.detail: Non-blanching, on a single observation.
Adds precision, not a trend.
One misreads blanching, one gives away nursing scope.

elimination.verdict: That leaves the absence of a trend.

questions.stem: A nurse evaluates the outcome 'patient will use the incentive spirometer ten times hourly while awake.' He has used it twice in four hours and his saturation has fallen from 96% to 92%. Which action does she take?

options.text: Request an order for a sedative so he rests more
options.rationale: Sedation worsens atelectasis rather than helping it.

options.text: Discontinue the intervention as ineffective and select a different approach
options.rationale: The intervention is appropriate. The dose is not.

options.text: Document that the patient is nonadherent with the prescribed intervention
options.rationale: Nothing in the stem suggests he refused. Labeling replaces problem solving.

options.text: Increase the frequency of coughing and deep breathing and add positioning
options.rationale: Adjusting frequency based on the patient's actual response is a standard revision.

questions.takeaway: Revision often means changing the frequency rather than abandoning the intervention.
questions.strategy: Before discarding an intervention, ask whether it was simply not done often enough.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Polarity is positive. No priority key word, so look for the single accurate option.
Nothing in the stem suggests he refused.
Sedation worsens atelectasis rather than helping it.
The intervention is appropriate.

elimination.verdict: That leaves D. Adjusting frequency based on the patient's actual response is a standard revision.

questions.stem: A nurse evaluates the outcome 'patient will verbalize three signs of hypoglycemia before discharge' and writes: 'Hypoglycemia teaching completed at 1400.' Which problem does this entry contain?

options.text: It records the nurse's action rather than the patient's achievement
options.rationale: The outcome named three signs the patient would verbalize. The entry proves teaching happened and says nothing about whether he learned.

options.text: It omits the patient's emotional response to the teaching session
options.rationale: Affective response is worth noting and is not what this outcome measured.

options.text: It should name the teaching materials and method used
options.rationale: Adds detail about the nurse's activity, which is already the wrong subject.

options.text: It gives a time without naming who delivered the teaching
options.rationale: Attribution matters for the record and does not address whether the outcome was met.

questions.takeaway: Evaluation documents the patient's achievement against the outcome, not the nurse's activity.
questions.strategy: Two distractors ask for more detail in the same wrong subject. Ask who the sentence is about.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The patient will verbalize three signs.
Teaching completed at 1400.
More detail about the nurse is still about the nurse.

elimination.verdict: That leaves documenting the action rather than the outcome.

questions.stem: Highlight the findings that provide data for evaluating whether the outcomes were met.
questions.takeaway: Evaluation compares outcomes against expected outcomes. Data without a matching outcome is not evaluation data.
questions.strategy: Two findings here are real observations with nothing in the plan to compare them to. Evaluation needs both halves. Two findings are genuine observations with no matching outcome in the plan.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Four findings have a stated target.
Kindness and a visit are not outcome data.
Each usable finding names both the result and the target.

questions.nursesNote: 1600: Patient is 79, day three after hip repair. Plan of care outcomes: ambulate 50 feet with a walker by day three; report pain of 3 or less within 60 minutes of analgesia; demonstrate independent dressing change before discharge; maintain intact skin. Today she ambulated 20 feet with a walker and rated pain 8 out of 10 during the attempt. Demonstrated the dressing change correctly twice. Sacral skin remains reddened and non-blanching. States the staff have been kind. Daughter visited for two hours.

segments.text: Ambulated 20 feet with a walker against an outcome of 50 feet by day three
segments.rationale: A measurable result compared against a measurable outcome, which is what evaluation requires.

segments.text: Rates pain 8 out of 10 during the attempt against an outcome of 3 or less
segments.rationale: Directly comparable to the written outcome and it explains why the mobility outcome was not reached.

segments.text: Demonstrated the dressing change correctly twice
segments.rationale: Return demonstration against an outcome of independent wound care.

segments.text: States she feels the staff have been kind
segments.rationale: Meaningful feedback about her experience and not data about any written outcome.

segments.text: Daughter visited for two hours
segments.rationale: Not connected to any outcome in the plan.

segments.text: Sacral skin remains reddened and non-blanching against an outcome of intact skin
segments.rationale: A measurable finding compared against a written outcome.

questions.caseTitle: Evaluating and revising the plan

questions.stem: For each outcome, determine whether it was MET, PARTIALLY MET, or NOT MET.
questions.takeaway: Met, partially met, or not met, with the data that supports the conclusion.
questions.strategy: Partially met exists so that progress is recorded rather than discarded. Twenty feet is not nothing.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Compare each result to its target
steps.detail: Every outcome has a number or a demonstration.
Ambulation moved toward the target without reaching it.
Non-blanching redness means not intact.

elimination.verdict: One met, one partially met, two not met.

rows.text: Ambulate 50 feet with a walker by day three
rows.rationale: She ambulated 20 feet, so progress occurred and the target was not reached. Partially met is the option students skip.

rows.text: Report pain of 3 or less within 60 minutes of analgesia
rows.rationale: She rated 8 out of 10 during the attempt, which is well above the target.

rows.text: Demonstrate independent dressing change before discharge
rows.rationale: Return demonstration performed correctly twice, which is the evidence the outcome specified.

rows.text: Maintain intact skin
rows.rationale: Non-blanching redness is a stage 1 pressure injury, so the skin has not remained intact.

questions.caseTitle: Evaluating and revising the plan

questions.stem: Complete the sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.takeaway: When outcomes are not fully met: reassess, reconsider the diagnosis or priority, adjust the outcome or timeframe, and select new interventions.
questions.strategy: Two outcomes failed and one caused the other. Find the upstream problem before revising the downstream plan.

strategies: Assessment before intervention

steps.detail: Pain and mobility both missed their targets.
The pain is why she stopped.
Extending the target or closing the plan.

elimination.verdict: Blank 1 is A and blank 2 is A.

questions.sentence: Before changing the mobility interventions, the nurse should first [[1]], because [[2]].

options.text: reconsider whether pain control is the actual barrier
options.rationale: When outcomes are not fully met the nurse reassesses for new or overlooked data and reconsiders whether the diagnosis or priority is still accurate. Pain at 8 out of 10 is why she stopped at 20 feet.

options.text: extend the ambulation target to day five
options.rationale: Adjusting the timeframe may follow, and doing it first treats the symptom rather than the cause.

options.text: record the outcome as not met and continue the current plan
options.rationale: Records the failure and changes nothing.

options.text: an unmet outcome may be caused by a different unresolved problem
options.rationale: The mobility outcome failed because the pain outcome failed, so revising the mobility interventions alone would not work.

options.text: outcomes should always be made easier when they are not met
options.rationale: Not the guidance, and it lowers the standard without finding the cause.

options.text: the plan should be closed once an outcome is not met
options.rationale: Evaluation data becomes new assessment data and the process loops.

questions.caseTitle: Evaluating and revising the plan

questions.stem: For each finding two days later, determine whether it reflects IMPROVEMENT, NO CHANGE, or DECLINE compared with day three, or whether it is a NEW FINDING not previously assessed.
questions.takeaway: Compare each finding against its own baseline. An outcome that was already met and remains met is unchanged, not improved.
questions.strategy: The dressing row is the discrimination. Still able is not the same as better, and recording it as improvement would misrepresent the plan. One outcome was already met and remains met. Consider whether that is improvement.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Four findings were recorded on day three.
The dressing change was correct then and now.
Mood was never assessed.

elimination.verdict: Three improved, one unchanged, one new finding.

questions.baseline: Day three: ambulated 20 feet, pain 8/10 during the attempt, dressing change demonstrated correctly, sacral skin non-blanching.

rows.text: Ambulated 55 feet with a walker
rows.rationale: Up from 20 feet, and beyond the original target.

rows.text: Rates pain 3 out of 10 during ambulation with scheduled analgesia
rows.rationale: Down from 8, which is why she walked further.

rows.text: Sacral skin blanches on pressure
rows.rationale: The stage 1 injury has resolved with pressure relief.

rows.text: Performs the dressing change independently
rows.rationale: She demonstrated it correctly on day three as well, so the outcome remains met rather than having improved further.

rows.text: Reports feeling low and tearful about going home alone
rows.rationale: Mood and her feelings about discharge were not assessed on day three, so there is no baseline. It requires assessment and may affect the discharge plan.

questions.caseTitle: Evaluating and revising the plan

questions.stem: Two of the four outcomes were not met. Which 2 actions does the nurse take?
questions.takeaway: Reassess, reconsider the diagnosis, adjust the outcome or timeframe, then select new interventions.
questions.strategy: Exactly two are requested. Four wrong options lower the standard, close the plan, or repeat what failed.

steps.detail: Mobility and pain, with one likely causing the other.
Discontinuing and replacing.
Neither responds to the data.

options.text: Reassess for new or overlooked data before changing any intervention
options.rationale: And the reported pain is the kind of data that may have been missed.

options.text: Reconsider whether pain, rather than mobility, is now the priority problem
options.rationale: If pain is the barrier the priority diagnosis may need to change before the interventions do.

options.text: Discontinue the mobility outcome entirely
options.rationale: Removes a legitimate goal rather than addressing why it was not reached.

options.text: Replace the outcome with one she has already achieved
options.rationale: Lowers the standard to match the result.

options.text: Record both outcomes as not met and close the plan

options.text: Continue the current interventions unchanged for another 48 hours
options.rationale: Repeats an approach that has already failed twice.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence by selecting from the choices below.

The outcome said intact.

questions.sentence: For the dressing change outcome the nurse records [[1]], and for the skin outcome she records [[2]].

questions.stem: A nurse has twice paged the provider about a patient whose blood pressure has fallen from 128/74 to 88/52 over four hours and who is now increasingly drowsy. Neither page was returned. Which tool does she use next?

options.text: The five rights of delegation
options.rationale: Belongs to delegation.

options.text: TeamSTEPPS
options.rationale: The broader teamwork framework CUS belongs to, with pillars of communication, team leadership, situation monitoring, and mutual support.

options.text: SBAR
options.rationale: The right tool for the first call and the wrong one for the third. Repeating a report that has already failed changes nothing.

options.text: CUS
options.rationale: Graded escalation language: I am concerned, I am uncomfortable, this is a safety issue. Each step raises the stakes explicitly.

questions.takeaway: SBAR reports. CUS escalates. SBAR structures a report: Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation. The recommendation is the part most often dropped. CUS escalates a concern with graded language: I am Concerned, I am Uncomfortable, this is a Safety issue. SBAR reports; CUS escalates when reporting has failed.

steps.detail: Two reports have already failed.
Repeating the same tool changes nothing.
A framework, not a moment-to-moment tool.
Wrong domain.

questions.stem: A manager introduces a new fall prevention protocol written entirely by the leadership team and circulated by email. Six weeks later an audit shows it is rarely followed, although staff report they are aware of it. Which factor most likely explains this?

options.text: The protocol was too short a document to be taken seriously by staff
options.rationale: Length does not determine adoption.

options.text: Nurses on the unit lack the training to follow it
options.rationale: Nothing in the stem suggests a knowledge gap, and assuming one locates the failure in the staff.

options.text: Audits are unreliable measures of what actually happens in practice
options.rationale: An audit finding is data, not an explanation to dismiss.

options.text: The nurses delivering the care did not participate in writing it
options.rationale: Shared governance exists because staff follow protocols they helped create, and adoption falls when they do not.

questions.takeaway: Shared decision-making is why protocols get followed. Adoption follows participation. Shared governance means the nurses who deliver care participate in the decisions that govern it, which is why protocols they helped write get followed.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Leadership alone.
Length and audit reliability.
No knowledge gap described.

elimination.verdict: That leaves D: shared governance exists because staff follow protocols they helped create, and adoption falls when they do not.

questions.concept: Shared governance means the nurses who deliver care participate in the decisions that govern it, which is why protocols they helped write get followed.

questions.stem: A nurse plans to delegate vital signs on a stable patient to assistive personnel so she can complete an admission assessment. She wants the delegation to be safe and defensible. Place the steps of delegation in the correct order, from FIRST to LAST.

options.text: Determine whether the task is appropriate to delegate

questions.stem: The nurse is preparing to call the provider about a postoperative patient whose condition has changed over the past four hours. She reviews her findings and must decide what to lead with. Highlight the three highest priority findings to emphasize to the provider.

segments.text: Blood pressure has fallen from 122/74 to 88/52 over four hours
segments.rationale: A downward trend in perfusion pressure, and trends outrank single values.

segments.text: Patient reports the room is too warm
segments.rationale: A comfort issue, not a priority to report.

segments.rationale: Compensatory tachycardia accompanying the falling pressure, and the two together suggest hypovolemia.

segments.rationale: Old, dried, and small. Expected postoperatively.

segments.text: Patient is increasingly difficult to rouse
segments.rationale: A change in level of consciousness, and altered mentation with falling pressure signals decompensation.

segments.text: Patient has not had a bowel movement since surgery two days ago
segments.rationale: Worth addressing and not among the three highest priorities.

segments.rationale: Not a clinical finding.
