elimination.verdict: Three rows are RN only, one is LPN/LVN, and two are assistive personnel.

rows.text: Initial assessment of the patient admitted at 0300
rows.rationale: The initial assessment establishes the baseline others judge against and cannot be delegated.

rows.text: Vital signs on bed 12, day two after appendectomy and afebrile
rows.rationale: Routine data collection on a stable patient with a predictable outcome.

rows.text: Ongoing assessment of bed 9, whose pressure is falling
rows.rationale: An unstable patient with an unpredictable outcome stays with the RN however routine the task appears.

rows.text: Assisting bed 17 to shower while on contact precautions
rows.rationale: Precautions change the PPE worn, not who may provide hygiene care.

rows.text: Discharge teaching on a new anticoagulant for bed 21
rows.rationale: Teaching is in the RN scope. The LPN may reinforce teaching already begun; initiating it is not delegable.

rows.text: Dressing change on bed 12 according to protocol
rows.rationale: The LPN assists with implementation of defined plans for physiologically stable patients with predictable conditions.

questions.takeaway: Compare each finding against its own baseline. Two findings here have none, and one of them is a delegation failure. The five rights of delegation are the right task, right circumstance, right person, right directions and communication, and right supervision and evaluation.
questions.strategy: The two rows without a baseline are the ones worth noticing: an unassessed symptom and an incomplete delegation. One new finding concerns the nurse's own delegation rather than the patient.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Three items were recorded at handover.
Four rows compare; two do not.
A delegation without a reporting threshold is incomplete.

rows.text: Bed 9: blood pressure 112/68 after intravenous fluids

rows.text: Bed 9: alert and oriented

questions.stem: A competent 67-year-old refuses his prescribed antihypertensive, saying it makes him dizzy on standing. His blood pressure remains elevated and he had a documented orthostatic drop yesterday. Which nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Determine the reason for the refusal
options.rationale: Often uncovers a side effect or misunderstanding that can be resolved.

options.text: Ensure the patient understands the risks of not taking it
options.rationale: A refusal is only informed if the patient knows what refusing costs.

options.text: Conceal the medication in food so the patient receives the dose
options.rationale: Removes consent entirely and is never acceptable, however compassionate the intent.

options.text: Notify the health care provider
options.rationale: So the plan can be reconsidered.

options.text: Document that the patient is noncompliant
options.rationale: Noncompliant is a judgment. Documentation must be factual: what was refused and what the patient said.

options.text: Document the refusal and the patient's stated reason
options.rationale: The factual entry that belongs in the record.

questions.takeaway: Confirm understanding, notify the provider, and document factually. Not to change the patient's mind.
questions.strategy: Two wrong options here are the compassionate violation and the judgmental charting entry. Both recur across legal and ethical material.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A competent patient refusing.
Concealment removes consent.
Noncompliant is a judgment, not a fact.

elimination.verdict: A, B, D, and F are selected.

questions.stem: A nurse educator teaches the framework used to reason through difficult decisions in patient care, asking students to distinguish it from the nursing process, the rights of delegation, and handoff tools. Which set names the ethical principles?

options.text: Right task, right circumstance, right person, right directions, right supervision
options.rationale: The five rights of delegation.

options.text: Autonomy, beneficence, nonmaleficence, justice, and fidelity
options.rationale: The five principles, with fidelity meaning keeping promises and commitments.

options.text: Assessment, diagnosis, planning, implementation, evaluation
options.rationale: The nursing process.

options.text: Situation, background, assessment, and recommendation, in that order
options.rationale: SBAR is a handoff structure for communicating about a patient, not a set of ethical principles.

questions.takeaway: Autonomy, beneficence, nonmaleficence, justice, fidelity. The nursing process has five steps in order: assessment, diagnosis, planning, implementation, evaluation. Each depends on the one before it.
questions.strategy: Distractors here are drawn from other five-part frameworks. Match the set to the name in the stem.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The ethical principles specifically.
The nursing process.
Delegation.
A handoff tool.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B: the five principles, with fidelity meaning keeping promises and commitments.

questions.concept: The LEARN model structures a cross-cultural encounter: Listen to the patient's perception, Explain your own, Acknowledge differences, Recommend a plan, Negotiate agreement. The nursing process has five steps in order: assessment, diagnosis, planning, implementation, evaluation. Each depends on the one before it.

questions.stem: A competent 78-year-old with a written advance directive declining intubation develops a saturation of 84% and rising carbon dioxide. His daughter demands intubation. Which ethical principle guides the nurse?

options.text: Beneficence
options.rationale: The most dangerous distractor in ethics. Doing what you believe is good for a competent person who has refused it is not beneficence, it is a violation of autonomy.

options.text: Autonomy
options.rationale: The competent patient decides. Confirming understanding first is what makes it autonomy rather than abandonment.

options.text: Fidelity
options.rationale: Keeping promises and commitments, which is not what is here.

options.text: Justice
options.rationale: Concerns fair distribution of resources, and no allocation question is present.

questions.takeaway: Beneficence never overrides autonomy for a competent patient. Autonomy is the patient's right to make their own decisions about their care, including decisions the team disagrees with.
questions.strategy: When a competent patient has stated a wish, autonomy usually wins. Look for the option that names the patient's authority.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Competent, informed, understanding confirmed.
Overriding an informed refusal is not doing good.
No allocation and no promise are in play.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B: the competent patient decides.

questions.concept: Autonomy is the patient's right to make their own decisions about their care, including decisions the team disagrees with.

questions.stem: A care team disagrees with a family about continuing aggressive treatment for a patient with an advance directive requesting comfort measures. Place the following actions in the correct order the nurse should take to work toward resolution, from FIRST to LAST.

options.text: Gather all relevant clinical, social, and spiritual information about the situation
options.rationale: You cannot reason about a situation you have not described. Gathering comes after recognizing there is an ethical question and before values are sorted.

options.text: Recognize that the situation involves an ethical problem, not just a clinical one
options.rationale: Nothing else can happen until the problem is ethical. Treated as purely clinical, the disagreement gets managed rather than resolved.

options.text: Clarify the values and key ethical principles and relationships involved
options.rationale: With the facts assembled, name whose values are in play and which principles collide. Here autonomy and beneficence pull against each other.

options.text: List the possible actions that could be taken to address the disagreement
options.rationale: Options are generated only after the values are clear, otherwise you are choosing between actions without knowing what you are optimizing for.

options.text: Develop and implement a plan that addresses the identified problem
options.rationale: Acting comes last, and it addresses the problem as defined rather than the surface disagreement.

questions.takeaway: Recognize it as ethical, gather information, clarify values, list options, then act. An ethical dilemma involves two defensible positions grounded in different principles, where nobody is behaving badly and the right action is contested. An advance directive documents a patient's own decisions about future care and speaks for them when they cannot. Family preference does not override it.
questions.strategy: Ordered-response items reward finding the first and last step before sorting the middle. Recognition almost always opens a process and implementation almost always closes it.

strategies: Assessment before intervention

steps.detail: Recognizing the problem as ethical must precede everything.
Implementing a plan is the only action step.
Information, then values, then options. Each depends on the one before it.

elimination.verdict: B, A, C, D, E.

questions.concept: An ethical dilemma involves two defensible positions grounded in different principles, where nobody is behaving badly and the right action is contested. An advance directive documents a patient's own decisions about future care and speaks for them when they cannot. Family preference does not override it.

questions.stem: A nurse tells a colleague she disagrees with one provision of the profession's code of ethics and does not consider it binding on her. Her colleague explains what a code of ethics is and what its four key principles are. Which statement is accurate?

options.text: It sets shared obligations that hold whether or not a member agrees
options.rationale: A code binds by membership in the profession. Individual disagreement is a reason to work to change it, not to opt out.

options.text: It carries the force of law and can be enforced in court
options.rationale: Codes inform legal standards without being statutes. This overstates their status.

options.text: It describes ideals to aspire to rather than obligations
options.rationale: Understates it. Provisions are expectations, not aspirations.

options.text: It applies to those in formal nursing roles rather than students
options.rationale: Students practicing nursing are held to it.

questions.takeaway: A professional code binds every member. Disagreement is grounds to seek change, not exemption.
questions.strategy: One distractor overstates the code's force, one understates it, one narrows who it covers.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Shared obligations of membership.
A code is not a statute.
One weakens it, one narrows it.

elimination.verdict: That leaves obligations binding regardless of agreement.

questions.concept: A code of ethics is a set of guiding principles all members of a profession accept. The Code of Ethics for Nursing rests on advocacy, responsibility, accountability, and confidentiality.

questions.scenario: A nurse works a medical unit shift and takes several actions during the day.
questions.stem: A nurse works a shift on a medical unit and takes several actions: repositioning a patient, withholding a medication, honoring a refusal, and allocating the last available sitter. Her educator asks her to identify the principle behind each. For each nursing action, indicate which ethical principle it BEST demonstrates.

rows.text: Repositions a patient every two hours to prevent skin breakdown
rows.rationale: An action taken to produce benefit.

rows.text: Holds a scheduled antihypertensive when the systolic pressure is 84
rows.rationale: Refraining in order to prevent foreseeable harm.

rows.text: Honors a competent patient's refusal of a bath after confirming she understands
rows.rationale: The patient decides, and understanding was confirmed.

rows.text: Assigns the last available one-to-one sitter to the patient at highest fall risk
rows.rationale: A scarce resource allocated on need rather than preference.

rows.text: Provides pain medication before a painful dressing change
rows.rationale: An action taken to produce benefit.

rows.text: Stops an infusion when the site shows signs of infiltration
rows.rationale: Stopping to prevent tissue injury.

questions.takeaway: Acting to help is beneficence. Refraining to prevent injury is nonmaleficence. The patient deciding is autonomy. Scarcity is justice. Autonomy is the patient's right to make their own decisions about their care, including decisions the team disagrees with. Nonmaleficence is the duty to avoid causing harm. Beneficence is the duty to act for the patient's benefit.
questions.strategy: Work each row by asking whether the nurse added something, withheld something, deferred to the patient, or divided a resource.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Provides and repositions are actions; holds and stops are refraining.
One sitter for several candidates is allocation.
Honoring a refusal is the patient deciding.

elimination.verdict: Two beneficence, two nonmaleficence, one autonomy, one justice.

questions.concept: Autonomy is the patient's right to make their own decisions about their care, including decisions the team disagrees with. Nonmaleficence is the duty to avoid causing harm. Beneficence is the duty to act for the patient's benefit.

questions.stem: A competent 62-year-old with a hemoglobin of 7.1 g/dL declines a transfusion his provider recommends. He states he understands he may become weaker. His son asks the nurse to persuade him. Which action is correct?

options.text: Explain the risks of untreated anemia to him again with his son present
options.rationale: Reasonable education used as leverage. He has already stated he understands he may become weaker.

options.text: Support him in stating his own wishes and record whom he designates
options.rationale: He is competent and has decided. The nursing role is to protect his voice and make sure the record reflects it.

options.text: Explain to the son that the decision is his father's to make
options.rationale: Accurate and it closes the conversation with the son rather than supporting the patient with him.

options.text: Arrange an ethics consultation given the disagreement
options.rationale: A competent patient's refusal is not an ethical dilemma. There are not two defensible positions here.

questions.takeaway: A competent refusal is not a dilemma. Protect his voice and document who speaks for him.
questions.strategy: Three options treat a settled decision as still open. Ask whether anything is actually in question.

strategies: Patient-centered option

steps.detail: Competent, informed, decided.
He has already demonstrated understanding.

steps.action: Cut the son-focused and ethics options
steps.detail: Neither supports him directly.

elimination.verdict: That leaves supporting his expression and documenting his designee.

questions.stem: A patient tells the nurse he does not want his adult daughter informed of his diagnosis, although she telephones the unit daily and is listed as his next of kin. He is alert and oriented. Which nursing action reflects the four principles of the nursing code of ethics?

options.text: Tell the daughter, since she is listed as his next of kin on the record
options.rationale: Next of kin identifies who is contacted in an emergency and does not authorize disclosure against a competent patient's wishes.

options.text: Encourage him to reconsider, since family involvement usually improves outcomes
options.rationale: Pressures a competent patient toward the nurse's preference rather than supporting his own decision.

options.text: Honor his decision, tell him what he wants his daughter to be told, and inform the team
options.rationale: Advocacy and confidentiality together. A competent patient decides who receives his health information, and the team needs to know so nobody discloses it by accident.

options.text: Tell the daughter only that her father is unwell without naming the diagnosis
options.rationale: Partial disclosure is still disclosure, and he has not authorized any of it.

questions.takeaway: The Code of Ethics for Nursing rests on four principles: advocacy, responsibility, accountability, and confidentiality. A competent patient decides who receives his information.
questions.strategy: Next of kin is a contact designation, not an authorization. Options that treat it as permission to disclose are the pattern here.

strategies: Patient-centered option

steps.detail: Alert and oriented, so the decision is his.
Next of kin is a contact, not an authorization.
Pressures him toward the nurse's preference.
Partial disclosure is still disclosure.

elimination.verdict: That leaves C: honor the decision, agree what may be shared, and tell the team so nobody discloses it inadvertently.

questions.concept: The Code of Ethics for Nursing rests on advocacy, responsibility, accountability, and confidentiality. All members of a profession accept it.

questions.stem: A nurse knows a patient's pain is undertreated, has raised it twice, and has been told the prescriber will not change the order. She continues to care for him each shift. Which term describes what she is experiencing?

options.text: A breach of fidelity
options.rationale: Fidelity concerns keeping commitments; nothing here describes a promise broken.

options.text: A collaborative problem
options.rationale: A clinical category rather than a description of her experience.

options.text: An ethical dilemma
options.rationale: A dilemma means two defensible positions. Here she knows what is right and cannot deliver it.

options.text: Moral distress
options.rationale: Knowing the right action and being constrained from taking it is the definition, and repeated exposure is what makes it accumulate.

questions.takeaway: A dilemma is not knowing which action is right. Moral distress is knowing and being prevented.
questions.strategy: Ask whether she is uncertain or constrained. Uncertainty is a dilemma; constraint is distress.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Not clarity, but the ability to act.
She is not uncertain about the right action.
One is a clinical category, one is a different principle.

elimination.verdict: That leaves D: moral distress.

questions.stem: A nurse and a colleague disagree about telling a patient something his family wants withheld. One argues from her own upbringing about honesty, the other from the profession's agreed standards. Which statement distinguishes morals from ethics?

options.text: Morals are personal judgments; ethics studies how they are determined
options.rationale: Morals are individually held. Ethics is the systematic study of how such judgments are determined and justified.

options.text: Morals are professional standards; ethics are personal judgments
options.rationale: Reverses the two terms.

options.text: Morals are legally binding; ethics are voluntary guidelines
options.rationale: Neither term describes a legal obligation.

options.text: Morals apply at work; ethics apply in private life
options.rationale: Setting does not distinguish them.

questions.takeaway: Morals are the judgments. Ethics is the reasoning behind them, and also a profession's agreed standards.
questions.strategy: Both senses of ethics appear on exams. If an option makes ethics purely legal or purely personal, it is wrong.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
Global or umbrella option

steps.detail: The question asks how the two differ.
Reverses the two terms.
Neither term describes a legal obligation.
Setting does not distinguish them.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A: morals are individually held.

questions.stem: A nurse reviews the chart of a patient with advanced illness whose family disagrees with the plan of care. The record contains laboratory values, routine care entries, a written directive, and notes about the disagreement. Highlight the findings that indicate an ethical problem rather than a purely clinical one.

segments.text: Patient has a written advance directive requesting comfort measures only
segments.rationale: A documented decision. On its own it is a clinical fact to follow, not a conflict.

segments.text: Adult daughter has asked staff to continue aggressive treatment against the directive
segments.rationale: Two defensible positions grounded in different principles, autonomy and beneficence.

segments.text: Hemoglobin is 9.2 g/dL
segments.rationale: A laboratory value requiring clinical judgment, not ethical reasoning.

segments.text: A staff nurse has told the patient's family that the directive can be ignored if they insist
segments.rationale: Misinformation that undermines the patient's documented autonomy.

segments.text: Patient received scheduled analgesia at 0800
segments.rationale: Routine care.

segments.text: Team members disagree about whether the patient's quality of life justifies further treatment
segments.rationale: Quality of life is contested because it is culturally shaped, individually defined, and largely unmeasurable.

segments.text: Patient is unresponsive and cannot participate in the discussion
segments.rationale: A clinical fact that raises the stakes and is not itself the ethical problem.

questions.takeaway: Recognizing that a situation involves an ethical problem is the first step in working toward resolution.
questions.strategy: An ethical problem exists where defensible positions conflict or where someone's documented autonomy is at risk. A difficult clinical fact is not the same thing. Several findings are clinically significant without being ethical problems. Highlight only the ethical ones.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Two parties wanting different things on principled grounds.
Misinformation about a directive threatens the patient's decision.
Laboratory values and routine care are clinical, not ethical.

elimination.verdict: Highlight s2, s4, and s6.

questions.stem: Two patients need the unit's only negative-pressure room. One has suspected tuberculosis with a three-week cough and a temperature of 38.1 C. The other is neutropenic with a white cell count of 0.6. Which ethical principle guides the decision?

options.text: Fidelity
options.rationale: Fidelity is keeping promises and commitments, which is not what a decision about allocating a scarce room turns on.

options.text: Beneficence
options.rationale: Would describe doing good for one patient, but the question is how to choose between two.

options.text: Justice
options.rationale: Fairness in the distribution of a scarce resource, allocated on clinical risk rather than on who advocated loudest.

options.text: Autonomy
options.rationale: Would apply if a patient were making a decision, and neither is.

questions.takeaway: Justice questions almost always involve scarcity. One bed, one room, limited staff, triage.
questions.strategy: Look for two claimants and one resource. That structure names the principle before you read the options.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Two patients, one room.
The question is allocation, not care of one.
No promise and no patient decision.

elimination.verdict: That leaves C: fairness in the distribution of a scarce resource, allocated on clinical risk rather than on who advocated loudest.

questions.stem: A family asks the nurse not to tell a patient about a new cancer diagnosis. The patient has asked the nurse three times what the tests showed. What is the nurse's BEST action?

options.text: Tell him what the tests showed, since he has asked three times
options.rationale: Honors his autonomy and takes on a disclosure decision that is not the nurse's to make alone.

options.text: Tell him the provider will discuss the results with him shortly
options.rationale: True as far as it goes, and it deflects a third request without addressing why he is not being told.

options.text: Agree to the family's request while continuing to support him
options.rationale: Takes a side without exploring it, and leaves him asking a question nobody will answer.

options.text: Explore what is behind the family's request and involve the provider
options.rationale: The request usually rests on a fear worth hearing, and disclosure is the provider's to make. This keeps his question alive without going around either party.

questions.takeaway: Explore the request, keep his question alive, and route disclosure to the provider.
questions.strategy: One option over-steps, one deflects, one concedes. Each is a real response nurses give.

strategies: Priority key word

steps.detail: He has asked three times.
Not the nurse's decision alone.
Both leave his question unanswered.

elimination.verdict: That leaves exploring the concerns and notifying the provider.

questions.stem: Four staff actions from the past week come up at a unit meeting: an error reported immediately, a workstation logged out before leaving the room, a patient's wishes relayed to a provider despite family objection, and a stated return time kept exactly. Match each nursing action with the ethical or legal term it BEST demonstrates. Each term is used only once.

items.text: A nurse discovers a medication error, immediately notifies the provider and manager, and completes an occurrence report
items.rationale: Accountability is answering for your own actions. Owning the error and reporting it is the definition in practice.

items.text: A nurse steps away from a shared workstation and logs out of the record before administering a medication in another room
items.rationale: Protecting information from those without a need to know. An open record under your login exposes data and attributes anything done next to you.

items.text: A nurse contacts the primary provider to relay a patient's wish for comfort care despite family objections
items.rationale: Advocacy promotes care that reflects the patient's wishes. It points outward at the patient, even when others disagree.

items.text: A nurse says, "I will be back in 20 minutes with your next dose," and returns at the stated time
items.rationale: Responsibility is following through on what you accepted. Keeping a stated commitment is the everyday form of it.

questions.takeaway: Accountability points back at you, responsibility points at the work, advocacy points at the patient, confidentiality protects the information.
questions.strategy: Matching items are answered by direction. Ask where each action points before reaching for a definition. Two of these terms are frequently confused. Decide whether the action answers for the past or delivers on the present.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Backward at yourself, at the work, outward at the patient, or at the information.
Logging out is unambiguously confidentiality.
Each term is used once, so the last pairing is fixed by elimination.

questions.stem: The 0900 medications include metoprolol 50 mg orally. The patient's apical rate is 44, down from 62 this morning, and his blood pressure is 96/54. She withholds the dose and notifies the provider. Which principle does this demonstrate?

options.text: Nonmaleficence
options.rationale: The nurse refrained in order to prevent harm. A rate of 44 with a drug that slows the heart is foreseeable injury.

options.text: Fidelity, keeping promises and honoring commitments made
options.rationale: Keeping promises and commitments, which is not what is here.

options.text: Justice, the fair distribution of benefits and burdens
options.rationale: Fairness in allocation.

options.text: Autonomy, the patient's right to make his own decisions
options.rationale: The pair-mate and the trap. Beneficence is acting to do good; this nurse withheld an action.

questions.takeaway: Ask whether the nurse acted or refrained. Adding something is beneficence; withholding to prevent injury is nonmaleficence. Nonmaleficence is the duty to avoid causing harm. Beneficence is the duty to act for the patient's benefit.
questions.strategy: When both principles appear as options, the verb in the stem decides it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Withholds is the key word.
Beneficence requires an action taken.
Neither truth-telling nor allocation is present.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A: the nurse refrained in order to prevent harm.

questions.concept: Nonmaleficence is the duty to avoid causing harm. Beneficence is the duty to act for the patient's benefit.

questions.stem: A disagreement about the goals of care for a patient with advanced illness cannot be resolved between the team and the family. Both positions are defensible, no law has been broken, and the discussion has stalled after two meetings. Which resource does the nurse recommend?

options.text: The State Board of Nursing, which regulates licensure
options.rationale: Handles licensure and discipline and enforces the standard of care. Legal, not philosophical, and it is the trap worth understanding.

options.text: The charge nurse, who oversees the unit that shift
options.rationale: Manages the shift, not the ethical question.

options.text: The multidisciplinary ethics committee
options.rationale: The body that determines an ethical course of action when a dilemma arises in patient care. Multidisciplinary matters, because the point is several perspectives on one hard case.

options.text: Risk management, which reviews incidents and hazards
options.rationale: Prevents harm and financial loss from liability, and is problem-focused rather than values-focused.

questions.takeaway: Ethical course of action means the ethics committee. Discipline or licensure means the Board.
questions.strategy: Sort by what the body does. One writes standards, one advises on a case, one disciplines licensees, one manages liability.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: An unresolved values disagreement in patient care.
A staffing role.
Discipline and licensure.
Liability prevention.

elimination.verdict: That leaves C: the body that determines an ethical course of action when a dilemma arises in patient care.

questions.stem: A care team is struggling to agree on a plan for a patient with a severe chronic illness because members disagree about the patient's quality of life. Which statements help explain why consensus on this term is difficult to reach? Select all that apply.

options.text: Community and cultural values shape definitions of quality, and these values shift over time
options.rationale: Quality of life is socially constructed, so the standard itself moves between groups and across decades.

options.text: A person's individual life experiences influence how they personally define quality of life
options.rationale: Two people with identical function can rate their lives very differently based on what they have lived.

options.text: Elements such as meaningful work and family relationships are difficult to measure objectively
options.rationale: The components that matter most to people resist measurement, which is why teams cannot simply check them.

options.text: Whether a person is employed is the single objective measure that should determine quality of life
options.rationale: Reduces a contested multidimensional concept to one variable, and employment status says nothing about meaning.

options.text: Outcomes that cannot be easily quantified are difficult to evaluate using standard statistical methods
options.rationale: Unmeasurable outcomes cannot be compared across patients, which is part of why evidence does not settle the disagreement.

questions.takeaway: Quality of life is contested because it is culturally shaped, individually defined, and largely unmeasurable.
questions.strategy: The wrong option in a quality-of-life item is usually the one offering a single objective substitute for the whole concept. One option offers a simple measurable substitute for a complex concept. That is the distractor pattern here.

strategies: Eliminate absolutes

steps.detail: The question asks why consensus is hard, so correct options explain difficulty.
Single and should determine are both absolutes, and employment is not a proxy for meaning.

questions.stem: A home health nurse notes multiple bruises in various stages of healing on the head, abdomen, and posterior legs of a nonambulatory 8-month-old infant. The caregiver states the bruises are from the infant rolling off the couch a few times. What is the nurse's FIRST priority action?

options.text: Report the reasonable suspicion of abuse to the appropriate child protective authority
options.rationale: Nurses are mandated reporters. A nonambulatory infant cannot produce bruises in varied stages across those sites, so the explanation is not plausible and the threshold for reporting is met now.

options.text: Discuss the situation with a colleague for a second opinion before acting
options.rationale: Delays a mandated report. The standard is reasonable suspicion, not certainty.

options.text: Confront the caregiver about the inconsistency in the explanation he gave
options.rationale: Risks the child's safety by alerting a possible perpetrator, and it is not the nurse's role to investigate.

options.text: Document the findings in detail and complete a full physical assessment
options.rationale: Essential and not first. Documentation supports the report; it does not substitute for making it.

questions.takeaway: Mandated reporting requires reasonable suspicion, not proof, and it is not delayed for confirmation.
questions.strategy: The detail that decides this is nonambulatory. An infant who cannot move independently cannot self-inflict bruises in multiple stages across several body regions. Documentation is essential, but consider which action is legally mandated FIRST given a nonambulatory infant with these findings.

strategies: Priority key word

steps.detail: Key word FIRST, with a nonambulatory infant and an implausible explanation.

options.text: Failure to document the change in neurovascular assessment findings
options.rationale: Documentation is part of the standard of care, and an undocumented finding is invisible to everyone who follows.

options.text: Failure to notify the provider about a significant change in condition
options.rationale: The change required an order to act on, and the omission is the direct link to the harm.

options.text: Failure to provide discharge teaching about cast care
options.rationale: Not relevant to this injury. The patient is in traction and the harm occurred during the admission.

options.rationale: A reasonably prudent nurse recognizes pale, cold, insensate toes as neurovascular compromise.

options.text: Failure to complete an occurrence report for the other patient's emergency
options.rationale: Unrelated to this patient's harm and not a breach of duty toward him.

questions.takeaway: Breach of duty means conduct fell below what a reasonably prudent nurse would do, and it must connect to the harm. The standard of care is what a reasonable nurse with similar training would have done in similar circumstances. Not the best nurse, and not the nurse's own opinion.
questions.strategy: Two options here describe real nursing responsibilities that are not connected to this patient's injury. Relevance to the harm is what makes an omission a breach.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

Concerns a different patient.

options.text: Documenting care accurately, completely, and at the time it is provided
options.rationale: The record is the evidence of what was done, and contemporaneous accurate documentation is the strongest protection.

options.rationale: Omission does not remove the event and undermines the record.

questions.stem: A nurse is named in a malpractice claim after a patient was harmed. Her attorney explains that her conduct will be compared against a defined benchmark rather than against her own view of the situation or the best nurse on the unit. Against which standard is her conduct measured?

options.text: The nurse's own judgment about what was appropriate at the time she acted
options.rationale: Would make the standard whatever each nurse believed, which is no standard at all.

options.text: What a reasonably prudent nurse would do under similar circumstances
options.rationale: The skill and knowledge commonly exercised by nurses currently practicing, with both qualifiers.

options.text: What the most experienced nurse in the facility would have done in that situation
options.rationale: Raises the bar to an ideal that no one meets and that is not the legal test.

options.text: Whatever the facility policy manual specifies for that particular procedure
options.rationale: Policy is one input alongside law and professional organizations, not the whole standard.

questions.takeaway: Reasonably prudent, similar circumstances, same geographical area. Malpractice is professional negligence causing harm, judged against what a reasonable nurse with similar training would have done in similar circumstances. The standard of care is what a reasonable nurse with similar training would have done in similar circumstances. Not the best nurse, and not the nurse's own opinion.
questions.strategy: Options that raise the standard to perfection or lower it to personal judgment are both wrong. The test is an ordinary competent nurse.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The legal test for conduct.
An ideal rather than a reasonable nurse.
Policy is one input.
No objective standard.

questions.concept: Malpractice is professional negligence causing harm, judged against what a reasonable nurse with similar training would have done in similar circumstances. The standard of care is what a reasonable nurse with similar training would have done in similar circumstances. Not the best nurse, and not the nurse's own opinion.

questions.stem: Three reported events come to the risk committee: a patient burned by a heating pad left on too long, a patient discussed by name in a lift where another passenger recognized her, and a patient harmed by care the nurse should have known was substandard. Match each event with the term it BEST illustrates. Each term is used only once.

items.text: A patient is burned by a heating pad left on too long
items.rationale: A tort is a civil wrong: a wrongful act or omission of care made against a person or property. This is the standard example.

items.text: A nurse discusses a patient by name in a lift and another passenger recognizes her
items.rationale: A quasi-intentional tort. You did not mean to cause harm and you did, through the nature of the act itself.

items.text: A patient is harmed by care the nurse knew or should have known was substandard
items.rationale: An unintentional tort. Harm arises where the person inflicting it knew, or should have known, that the care fell below standard.

questions.takeaway: A tort is a civil wrong. Quasi-intentional means you did not mean harm and caused it. Unintentional means you knew or should have known the care was substandard.
questions.strategy: Sort by what the nurse knew. Harm through the nature of the act is quasi-intentional; harm you should have foreseen is unintentional. Two of these involve harm the nurse did not intend. What separates them is whether it was foreseeable.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Disclosure in a lift causes harm through the act itself.
Knew or should have known is the unintentional tort wording.
Each term is used once.

questions.concept: CUS escalates a concern with graded language: I am Concerned, I am Uncomfortable, this is a Safety issue. SBAR reports; CUS escalates when reporting has failed. A tort is a civil wrong. Quasi-intentional torts cause harm through the nature of the act. Unintentional torts arise where the person knew or should have known the care was substandard.

questions.stem: A nurse observes a colleague repeatedly documenting assessments she did not perform. She has raised it with the colleague directly and nothing has changed. The colleague tells her that reporting it would damage the unit. Which action is correct?

options.text: Report it through the appropriate channel, since falsified records are a patient safety issue
options.rationale: Documentation that assessments occurred when they did not means decisions are being made on invented data.

options.text: Raise it with the colleague once more, making clear it will be reported if it continues
options.rationale: She has already raised it directly and nothing changed. A further warning delays action on a safety problem.

options.text: Check whether other nurses have noticed the same pattern before reporting
options.rationale: Corroboration feels prudent and is how a concern becomes unit gossip while the practice continues.

options.text: Document her own observations of the colleague's practice in the patients' records
options.rationale: The medical record is for patient care, not for recording concerns about a colleague.

questions.takeaway: Falsified documentation is reported through the proper channel, not handled informally.
questions.strategy: Two distractors are reasonable-sounding delays. Ask what is happening to patients while she waits.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Direct conversation, no change.
Already attempted.
One delays, one misuses the record.

elimination.verdict: That leaves reporting through the appropriate channel.

questions.concept: Nurses have a duty to report unsafe or unethical practice. Raise it directly first, and escalate through the appropriate channel when it is not resolved.

questions.stem: An order reads heparin 25,000 units subcutaneously every 12 hours for a 70 kg patient. The usual prophylactic dose is 5,000 units. The prescriber is unavailable and the dose is due now. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Give the prophylactic 5,000 units, since that is the usual dose
options.rationale: Substitutes her own judgment for a prescription, which is prescribing.

options.text: Hold the dose and document that the prescriber was unavailable
options.rationale: Avoids the unsafe dose and leaves the patient without anticoagulation and the order unresolved.

options.text: Follow the chain of command to clarify before the dose is given
options.rationale: Five times the prophylactic dose is a discrepancy the nurse must resolve, and an unavailable prescriber escalates rather than excuses.

options.text: Administer it as written and monitor closely for bleeding
options.rationale: A signed order does not transfer accountability. Monitoring does not make an unsafe dose safe.

questions.takeaway: Question an unsafe order through the chain of command. Do not give it, change it, or simply hold it.
questions.strategy: One option prescribes, one abandons, one defers to the order. Only escalation resolves it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 25,000 against a usual 5,000.
That is prescribing.
One leaves it unresolved, one gives it anyway.

elimination.verdict: That leaves the chain of command.

questions.stem: A patient admitted with a hemoglobin of 6.4 g/dL has a written advance directive declining blood products. He is alert and oriented. His spouse tells the nurse he did not mean it and asks her to proceed with the transfusion. Which action is correct?

options.text: Withhold the transfusion based on the spouse's statement about his beliefs
options.rationale: Acts on an unverified report of the patient's wishes. A spouse does not automatically hold decision-making authority.

options.text: Gather more information, including whether a power of attorney or directive exists
options.rationale: Both extremes act before the facts are known. A documented advance directive or a health care power of attorney converts the spouse's claim into a legally binding one.

options.text: Administer the blood as ordered since the patient has not personally refused
options.rationale: Ignores credible evidence about the patient's values and treats silence as consent.

options.text: Contact the hospital ethics committee before taking any further action on the order
options.rationale: Appropriate later if a genuine conflict remains, and it is not the first step in a hemorrhage.

questions.takeaway: Verify decision-making authority before acting on a surrogate's report of what a patient would want. An advance directive documents a patient's own decisions about future care and speaks for them when they cannot. Family preference does not override it.
questions.strategy: When two options are opposite actions, the answer is often the one that establishes the facts first. Both poles are wrong for the same reason. More than one action may eventually be needed. Select the correct FIRST step.

strategies: Assessment before intervention

steps.detail: Key word FIRST. The patient cannot speak and the spouse is reporting.
Both act on an incomplete picture, in opposite directions.
A reasonable later step, not the first one in an emergency.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B: both extremes act before the facts are known.

questions.concept: An advance directive documents a patient's own decisions about future care and speaks for them when they cannot. Family preference does not override it.

questions.stem: A nurse gives metoprolol 50 mg to a patient whose apical rate is 48 without checking the hold parameter. He becomes symptomatic with a rate of 38 and requires transfer. Which legal concept does this illustrate?

options.text: A quasi-intentional tort
options.rationale: Covers acts such as breaching confidentiality, where harm was not intended but resulted from the nature of the act.

options.text: An intentional tort
options.rationale: Requires intent, which is absent.

options.text: Negligence only
options.rationale: Not wrong so much as imprecise. Negligence is the broad category, and when a licensed professional commits it in that role the specific term is malpractice.

options.text: Malpractice
options.rationale: Negligence committed by a professional acting in that role. Duty existed, the armband check was omitted, conduct fell below the standard, and harm followed.

questions.takeaway: Malpractice is the professional species of negligence. Name a licensed professional in the stem and the answer is malpractice. Negligence is failing to act as a reasonable nurse would in similar circumstances. Malpractice is professional negligence causing harm. Malpractice is professional negligence causing harm, judged against what a reasonable nurse with similar training would have done in similar circumstances.
questions.strategy: The standard is what a reasonably prudent nurse would do under similar circumstances in the same geographical area.

strategies: Favor qualifiers

steps.detail: A licensed nurse acting in that role, with harm resulting.
Correct but not the specific term.
Neither intent nor a quasi-intentional act is present.

elimination.verdict: That leaves D: negligence committed by a professional acting in that role.

questions.concept: Negligence is failing to act as a reasonable nurse would in similar circumstances. Malpractice is professional negligence causing harm. Malpractice is professional negligence causing harm, judged against what a reasonable nurse with similar training would have done in similar circumstances.

questions.stem: A nurse admits a 76-year-old for elective surgery and asks whether he has documented his wishes about future care. He says his daughter will decide if anything goes wrong, but has signed nothing. Which statements about advance directives are accurate? Select all that apply.

options.text: They allow a competent adult to state wishes about future care
options.rationale: The purpose of the document.

options.text: A health care power of attorney designates a person to make decisions if the patient cannot
options.rationale: A durable power of attorney for health care names the surrogate.

options.text: They take effect only when the patient can no longer make or communicate decisions
options.rationale: A competent patient continues to decide for themselves regardless of what the document says.

options.text: A family member automatically has authority to override a written directive
options.rationale: Family standing does not override a documented directive, and this is the assumption that creates the conflicts requiring ethics committees.

options.text: The nurse should confirm whether a directive exists on admission
options.rationale: Part of admission assessment, and finding out at the point of crisis is too late.

questions.takeaway: The directive speaks for the patient when the patient cannot. Family preference does not override it. An advance directive documents a patient's own decisions about future care and speaks for them when they cannot. A crisis is a turning point where previous coping methods no longer work.
questions.strategy: Any option granting family automatic authority over a written directive is wrong, and it appears frequently.

strategies: Eliminate absolutes

steps.detail: The question asks which statements are accurate.
Automatically is absolute, and family standing does not override the document.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, and E are selected.

questions.concept: An advance directive documents a patient's own decisions about future care and speaks for them when they cannot. Family preference does not override it. A crisis is a turning point where previous coping methods no longer work. Developmental follows a life transition, situational follows an external event, adventitious is catastrophic and rare.

questions.stem: A nurse asks her manager which body of law defines what she may legally do as a nurse and which defines the duty she owes an individual patient. She has been told that agency policy also governs her practice. Which statement is accurate?

options.text: Agency policy carries the same force as statute within the organization
options.rationale: Policy narrows practice within the law; it does not have the force of law.

options.text: All nursing obligations come from statute passed by the legislature
options.rationale: Common law establishes much of the duty of care.

options.text: Common law defines scope of practice through accumulated precedent
options.rationale: Scope is set by statute.

options.text: Statute defines scope through the practice act; common law establishes duty
options.rationale: Two sources operating at different levels, and both apply to nursing practice.

questions.takeaway: Statutory law sets scope. Common law establishes duty through precedent. Policy narrows both. A Nurse Practice Act is state law overseen by the State Board of Nursing. It defines scope of practice and exists to protect public health, safety, and welfare, not to protect the nurse or the employer.
questions.strategy: Three levels, and the one students conflate is policy with law. Policy can be stricter and never looser.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Statute for scope, common law for duty.
Each assigns both roles to one source.
Policy is not law.

elimination.verdict: That leaves D: two sources operating at different levels, and both apply to nursing practice.

questions.concept: A Nurse Practice Act is state law overseen by the State Board of Nursing. It defines scope of practice and exists to protect public health, safety, and welfare, not to protect the nurse or the employer.

questions.stem: A patient scheduled for surgery is unable to describe the procedure and asks the nurse what will be done. The consent form is unsigned. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Stop the process and contact the provider
options.rationale: The nurse verifies that the patient is competent, that the signature is voluntary, and that the patient understands what the provider explained. Not understanding means the third condition has failed.

options.text: Ask another nurse to witness the signature
options.rationale: Witnesses a consent you know is not informed.

options.text: Have the patient sign and document that teaching will follow
options.rationale: Reverses the order and records a consent obtained without understanding.

options.text: Explain the procedure so the consent can be signed
options.rationale: Generous and outside your role. Explaining the procedure belongs to the provider, and doing it yourself produces a signature on an explanation the provider never gave.

questions.takeaway: Confusion or not understanding is a stop signal, not a teaching opportunity. Informed consent requires three conditions: a competent patient, given voluntarily, who understands what the provider explained. The nurse witnesses that understanding.
questions.strategy: The nurse's role in consent is verification, not explanation. Any option that has you explaining the procedure is wrong.

strategies: Assessment before intervention

steps.detail: The patient cannot describe the procedure.
Explaining is the provider's role.
Both proceed with a consent known to be uninformed.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A. The same applies at any hint of coercion.

questions.concept: Informed consent requires three conditions: a competent patient, given voluntarily, who understands what the provider explained. The nurse witnesses that understanding.

questions.stem: A nurse sustains a needlestick from a used subcutaneous needle while recapping it. Place her actions in the correct order.

options.text: Wash the site immediately with soap and water
options.rationale: Step 1 of the sequence.

options.text: Report the injury to the supervisor without delay
options.rationale: Step 2 of the sequence.

options.text: Seek evaluation and post-exposure prophylaxis within the required window
options.rationale: Step 3 of the sequence.

options.text: Complete the occurrence report and exposure documentation
options.rationale: Step 4 of the sequence.

options.text: Follow up with the scheduled serological testing
options.rationale: Step 5 of the sequence.

questions.takeaway: Wash, report, seek prophylaxis within the window, document, then complete serological follow-up.
questions.strategy: Prophylaxis is time-limited, which is why reporting comes before paperwork. Recapping is the cause of this injury.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Wash immediately.
Report, then prophylaxis.
Documentation and serology follow.

elimination.verdict: Wash, report, prophylaxis, document, follow up.

questions.concept: An occurrence report is a risk management tool for identifying hazards. It is not part of the medical record and must never be referenced in the chart.

questions.stem: An off-duty nurse stops at the scene of a car crash and provides care until paramedics arrive. She receives no payment and acts within what she knows. Afterward she asks her manager what legal protection applies. Which statement is accurate?

options.text: She was obliged to stop, since a nurse always has a duty to render aid to anyone
options.rationale: Always is absolute. A duty to act arises from an established relationship or from employment, not from holding a license.

options.text: Her nurse practice act does not apply outside her place of employment, so no standard governs her
options.rationale: Her license and its scope travel with her. The act is not confined to her workplace.

options.text: Protection applies to voluntary aid given in good faith at an emergency scene, within the limits of her training
options.rationale: The protection covers voluntary emergency aid given without payment and in good faith. It does not extend to acts beyond her competence or to grossly negligent care.

options.text: She is fully protected regardless of what she does, since the situation was an emergency
options.rationale: Absolute, and the protection does not cover acts outside her training or grossly negligent care.

questions.takeaway: Voluntary aid, given in good faith, without payment, within the limits of your training.
questions.strategy: Two options here are absolutes. Fully protected regardless and always has a duty are both too broad.

strategies: Eliminate absolutes

steps.detail: Off duty, voluntary, no payment, within her knowledge.
Her license travels with her.
Regardless is absolute.
Always is absolute.

elimination.verdict: That leaves C: voluntary good-faith aid within the limits of her training.

questions.concept: Good Samaritan protection covers voluntary aid rendered in good faith at an emergency scene without payment. It does not cover acts beyond the nurse's training or grossly negligent care.

questions.stem: A nurse completes an occurrence report after a patient's minor fall with no injury. A colleague tells her she should not have filed it because it will be used against her, and asks whether it belongs in the chart. Which statement about the occurrence report is correct?

options.text: It becomes part of the patient's medical record
options.rationale: It is a risk management tool and is not part of the record, which is why it can capture system detail the chart does not.

options.text: It is used to identify problems and take corrective action
options.rationale: Risk management is a systems process aimed at preventing recurrence, and review of these reports is its basic component.

options.text: It is completed only when a patient is injured
options.rationale: Near-misses are reported precisely so harm can be prevented.

options.text: The nurse documents in the chart that a report was completed
options.rationale: The subtle error. Chart the clinical facts only; referencing the report pulls it toward the legal record.

questions.takeaway: The occurrence report is a systems tool, not part of the record, and not a disciplinary instrument. An occurrence report is a risk management tool for identifying hazards. It is not part of the medical record and must never be referenced in the chart.
questions.strategy: Treating these reports as punishment is what stops people filing them, which is the lesson of every high-profile medication error case.

strategies: Eliminate absolutes

steps.detail: The question asks what the report is for.
It sits outside the medical record.
Referencing it in the chart defeats its protection.
Only is absolute, and near-misses are reportable.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B: risk management is a systems process aimed at preventing recurrence, and review of these reports is its basic component.

questions.concept: An occurrence report is a risk management tool for identifying hazards. It is not part of the medical record and must never be referenced in the chart.

questions.scenario: A home health nurse visits a 79-year-old who has lost 6 kg since the last visit. She is wearing soiled clothing, has bruising on both upper arms, and flinches when her son enters the room. The son answers every question directed at her and says she has been refusing to eat. Her monthly pension has been withdrawn in full each month with no receipts for groceries or medications.
questions.stem: Complete the diagram by selecting from the choices below.

options.text: Interview the patient privately, away from the son
options.rationale: She cannot disclose while the possible perpetrator is answering for her, and a caregiver controlling communication is itself a red flag.

options.text: Report the reasonable suspicion to the appropriate adult protective authority
options.rationale: Nurses are mandated reporters, and reasonable suspicion is the threshold rather than proof.

options.text: Confront the son about the inconsistencies in his account
options.rationale: Investigation is not the nurse's role, and it may increase the risk to the patient after the visit ends.

options.text: Wait until the next scheduled visit to see whether the findings persist
options.rationale: Delays a mandated report and leaves her in the situation.

options.text: Advise the son on better nutrition and rebook in two weeks
options.rationale: Treats a possible neglect situation as an education gap.

options.text: Suspected elder mistreatment, including possible neglect and financial abuse
options.rationale: Weight loss, poor hygiene, unexplained bruising, fearfulness, a caregiver controlling communication, and unexplained financial withdrawals together.

options.text: Expected changes of aging
options.rationale: None of these findings is an expected change, and several are red flags.

options.text: A patient exercising the right to refuse care
options.rationale: The refusal is reported by the son, not by the patient, and she has not been asked alone.

options.text: Early dementia affecting appetite
options.rationale: Would not explain the bruising, the fearfulness, or the missing funds.

options.text: Weight, hydration, and skin integrity
options.rationale: Objective markers of whether the neglect is ongoing.

options.text: The patient's account when interviewed alone
options.rationale: The information that has been unavailable so far, and the reason private interview is the first action.

options.text: The son's satisfaction with the care plan
options.rationale: Not a clinical parameter.

options.text: Serum amylase
options.rationale: Not indicated.

options.text: Visual acuity
options.rationale: Unrelated to the findings described.

questions.takeaway: Reasonable suspicion is the threshold for a mandated report, and the assessment happens privately.
questions.strategy: Two wrong actions here delay or investigate. Nurses report; they do not investigate, and delay leaves the patient where she is.

strategies: Assessment before intervention

steps.detail: Multiple specified red flags occurring together.
Investigation is not the nurse's role and may raise the risk.
Both leave her in the situation.

elimination.verdict: Actions A and B, condition A, parameters A and B.

questions.stem: Highlight the findings that support a concern for elder mistreatment.
questions.takeaway: Red flags: unexplained injury, poor hygiene, unmet needs, fearfulness, inconsistent explanations, a caregiver controlling communication, and financial concerns.
questions.strategy: Two findings here are context or consequence. The living arrangement is not evidence and the raised pressure has an obvious explanation. Two findings are context or consequence rather than red flags.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Five findings appear on the list.
Living arrangement and a consequence of missed medication.
Injury, neglect, fear, control, and money together.

elimination.verdict: Highlight s1, s2, s3, s4, and s5.

questions.nursesNote: 1015: Home health visit. Patient is 79, lives with her adult son. Since the last visit five weeks ago she has lost 6 kg. Wearing clothing soiled with urine. Bruising noted on both upper arms in a grip pattern and on the left flank, in differing stages of healing. Patient flinches when her son moves closer and looks to him before answering. Son answers every question directed at her and states she has been refusing to eat. His account of the arm bruising changes twice during the visit. Patient's monthly pension has been withdrawn in full each month with no receipts for groceries or medication. Prescribed antihypertensive bottle is full and dated seven weeks ago. VS: T 36.2 C; HR 96; BP 158/92; SpO2 97%.

segments.text: Bruising on both upper arms in a grip pattern and on the flank, in differing stages
segments.rationale: Unexplained injuries are a specified red flag, and the bilateral grip pattern with varied ages is not consistent with a single accidental cause.

segments.text: Clothing soiled with urine and 6 kg weight loss
segments.rationale: Poor hygiene and unmet basic needs are red flags and both point toward neglect.

segments.text: Patient flinches when her son moves closer
segments.rationale: Fearfulness is a red flag.

segments.text: Son answers every question and his account changes twice
segments.rationale: A caregiver controlling communication and inconsistent explanations are both specified red flags.

segments.text: Pension withdrawn in full each month with no receipts
segments.rationale: Financial abuse is one of the four specified types.

segments.text: Blood pressure 158/92
segments.rationale: Consistent with an untaken antihypertensive. It is a consequence to address rather than a red flag in itself.

segments.text: Patient lives with her adult son
segments.rationale: A living arrangement. It is context, and it is not a finding.
