questions.stem: A nurse tells a patient she is listening while she continues to type and does not look up. He stops mid-sentence and says it can wait. Which term describes what happened?

options.text: A channel problem, since the message was spoken rather than written
options.rationale: The channel carried the words perfectly well. The conflict was with what her body was saying.

options.text: Ineffective feedback, because she did not respond to his message
options.rationale: She did respond. The problem is that her two responses contradicted each other.

options.text: Incongruent communication, where the verbal and nonverbal messages conflict
options.rationale: Her words said listening and her behavior said otherwise. When the two disagree the patient believes the behavior, which is why he stopped.

options.text: Environmental interference from competing demands on her attention
options.rationale: The environment is a real factor, and what he reacted to was her behavior rather than the room.

questions.takeaway: Congruent means verbal and nonverbal agree. When they conflict, the patient believes the nonverbal.
questions.strategy: Three options name a part of the communication process that is working fine here. Find the one actually in conflict.

strategies: Patient-centered option

steps.detail: Words say listening, behavior says busy.
Both functioned; they carried contradictory content.
He reacted to her, not the room.

elimination.verdict: That leaves C: incongruent communication.

questions.concept: Congruence is whether verbal and nonverbal messages agree. When they disagree, the nonverbal is usually the more reliable.

questions.stem: A nurse notes a patient's urine output has fallen from 60 mL/hr to 15 mL/hr and his blood pressure from 132/78 to 94/56. At handover she says he seemed a bit off, without giving the figures or stating her concern. The oncoming nurse does not recognize the change. Which statement best describes this?

options.text: A documentation problem rather than a communication problem
options.rationale: The values may well be documented. What failed was the transfer.

options.text: A safety concern: a change nobody can act on is not communicated
options.rationale: The handoff exists to transfer actionable information. Saying he seemed off transfers an impression, not a finding.

options.text: Acceptable, since the oncoming nurse will assess the patient herself
options.rationale: She will, without knowing what to compare against.

options.text: An incomplete handoff that the written record will compensate for
options.rationale: The record holds the numbers and the oncoming nurse does not know to look for them.

questions.takeaway: A handoff transfers actionable findings. An impression is not actionable.
questions.strategy: Each distractor assumes something downstream will catch it. Ask what the oncoming nurse actually knows.

strategies: Negative polarity
Priority key word

steps.detail: An impression, not the values.
Neither tells her to look.
No baseline to compare against.

elimination.verdict: That leaves a safety concern in the handoff itself.

questions.stem: An 87-year-old admitted with pneumonia has hearing loss and wears aids that he has left at home. He is answering questions inconsistently and appears to be guessing. The room television is on and two staff members are talking in the doorway. Which action best supports communication with this patient?

options.text: Face the patient with your mouth visible and speak at normal volume
options.rationale: Normal volume, visible mouth, and reduced background noise are the correct measures.

options.text: Repeat the same words more slowly if he appears to misunderstand
options.rationale: Rephrase rather than repeat. The same sounds will fail again.

options.text: Speak loudly and exaggerate lip movements so he can follow along
options.rationale: Shouting distorts speech and exaggerated movement makes lip reading harder.

options.text: Communicate primarily in writing to avoid confusion
options.rationale: Assumes a reading level and removes the interpersonal element unnecessarily.

questions.takeaway: Normal volume, visible mouth, quiet environment, and rephrase rather than repeat.
questions.strategy: Any option involving shouting is wrong.

strategies: Priority key word

steps.detail: Polarity is positive. Key word: best. More than one option may be true, so you are ranking them.
Rephrase rather than repeat.
Assumes a reading level and removes the interpersonal element unnecessarily.
Shouting distorts speech and exaggerated movement makes lip reading harder.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A. Normal volume, visible mouth, and reduced background noise are the correct measures.

questions.stem: A nurse observes a colleague using a wound care technique she believes may harm the patient, in front of the patient and his visiting family. She is certain about the clinical concern and unsure how to raise it. Which 2 actions reflect professional communication?
questions.takeaway: Raise concerns directly and privately, and escalate if they are not resolved.
questions.strategy: Exactly two are requested. The wrong options are the four things people actually do: correct publicly, stay silent, chart it, or tell everyone else.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Privately, with the colleague.
Charge nurse if unresolved.
Public, silent, charted, or sideways.

elimination.verdict: A and B are selected.

options.text: Raise the concern directly and privately with the colleague
options.rationale: Concerns about a colleague's practice are addressed away from the patient.

options.text: Escalate to the charge nurse if the concern is not resolved
options.rationale: The pathway continues when the first conversation does not resolve a safety issue.

options.text: Correct the colleague at the bedside so the patient hears it addressed
options.rationale: Undermines confidence in the whole team and embarrasses the colleague.

options.text: Say nothing, since disagreement between nurses is unprofessional
options.rationale: Disagreement is appropriate and necessary; the setting is what matters.

options.text: Document the disagreement in the patient's record
options.rationale: The record is for clinical facts, not interprofessional disagreement.

options.text: Discuss the concern with other staff on the unit first
options.rationale: Talks about a colleague rather than to her.

questions.stem: Two nurses are providing morning care for a patient who is unresponsive following a cardiac arrest three days ago. His family visits daily. One nurse begins discussing her weekend plans across the bed while they work. Which action is appropriate?

options.text: Discuss the patient's poor prognosis quietly at the bedside
options.rationale: Never talk about a patient to others in the patient's presence. Hearing may be intact.

options.text: Call the patient by name and explain each procedure as it is performed
options.rationale: Speak to the patient as though he can hear, and explain procedures and sensations.

options.text: Work in silence to avoid confusing the patient further
options.rationale: Silence removes orientation and the human contact he may still perceive.

options.text: Communicate only through touch, since speech is no longer useful
options.rationale: Touch is valuable and does not replace verbal explanation.

questions.takeaway: Speak to an unresponsive patient as though he can hear, and never talk about him in his presence. Presence is being physically and emotionally available to a patient, and sitting down is what signals you are not about to leave.
questions.strategy: Any option treating an unresponsive patient as absent from the room is wrong.

strategies: Eliminate absolutes

steps.detail: Polarity is positive. No priority key word, so look for the single accurate option.
Touch is valuable and does not replace verbal explanation.
Silence removes orientation and the human contact he may still perceive.
Never talk about a patient to others in the patient's presence.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B. Speak to the patient as though he can hear, and explain procedures and sensations.

questions.concept: Presence is being physically and emotionally available to a patient, and sitting down is what signals you are not about to leave. CUS escalates a concern with graded language: I am Concerned, I am Uncomfortable, this is a Safety issue. SBAR reports; CUS escalates when reporting has failed.

questions.stem: A nurse explains a discharge plan at the bedside and the patient repeats back something quite different from what she said. Her educator asks her to identify which element of the communication process tells her the message did not land. Which element is it?

options.text: The referent
options.rationale: What prompts the communication in the first place.

options.text: The sender
options.rationale: The person conveying the message.

options.text: The channel
options.rationale: The route the message travels, such as speech, writing, or touch.

options.text: Feedback
options.rationale: The response that tells you what got through. Without it you know what you said, not what was received.

questions.takeaway: Feedback is the response that tells you what got through.
questions.strategy: This is why teach-back exists. Delivering a message and confirming receipt are separate acts.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: His repeating it back.
Route and source.
The prompt for communicating.

elimination.verdict: That leaves D: the response that tells you what got through.

questions.stem: A patient says, "I don't understand any of this, everyone is using words I don't know." He has received discharge instructions from three team members and has nodded through each one. Which barrier is present?

options.text: Unwillingness to participate in his own care and discharge planning
options.rationale: He has just told the nurse he wants to understand, which is participation.

options.text: Cognitive impairment affecting his ability to learn
options.rationale: Nothing suggests impaired cognition, and assuming it locates the failure in the patient.

options.text: Language and health literacy, produced by excessive medical jargon
options.rationale: A verbal communication failure on the team's part, not a comprehension failure on his. The jargon created the barrier.

options.text: A hearing impairment that requires a different communication channel
options.rationale: He heard the words. He did not know them, which is a different problem with a different fix.

questions.takeaway: Excessive medical jargon creates a language and health literacy barrier. It is the team's failure, not the patient's. Health literacy is the ability to obtain, understand, and act on health information. Blank forms, missed appointments, and not knowing your own medications are indicators.
questions.strategy: Locate the failure. Options placing it in the patient are usually wrong when the patient has said he wants to understand.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: He heard the words and did not know them.
Hearing is not the problem.
No evidence of impaired cognition.
He is asking to understand, which is participation.

elimination.verdict: That leaves C: the jargon produced the barrier, and the fix is plain language.

questions.concept: Health literacy is the ability to obtain, understand, and act on health information. Blank forms, missed appointments, and not knowing your own medications are indicators.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old has moderate dementia and becomes agitated during morning care. She understands short phrases and loses track of longer explanations. Which actions support communication with her? Select all that apply.

options.text: Give one instruction at a time and wait
options.rationale: Reduces what she must hold in mind at once, which is where longer explanations fail.

options.text: Approach from the front and say who you are
options.rationale: Being approached unseen is a common trigger for agitation during personal care.

options.text: Use short sentences with familiar words
options.rationale: Matches the length of phrase she can follow.

options.text: Explain the whole sequence before starting so she knows what to expect
options.rationale: A long explanation is exactly what she loses track of.

options.text: Correct her when she says something factually wrong
options.rationale: Repeated correction increases agitation without improving orientation.

options.text: Ask the family to provide her personal care instead
options.rationale: Hands over nursing care rather than adapting how it is delivered.

questions.takeaway: One instruction at a time, approach from the front, short familiar phrasing.
questions.strategy: Two distractors give her more to process, not less. One removes the nurse entirely.

strategies: Assessment before intervention

steps.detail: Short phrases, one at a time.
A full sequence is more than she can follow.
One escalates, one hands over care.

elimination.verdict: A, B, and C are selected.

questions.stem: A patient scheduled for surgery tomorrow tells the nurse he is fine about it. He is sitting rigidly with his hands clenched, avoids eye contact, and has not touched his dinner. His words and his behavior do not match. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Tell him it is normal to be nervous before surgery
options.rationale: Normalizes without inviting him to say anything, and it names the feeling for him.

options.text: Document that the patient denies anxiety
options.rationale: Records only half the data and ignores the observed behavior.

options.text: Accept his statement and continue with routine care
options.rationale: Believes the words over the body when they conflict.

options.text: Share the observation and invite him to say more
options.rationale: Metacommunication. Name the mismatch without accusing and open the door.

questions.takeaway: When verbal and nonverbal conflict, the nonverbal is the true message.
questions.strategy: The right answer usually starts with what the nurse observed rather than what the patient said.

strategies: Negative polarity

steps.detail: No priority key word, so look for the single accurate option.
Normalizes without inviting him to say anything, and it names the feeling for him.
Records only half the data and ignores the observed behavior.
Believes the words over the body when they conflict.

elimination.verdict: That leaves D. Metacommunication.

questions.concept: CUS escalates a concern with graded language: I am Concerned, I am Uncomfortable, this is a Safety issue. SBAR reports; CUS escalates when reporting has failed.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old admitted for chemotherapy tells the nurse she is frightened about how her family will manage if the treatment does not work. Four nurses respond differently to the same statement, and the charge nurse uses the exchange to teach about therapeutic responses. Which nurse statement is a blocking response?

options.text: Why did you stop taking your medication?
options.rationale: A why question, which reads as accusation and produces defensiveness.

options.text: Tell me more about what happened at home
options.rationale: Open-ended and encourages elaboration.

options.text: It sounds like this has been frightening for you
options.rationale: Reflection, which is therapeutic.

options.text: I will sit with you for a while
options.rationale: Offering self, which is therapeutic.

questions.takeaway: Rephrase why into what. Not why are you anxious, but you seem upset, what is on your mind.
questions.strategy: Scan for the word why. It is a blocking technique nearly every time it appears.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Polarity is positive. No priority key word, so look for the single accurate option.
Open-ended and encourages elaboration.
Reflection, which is therapeutic.
Offering self, which is therapeutic.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A. A why question, which reads as accusation and produces defensiveness.

questions.concept: CUS escalates a concern with graded language: I am Concerned, I am Uncomfortable, this is a Safety issue. SBAR reports; CUS escalates when reporting has failed.

questions.stem: A patient three days after a stroke understands what is said to him but cannot find the words to reply. He becomes visibly frustrated when the nurse finishes his sentences for him. Which approach is most appropriate?

options.text: Let him rest and return when he is less frustrated
options.rationale: Kind and it leaves him without the adaptations that would make the next attempt work.

options.text: Allow time, use yes-or-no questions, and offer a communication board
options.rationale: Expressive aphasia spares comprehension, so the adaptations reduce what he must produce rather than simplifying what he receives.

options.text: Speak slowly and simplify your wording so he can follow
options.rationale: Addresses comprehension, which is intact. It treats the wrong half of the problem.

options.text: Supply the word when he pauses, so the exchange stays fluent
options.rationale: Reduces the pause and removes his attempt, which is the thing already frustrating him.

questions.takeaway: Expressive aphasia: comprehension is intact, production is not. Adapt what he must produce.
questions.strategy: One distractor helps comprehension he does not need. One removes his attempt. One postpones.

strategies: Patient-centered option

steps.detail: He understands; he cannot retrieve words.
Not where the deficit is.
One takes over, one defers.

elimination.verdict: That leaves time, yes-or-no questions, and a board.

questions.stem: A nurse educator is teaching new graduates why messages between staff and patients are so often misunderstood. She breaks a single bedside exchange into its component parts to show where meaning can be lost. Which are elements of the communication process? Select all that apply.

options.text: Sender
options.rationale: Encodes and initiates the message.

options.text: Message
options.rationale: The content being conveyed.

options.text: Diagnosis
options.rationale: A clinical conclusion rather than an element of the communication process.

options.text: Receiver
options.rationale: Decodes and interprets.

options.text: Documentation
options.rationale: A record of what occurred rather than an element of the process itself.

options.text: Prognosis
options.rationale: A clinical prediction rather than an element of the communication process.

questions.takeaway: Two lists of six are taught. One adds context and environment, the other adds referent. Learn all seven.
questions.strategy: If asked for six, check which list the stem is using. If simply asked to name them, give all seven.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Polarity is positive. This is a select all that apply, so there is no single best answer. Judge each option separately.
A step of the nursing process, not an element of communication.

elimination.verdict: A, B and D are selected.

questions.concept: The LEARN model structures a cross-cultural encounter: Listen to the patient's perception, Explain your own, Acknowledge differences, Recommend a plan, Negotiate agreement.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old scheduled for a mastectomy tomorrow tells the nurse she is frightened her husband will find her repulsive afterward. She has not slept for two nights. Which response is most therapeutic?

options.text: "You are worried about how this will change how he sees you."
options.rationale: Reflection. It hands the feeling back so she can look at it and keeps her talking.

options.text: "Many women feel this way beforehand and do very well afterward."
options.rationale: A cliche that minimizes her specific fear.

options.text: "Have you talked to your husband about how you are feeling?"
options.rationale: Redirects to someone else rather than exploring what she just said.

options.text: "Your husband loves you and that will not change."
options.rationale: False reassurance, and she cannot know it. It closes the conversation.

questions.takeaway: The kindest-sounding option is usually wrong. The correct one often sounds flatter because it does not resolve anything.
questions.strategy: Ask whether the response invites more or ends the conversation.

strategies: Negative polarity
Priority key word

steps.detail: Key word: best. More than one option may be true, so you are ranking them.
False reassurance, and she cannot know it.
A cliche that minimizes her specific fear.
Redirects to someone else rather than exploring what she just said.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A. Reflection.

questions.stem: A patient has just learned his cancer has recurred. He stops speaking mid-sentence and stares out of the window. Several minutes pass. The nurse has other patients waiting but nothing urgent. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Offer to call the chaplain
options.rationale: A reasonable later referral used here to hand the moment to someone else.

options.text: Remain present and allow the silence
options.rationale: Silence gives him time to think and feel, and allowing the patient to break it shows patience.

options.text: Ask him what he is thinking about
options.rationale: Interrupts a silence he initiated and may feel intrusive.

options.text: Explain the treatment options available
options.rationale: Information he cannot absorb right now.

questions.takeaway: Silence is an intervention, and it is especially therapeutic during profound sadness or grief.
questions.strategy: When the patient initiated the silence, let the patient break it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Polarity is positive. No priority key word, so look for the single accurate option.
Information he cannot absorb right now.
A reasonable later referral used here to hand the moment to someone else.
Interrupts a silence he initiated and may feel intrusive.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B. Silence gives him time to think and feel, and allowing the patient to break it shows patience.

questions.concept: The LEARN model structures a cross-cultural encounter: Listen to the patient's perception, Explain your own, Acknowledge differences, Recommend a plan, Negotiate agreement.

questions.stem: An order is written to catheterize for a 34-year-old with 700 mL of retained urine on bladder scan. His roommate is behind a curtain and two visitors are present. He looks away when the procedure is mentioned. Which action best demonstrates respect for personal space?

options.text: Ask a family member to stay with him for reassurance during it
options.rationale: Presumes he wants family present for intimate care.

options.text: Work efficiently and say as little as possible
options.rationale: Silence during intimate care increases vulnerability.

options.text: Explain what will happen and what he will feel, then ask permission before beginning
options.rationale: The genitalia involve exposure of the genital area, which requires permission and great sensitivity.

options.text: Complete the procedure and explain what happened afterward
options.rationale: Explanation after the fact is not consent.

questions.takeaway: Announce what you will touch and why, and ask permission before exposing a patient. Protect privacy and promote dignity during every skill.
questions.strategy: Any option that skips explanation before intimate contact is wrong.

strategies: Priority key word
Opposite pair, look closely

steps.detail: Polarity is positive. Key word: best. More than one option may be true, so you are ranking them.
Explanation after the fact is not consent.
Silence during intimate care increases vulnerability.
Presumes he wants family present for intimate care.

elimination.verdict: That leaves C. The genitalia are in the intimate zone, which requires permission and great sensitivity.

questions.stem: Four patients are assigned to a nurse: one with hearing impairment, one with vision impairment, one with cognitive impairment, and one with aphasia after a stroke. Which adaptations match the needs described? Select all that apply.

options.text: Face the patient, reduce background noise, and do not shout
options.rationale: Correct for hearing impairment. Shouting distorts speech rather than clarifying it.

options.text: Say who you are on entering and describe what you are doing
options.rationale: Correct for vision impairment.

options.text: Use short sentences and one instruction at a time
options.rationale: Correct for cognitive impairment.

options.text: Allow time and offer other channels such as writing or pictures
options.rationale: Correct for aphasia.

options.text: Speak to the family member instead when communication is difficult
options.rationale: Bypasses the patient, and each of these patients can communicate with the right adaptation.

questions.takeaway: Adapt the channel to the need. Shouting, rushing, and bypassing the patient all fail for different reasons. A tort is a civil wrong. Quasi-intentional torts cause harm through the nature of the act. Unintentional torts arise where the person knew or should have known the care was substandard.
questions.strategy: The wrong option is the shortcut used when communication is hard, and it removes the patient from their own care.

strategies: Patient-centered option

steps.detail: Four needs, four specified adaptations.
Bypassing the patient is not an adaptation.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, and D are selected.

questions.concept: A tort is a civil wrong. Quasi-intentional torts cause harm through the nature of the act. Unintentional torts arise where the person knew or should have known the care was substandard.

questions.stem: A patient begins describing her fear about a new diagnosis. The nurse sits down, maintains eye contact, and says nothing until the patient finishes. Which technique is she using?

options.text: Giving advice
options.rationale: Substitutes the nurse's solution for the patient's own reasoning.

options.text: False reassurance
options.rationale: Closes the conversation she has just opened.

options.text: Summarizing
options.rationale: Restates the main points, which comes after she has finished rather than during.

options.text: Active listening
options.rationale: Attending fully and signaling attention without steering the content, which is what allows a patient to volunteer what she had not planned to say.

questions.takeaway: Active listening attends fully and signals attention without steering the content. Active listening attends fully and signals attention without steering the content, which is what allows a patient to volunteer what they had not planned to say.
questions.strategy: The evidence it worked is in the stem: she volunteered something she had not said before.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Attended, did not interrupt, signaled attention.
Substitutes the nurse's solution for the patient's own reasoning.
Closes the conversation she has just opened.
Restates the main points, which comes after she has finished rather than during.

elimination.verdict: That leaves D: attending fully and signaling attention without steering the content, which is what allows a patient to volunteer what she had not planned to say.

questions.concept: Active listening attends fully and signals attention without steering the content, which is what allows a patient to volunteer what they had not planned to say.

questions.stem: A nurse calls a provider about a patient whose blood pressure has dropped from 128/76 to 88/52 over four hours. She describes the situation, the background, and her assessment, then stops and waits. The provider asks what she wants him to do. What has she omitted?

options.text: Her own credentials and years of experience on the unit
options.rationale: That belongs to the Identify step in ISBAR, used when people do not know each other.

options.text: The patient's current code status and advance directive
options.rationale: Relevant in some calls and not a component of SBAR.

options.text: A recommendation for what she wants done
options.rationale: The R is the step people drop. Stating what you want is within your scope and is what changes the outcome.

options.text: The patient's full medical history
options.rationale: Background covers the relevant history, and the full history is not the point of the call.

questions.takeaway: Say what you want. I need you to come see him is a legitimate nursing recommendation. SBAR structures a report: Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation. The recommendation is the part most often dropped.
questions.strategy: When a stem walks through SBAR and stops early, the missing letter is the answer.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Polarity is positive. No priority key word, so look for the single accurate option.
That belongs to the Identify step in ISBAR, used when people do not know each other.
Background covers the relevant history, and the full history is not the point of the call.
Relevant in some calls and not a component of SBAR.

elimination.verdict: That leaves C. The R is the step people drop.

questions.concept: SBAR structures a report: Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation. The recommendation is the part most often dropped.

questions.stem: A nurse precepts a student after a conversation with a patient who had just learned her treatment was not working. The student describes how she responded and what she was trying to achieve. Which student statement indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "Reassuring her that most people do well was the kindest thing I could say."
options.rationale: False reassurance closes the conversation she had just opened. Therapeutic communication reflects the feeling and invites her to say more.

options.text: "Naming the feeling she expressed keeps the conversation open."
options.rationale: Accurate. Reflecting feelings is the hallmark of therapeutic communication.

options.text: "Silence gave her room to continue rather than being awkward."
options.rationale: Accurate. Silence invites the patient to add to what they have said.

options.text: "When her words and her posture disagreed, the posture was the more reliable message."
options.rationale: Accurate. Nonverbal communication generally carries the truer message.

questions.takeaway: False reassurance feels kind and ends the conversation. Reflect the feeling instead.
questions.strategy: Both wrong answers in communication items are usually kind: reassurance and advice. Neither keeps the patient talking.

strategies: Negative polarity
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Find the non-therapeutic response.
Reassurance ends the exchange.
Reflecting, silence, and congruence are correct.

elimination.verdict: A is the statement needing correction: reassurance closes the conversation.

questions.stem: Highlight the findings that represent barriers to this patient's understanding.
questions.takeaway: Nodding is not understanding, and a blank form is rarely about glasses.
questions.strategy: Two findings here are not barriers: one is a comfort issue and one is the remedy. Read each for whether it blocks comprehension. One finding is the solution rather than a barrier.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Four findings interfere with understanding.
The interpreter is the solution.
Mild shoulder pain is not a comprehension barrier.

elimination.verdict: Highlight s1, s2, s3, and s4.

questions.nursesNote: 1330: Patient is 63, admitted for elective bowel surgery tomorrow. Speaks limited English. Consent has not been signed. Preoperative teaching and a medication history remain outstanding. Teenage son present and offering to interpret, stating he does so at every appointment. Patient nods at each explanation and says he understands, but cannot describe the procedure when asked. Registration form returned with several sections blank; patient states he forgot his glasses. Has missed two previous outpatient appointments. Rates pain from an unrelated shoulder injury 4 out of 10. A qualified interpreter is available in twenty minutes.

segments.text: Limited English proficiency with a teenage son offering to interpret
segments.rationale: A minor may lack medical vocabulary, may be uncomfortable with sensitive content, and may unintentionally alter the message.

segments.text: Nods and says he understands but cannot describe the procedure
segments.rationale: Nodding is not comprehension. Understanding is confirmed by teach-back, not by agreement.

segments.text: Registration form returned with sections blank
segments.rationale: A specified indicator of possible low health literacy, and forgot my glasses is the usual explanation given.

segments.text: Two missed outpatient appointments
segments.rationale: Another specified indicator, and it often reflects difficulty reading a reminder rather than indifference.

segments.text: Shoulder pain rated 4 out of 10
segments.rationale: Worth addressing for comfort and not a barrier to understanding at this level.

segments.text: A qualified interpreter available in twenty minutes
segments.rationale: The solution rather than a barrier.

questions.caseTitle: Preoperative teaching across a language barrier

questions.stem: Which 2 actions should the nurse take FIRST?
questions.takeaway: Confusion or an inability to describe the procedure is a stop signal, not a reason to proceed.
questions.strategy: Exactly two are requested. Three wrong options proceed with a consent the nurse already knows is not informed.

strategies: Assessment before intervention

steps.detail: He cannot describe the procedure.
Topic-based and time-based exceptions do not exist.
That is the provider's role.

elimination.verdict: A and B are selected.

options.text: Wait for the qualified interpreter before proceeding with consent or teaching
options.rationale: Consent depends on the patient understanding what the provider explained, and that cannot be established through a minor.

options.text: Explain to the patient and his son why a professional interpreter is used
options.rationale: Declining the son's offer without explanation may be experienced as rejecting the family, and the family clearly expects this arrangement.

options.text: Allow the son to interpret the medication history only, since it is straightforward
options.rationale: The concerns apply to every topic, and a medication history is where an altered message causes harm.

options.text: Witness the consent now, since the provider has already explained the procedure
options.rationale: The nurse verifies that the patient understands what was explained. He cannot describe it, so that condition has failed.

options.text: Explain the procedure herself so consent can be obtained before the interpreter arrives
options.rationale: Explaining the procedure is the provider's role, and doing it produces a signature on an explanation the provider never gave.

options.text: Document that the patient understands and proceed
options.rationale: Records a conclusion the evidence contradicts.

questions.caseTitle: Preoperative teaching across a language barrier

questions.stem: For each nursing action, determine whether it SUPPORTS or UNDERMINES effective teaching for this patient.
questions.takeaway: Plain language, teach-back, short sessions, and family included at the patient's direction. Teach-back asks the patient to explain the plan in their own words. It confirms understanding rather than confirming that teaching was delivered.
questions.strategy: Two actions here hand the work back to the patient or his family. Both look practical and both reproduce the original barrier. Two actions reintroduce the barrier the interpreter was arranged to remove.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Four actions confirm or ease understanding.
English written material and a son teaching at home.

elimination.verdict: Four actions support teaching and two undermine it.

questions.scenario: The interpreter is present, consent has been obtained appropriately, and the nurse is planning preoperative teaching. The patient asks that his wife be included.

rows.text: Use plain language rather than clinical terms through the interpreter
rows.rationale: Excessive medical jargon creates a language and health literacy barrier, and it is the team's failure rather than the patient's.

rows.text: Ask him to explain the plan back in his own words
rows.rationale: Teach-back confirms understanding rather than assuming it, and nodding has already proved unreliable here.

rows.text: Provide the written material in English for him to read later
rows.rationale: Assumes both reading ability and language, and he has already returned a form incomplete.

rows.text: Break the teaching into short sessions rather than one long one

questions.stem: A nurse must record that a patient declined his morning bath, saying he was too tired, and later accepted it in the afternoon. She wants the entry to be usable by the next nurse and defensible if the record is reviewed. Which entry meets the guidelines for quality documentation?

questions.stem: A patient is admitted following a house fire and remains in hospital for several days. The nurse observes an initial surge in heart rate and blood pressure, a period where the vital signs settle while the patient remains under strain, and later a decline in her physical condition. Place the stages of the general adaptation syndrome in the correct order, from FIRST to LAST.

options.text: The body recognizes a stressor and activates the fight-or-flight response
options.rationale: Alarm. The sympathetic nervous system activates, producing increased heart rate, respirations, blood pressure, and blood glucose, plus sweating, muscle tension, dilated pupils, increased alertness, and decreased digestion.

options.text: The body attempts to adapt and stabilize while the stressor continues
options.rationale: Resistance. Vital signs may return toward normal while resources are being consumed, which is why a patient can look stable and still be depleting.

options.text: Adaptive resources are depleted and physiological functioning declines
options.rationale: Exhaustion. When the stressor persists beyond the body's capacity to adapt, illness and organ effects follow.

questions.takeaway: Alarm, resistance, exhaustion. Resistance is where a patient looks fine and is spending reserves. The general adaptation syndrome has three stages: alarm with sympathetic activation, resistance where the body adapts while the stressor continues, and exhaustion when adaptive resources are depleted.
questions.strategy: The stage most often misread is resistance, because normalized vital signs are mistaken for recovery. A patient in the resistance stage may have near-normal vital signs. Stability is not the same as recovery.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Recognition and sympathetic activation open the response.
Depletion closes it.
Adaptation while the stressor continues.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C. Alarm activates the sympathetic response, resistance adapts while the stressor continues, and exhaustion follows when adaptive resources run out.

questions.concept: The general adaptation syndrome has three stages: alarm with sympathetic activation, resistance where the body adapts while the stressor continues, and exhaustion when adaptive resources are depleted.

questions.scenario: A nurse reviews several patient situations during a shift.
questions.stem: Each situation below involves a different pattern and duration of stress. rows.text: A patient feels tense before a scheduled family meeting this afternoon
rows.rationale: Short-term stress from an immediate event, and it resolves when the event passes.

rows.text: A patient has managed housing instability and debt for three years
rows.rationale: Ongoing stress persisting over time, and it is what produces allostatic load.

rows.text: A patient loses his job of twenty years and says his usual ways of coping no longer work
rows.rationale: The event itself is acute, and the failure of previous coping makes it a crisis. It is situational because an external event provoked it.

rows.text: A patient's home is destroyed by flooding and she cannot see a way forward
rows.rationale: An external event producing an immediate stress response, with coping that has stopped working.

rows.text: A caregiver has supported a spouse with dementia for four years and now reports exhaustion
rows.rationale: Persistent over time. It becomes a crisis only if previous coping methods stop working.

rows.text: A patient describes years of financial strain that recently became unmanageable after an eviction notice
rows.rationale: Long-standing stress that has reached a turning point where coping no longer works.

options.rationale: Requires a longer symptom duration and a defined symptom cluster. Three weeks is too early.

options.rationale: Distress is expected. Coping that has stopped working is the line between response and crisis.

rows.text: "I have not slept properly in two weeks."
rows.rationale: The patient's own report about sleep, and only he can supply it.

rows.text: Tearful during the admission interview
rows.rationale: An observed behavior.

rows.rationale: A statement about coping.

rows.rationale: Measured and observed.

rows.rationale: Observed hygiene, a specified objective cue.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old newly diagnosed with type 2 diabetes and an A1C of 9.2% enrolls in a self-management course, buys a glucose meter, and books a dietitian appointment. Which coping strategy is he using?

questions.stem: Three weeks after losing her home in a fire, a 46-year-old talks with the nurse about how she is managing. She describes how she has been coping and what she plans to do next. Which patient statement indicates a need for further teaching?

options.rationale: Accurate. A crisis is defined by coping that no longer works.

options.rationale: Suppression is not coping. It removes the chance to work the problem, and avoidance is not among the effective strategies.

options.text: "Talking with my sister does not change what happened, but it helps me manage it."
options.rationale: Accurate. Emotion-focused coping is the fitting strategy when the stressor cannot be altered.

options.text: "How I read a situation affects how hard it hits me."
options.rationale: Accurate. Appraisal is why the same event affects two people differently.

questions.takeaway: Suppression is not coping. Problem-focused changes the stressor; emotion-focused manages the response to it.

questions.stem: Two patients are admitted with the same diagnosis on the same day. One manages the admission calmly and the other is overwhelmed within hours. The nurse considers what differs between them beyond the diagnosis itself. Which factors influence a person's ability to cope with stress? Select all that apply.

options.text: Age and developmental stage
options.rationale: Age and developmental stage shape what a person has already faced and what resources they have built by this point in life.

options.text: Culture and beliefs
options.rationale: Culture and beliefs shape what counts as a stressor at all, and what responses are acceptable to the person.

options.text: Past experiences
options.rationale: Past experience tells the person whether they have survived something like this before, which affects appraisal directly.

options.text: Height and body build
options.rationale: Not among the factors, and it has no bearing on coping capacity.

options.text: Support system
options.rationale: Correct factor, alongside financial and personal resources.

options.text: Problem-solving skills and personal outlook
options.rationale: Problem-solving skills determine what options a person can see, and outlook determines whether they expect any of them to work.

options.text: Blood type
options.rationale: Unrelated to stress appraisal or coping capacity.

questions.takeaway: Eight factors: age and stage, culture and beliefs, past experiences, health and energy, support system, resources, problem-solving skills, and outlook. Appraisal is how a person interprets the impact of a stressor, which is why the same event affects two people differently.

steps.detail: Factors influencing coping ability.
A physical characteristic unrelated to coping.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old is admitted after a house fire destroyed her home. The nurse assesses her orientation, mood, sleep, vital signs, intake, and contact with family. Highlight the findings that require immediate nursing intervention.

segments.text: Patient is alert and oriented to person, place, and time
segments.rationale: A normal finding and a useful baseline.

segments.rationale: Expressed hopelessness with failed coping. Safety is prioritized first in planning.

segments.text: Reports she has not slept in three days
segments.rationale: Sleep loss impairs judgment and coping capacity and is a marker in evaluation.

segments.text: Tearful during the admission interview
segments.rationale: An expected emotional response to a catastrophic loss, and it is an objective cue rather than an emergency.

segments.text: Heart rate 104 and hands trembling
segments.rationale: Consistent with sympathetic activation in the alarm stage, and expected in this situation.

segments.text: Has declined all contact with her sister and her closest friend
segments.rationale: Withdrawal from the support system, which is a factor influencing coping and removes a protective resource.

segments.text: Reports she ate a small meal this morning
segments.rationale: A reassuring finding.

questions.stem: A 54-year-old who has cared for a spouse with advanced illness for three years reports exhaustion, a resting pulse of 96, and four upper respiratory infections this winter. Which effects of prolonged stress apply? Select all that apply.

options.rationale: Leaving the body less able to fight pathogens.

options.rationale: A direct consequence of the reduced immune response.

options.rationale: Which is why chronic stress also appears as a risk factor for infection.

options.text: Document that she is coping adequately now that safety is established
options.rationale: Records a conclusion that the findings do not support.

questions.caseTitle: Adult in crisis after catastrophic loss

questions.stem: For each finding, determine whether it reflects the ALARM STAGE, FAILED COPING, or an EXPECTED GRIEF RESPONSE.
questions.takeaway: Alarm is physiological, failed coping is what she says she can no longer do, and grief is an appropriate response.
questions.strategy: Two rows look like problems and are not. Tearfulness and talking about the loss are how grief works.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Sympathetic activation is the alarm stage.
Her own words and her withdrawal.
Crying and talking are appropriate.

elimination.verdict: Two alarm stage, two failed coping, two expected grief response.

questions.scenario: The nurse reviews her findings and separates what requires intervention from what is an appropriate response to loss.

rows.text: Heart rate 104 with trembling hands
rows.rationale: Sympathetic activation in response to an acute stressor.

rows.text: "Nothing I do works anymore"
rows.rationale: The defining feature of a crisis is that previous coping has stopped working.

rows.text: Tearful when describing the loss of her home
rows.rationale: An appropriate response to a catastrophic loss.

rows.text: Declining contact with her sister and closest friend
rows.rationale: Withdrawal removes a factor in coping capacity.

rows.rationale: Correct alarm findings alongside the raised heart rate.
