questions.stem: A 74-year-old with heart failure tells the nurse he wakes most nights with chest pain rated 6 of 10 that eases when he sits up. He has not reported it before, assuming it was indigestion. Which condition should the nurse suspect?

options.text: A parasomnia
options.rationale: Undesirable physical events during sleep such as sleepwalking.

options.text: Sleep latency
options.rationale: The time it takes to fall asleep.

options.text: Nocturnal angina
options.rationale: Chest pain from the heart occurring at night, and it occurs alongside heart failure-related apnea as a cardiac cause of disrupted sleep.

options.text: Obstructive sleep apnea
options.rationale: Airway obstruction producing snoring and apneic episodes, which is a different mechanism.

questions.takeaway: Cardiac disease disrupts sleep through nocturnal angina and heart failure-related apnea.
questions.strategy: Chest pain waking a patient at night is a finding to report, not a sleep complaint to manage with hygiene teaching.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Chest pain occurring at night in heart failure.
A behavioral event, not pain.
Obstruction rather than cardiac pain.
A measure of time to fall asleep.

elimination.verdict: That leaves C: chest pain from the heart occurring at night, and it occurs alongside heart failure-related apnea as a cardiac cause of disrupted sleep.

questions.stem: A nurse plans to protect a patient's sleep overnight on a busy medical unit. Place the following actions in the correct order across the evening and night, from FIRST to LAST.

options.text: Assess the patient's usual bedtime routine and what has helped at home
options.rationale: Sleep is subjective and individual, so the plan starts with what already works for this person.

options.text: Dim the lights during evening hours to support melatonin release
options.rationale: Light suppresses melatonin, so lowering it in the evening supports the natural onset of sleep.

options.text: Cluster nursing care so assessments and medications are grouped rather than scattered
options.rationale: Reduces the number of separate interruptions, which is the largest controllable cause of hospital sleep loss.

options.text: Control noise by closing doors, lowering alarm volumes, and keeping night conversations quiet
options.rationale: And alarm volume is the part staff most often overlook.

options.text: Position the patient for comfort and airway safety
options.rationale: The final step before sleep, and airway safety is why positioning is not purely a comfort measure.

questions.takeaway: Assess the routine, dim the lights, cluster care, control noise, position for comfort and airway safety.
questions.strategy: Sleep bundles work because they combine these rather than relying on any one. Clustering care is the highest-yield single action. All five are appropriate interventions. Consider which one must come FIRST if the plan is to fit this patient.

strategies: Assessment before intervention

steps.detail: Assessment of the usual routine precedes any intervention.
Positioning immediately precedes sleep.
Light, then interruptions, then noise.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, D, E.

questions.stem: A patient recovering from surgery asks why the nurse keeps emphasizing sleep when he would rather stay up watching television. His wound is healing slowly and his pain is 5 of 10. Which response is accurate?

options.text: "Growth hormone is released during sleep, which supports tissue repair and wound healing."
options.rationale: A direct mechanism. Poor sleep also impairs immune function, wound healing, and pain tolerance.

options.text: "Sleep prevents you from needing pain medication."
options.rationale: Sleep improves pain tolerance; it does not remove the need for analgesia.

options.text: "It reduces the number of times we need to check on you."
options.rationale: Describes a staffing convenience rather than the patient's benefit.

options.text: "Sleep helps the time pass more quickly during recovery."
options.rationale: Trivializes a physiological process with measurable clinical effects.

questions.takeaway: Growth hormone releases during sleep, driving tissue repair and wound healing.
questions.strategy: Sleep protection is a clinical intervention with a mechanism, not a comfort measure. Answer with the mechanism.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Why sleep is protected after surgery.
No mechanism.
Overstates the effect on pain.
A convenience, not a benefit.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A. REM sleep also supports memory consolidation and emotional processing.

questions.stem: A 76-year-old takes a diuretic each morning and reports waking three or four times each night to void, then struggling to fall back asleep. He is becoming drowsy during the day and has stumbled twice on the way to the bathroom. Which nursing action is most appropriate?

options.text: Restrict his fluid intake after the early evening
options.rationale: Commonly suggested and it risks dehydration in an older adult without addressing the diuretic.

options.text: Discuss moving the diuretic earlier in the day with the provider
options.rationale: The nocturia is drug-timed, and changing the timing removes the cause. He is now falling on the way to the bathroom.

options.text: Provide a bedside commode to shorten the walk
options.rationale: Reduces the fall risk and accepts three or four awakenings as unchangeable.

options.text: Review his sleep hygiene and evening routine
options.rationale: Appropriate where sleep habits are the issue. His awakenings have a pharmacological cause.

questions.takeaway: When a drug is causing the symptom, change the drug timing rather than working around it.
questions.strategy: Three options manage the consequence. Ask what is producing the awakenings.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A morning diuretic still working at night.
Dehydration risk without touching the cause.
Both accept the awakenings.

elimination.verdict: That leaves discussing the timing with the provider.

questions.concept: CUS escalates a concern with graded language: I am Concerned, I am Uncomfortable, this is a Safety issue. SBAR reports; CUS escalates when reporting has failed.

questions.stem: A 69-year-old on a medical unit reports he has not slept since admission four nights ago. The nurse reviews his medications, pain, the ward environment, his intake, and his age and medical history. Highlight the findings that represent modifiable causes the nurse can address.

segments.text: Receives a diuretic at 2000 and wakes three to four times to void
segments.rationale: Diuretic timing affects nocturia and night-time awakenings, and the timing can be changed.

segments.text: Rates his pain as 6 out of 10 at night
segments.rationale: Unrelieved pain is a cause of disrupted sleep and is treatable.

segments.text: Reports the overhead light is switched on whenever staff enter
segments.rationale: Light suppresses melatonin, and dimming lights during evening hours is an intervention.

segments.text: Is 68 years old
segments.rationale: Age is not modifiable, and reduced sleep in older adults is expected rather than correctable.

segments.text: Has a history of hypertension managed with medication
segments.rationale: Not itself a sleep disruptor in this scenario.

segments.text: Reports staff enter the room separately for vital signs, medications, and blood draws
segments.rationale: Clustering nursing care reduces interruptions, which is the largest controllable cause of hospital sleep loss.

segments.text: Drinks two cups of coffee with his evening meal
segments.rationale: Caffeine close to bedtime is a disruptor and is straightforward to change.

questions.takeaway: Find the treatable causes before reaching for a sleeping tablet.
questions.strategy: Ask of each finding whether a nurse could change it this week. Age and a chronic diagnosis are context; timing, light, noise, and caffeine are levers. Two findings are relevant background rather than modifiable causes.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Read for what can be changed
steps.detail: Timing, pain control, light, clustering, and caffeine all can.
Age and an existing diagnosis are not modifiable.
Five modifiable causes appear in this passage.

elimination.verdict: Highlight s1, s2, s3, s6, and s7.

questions.scenario: The nurse reviews the home substance and medication history of a patient reporting poor sleep.
questions.stem: For each item, click to specify which effects apply. Each item may have more than one effect.
columns: Raises fall risk in older adults

rows.text: Caffeine
rows.rationale: A common and underreported disruptor, alongside nicotine and alcohol.

rows.text: Alcohol
rows.rationale: It shortens sleep latency and then fragments the night, and it reduces REM.

rows.text: Benzodiazepines
answer: Raises fall risk in older adults
rows.rationale: Short-term use only, with a specific risk of falls and confusion in older adults.

rows.text: Opiates
answer: Raises fall risk in older adults
rows.rationale: Correct as a REM suppressant causing daytime drowsiness, and sedation raises fall risk.

rows.text: Nicotine
rows.rationale: A stimulant, and the most commonly overlooked of the three disruptors.

rows.text: Antidepressants
rows.rationale: Occurs alongside opiates and anticonvulsants, with daytime drowsiness as a consequence.

questions.constraint: Each column must have at least one response selected.
questions.takeaway: Caffeine, nicotine, and alcohol disrupt. Antidepressants, opiates, and anticonvulsants suppress REM. Sedating agents raise fall risk.
questions.strategy: Two items belong in more than one column. Alcohol both disrupts and suppresses REM, and opiates both suppress REM and sedate. Each column must have at least one response selected, and some items belong in more than one.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Caffeine, alcohol, nicotine.
Alcohol, opiates, antidepressants.
Anything sedating in an older adult.

elimination.verdict: Four rows map to one column and two map to two.

r3: Raises fall risk in older adults
r4: Raises fall risk in older adults

questions.stem: A 59-year-old admitted for elective surgery has a bed partner who reports loud snoring with pauses in breathing most nights. He falls asleep during meetings and once while stopped in traffic, though he believes he sleeps enough. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Teach sleep hygiene and reassess in one month
options.rationale: Hygiene will not resolve airway obstruction, and delay allows the cardiovascular consequences to continue.

options.text: Reassure the patient that snoring is common and not concerning
options.rationale: Snoring with witnessed apnea and daytime sleepiness is not a benign finding.

options.text: Report the findings and discuss evaluation for obstructive sleep apnea
options.rationale: Snoring with apneic episodes plus daytime sleepiness is the described pattern, and it warrants evaluation rather than hygiene teaching alone.

options.text: Advise the patient to sleep alone so the partner is not disturbed
options.rationale: Addresses the partner's sleep and ignores the patient's airway.

questions.takeaway: Snoring plus witnessed apnea plus daytime sleepiness is a pattern to report, not a hygiene problem. Obstructive sleep apnea is repeated airway obstruction during sleep, producing snoring, witnessed apneic episodes, and daytime sleepiness.
questions.strategy: The bed partner's report is valuable here precisely because the patient cannot observe their own breathing during sleep.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Snoring, apneic pauses, daytime sleepiness.
Hygiene does not address obstruction.
Addresses the wrong person.
Dismisses a significant pattern.

elimination.verdict: That leaves C: snoring with apneic episodes plus daytime sleepiness is the described pattern, and it warrants evaluation rather than hygiene teaching alone.

questions.concept: CUS escalates a concern with graded language: I am Concerned, I am Uncomfortable, this is a Safety issue. SBAR reports; CUS escalates when reporting has failed. Obstructive sleep apnea is repeated airway obstruction during sleep, producing snoring, witnessed apneic episodes, and daytime sleepiness.

questions.stem: A 51-year-old with difficulty falling asleep tells the nurse she watches television in bed until she feels drowsy, has coffee after dinner, and exercises at 2200 because it is the only time she has. Which instructions does the nurse include when teaching sleep hygiene? Select all that apply.

options.text: Keep a consistent bedtime and wake time daily, including weekends
options.rationale: Consistency supports the circadian rhythm, and weekend variation undoes it.

options.text: Take a warm bath immediately before getting into bed
options.rationale: A warm bath raises core temperature; it helps only if taken well before bed.

options.text: Limit screen time for 30 minutes before bed
options.rationale: Screens delay sleep onset through light exposure and through mental stimulation, so the instruction addresses both.

options.text: Stay in bed reading or watching television until sleep comes
options.rationale: The bed is reserved for sleep only. Using it for other activities weakens the association.

options.text: Exercise during the day, but not within 1 to 2 hours of bedtime
options.rationale: Daytime activity helps; activity too close to sleep does not.

options.text: Use relaxation techniques before bed
options.rationale: Relaxation techniques lower the arousal that keeps a person awake, which is the barrier when sleep hygiene alone has not worked.

questions.takeaway: Consistent timing, no caffeine or alcohol late, screens off 30 minutes before, bed for sleep only, daytime exercise, relaxation.
questions.strategy: The wrong option here is the one patients most commonly do. Reading in bed until sleep arrives feels productive and weakens the bed-sleep association.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Sleep hygiene instructions.
The bed is reserved for sleep only.

elimination.verdict: A, C, E and F are selected.

questions.stem: A provider considers prescribing a benzodiazepine for a 75-year-old with insomnia. She is unsteady on standing, takes five other medications, and fell once at home this year. Which concern is most important to raise?

options.text: No effect on sleep architecture at all
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines reduce deep and REM sleep.

options.text: Falls and confusion risk, and short-term use only
options.rationale: Both cautions are, and they matter more in this population than in younger adults.

options.text: Permanent suppression of REM sleep
options.rationale: REM suppression is associated with antidepressants, opiates, and anticonvulsants, and no effect is permanent.

options.text: Need to take it with caffeine to avoid drowsiness
options.rationale: Caffeine is a sleep disruptor and would work against the goal.

questions.takeaway: Benzodiazepines are short-term only, with falls and confusion the specific risk in older adults.
questions.strategy: Sedatives are a fall-risk class.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A benzodiazepine considered for a 75-year-old.
REM suppression is associated with antidepressants, opiates, and anticonvulsants, and no effect is permanent.
Benzodiazepines reduce deep and REM sleep.
Caffeine is a sleep disruptor and would work against the goal.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B: both cautions are, and they matter more in this population than in younger adults.

questions.stem: Patient complaints about sleep are reviewed on a busy medical unit. Staff enter rooms separately for vital signs, medications, and blood draws through the night, and alarms and hallway conversation continue after 2300. Which action has the greatest effect on nighttime interruptions?

options.text: Complete all documentation at the bedside overnight
options.rationale: Increases presence in the room during sleeping hours.

options.text: Keep hallway lights bright so staff can work without entering rooms
options.rationale: Light suppresses melatonin, and hallway light reaches patient rooms.

options.text: Offer a sleep medication to every patient at bedtime
options.rationale: Medicates a problem the environment is causing, and it adds risk in older adults.

options.text: Cluster nursing care so assessments and medications are grouped
options.rationale: Reduces the number of separate entries into the room, which is the largest controllable cause of hospital sleep loss.

questions.takeaway: Cluster care, dim lights, control noise, and position for comfort. Sleep bundles combine these.
questions.strategy: The pattern across all four options is whether the action reduces or increases stimulation in the room at night.

strategies: Priority key word

steps.detail: Greatest effect on nighttime interruptions.
Medicates an environmental problem.
Light suppresses melatonin.
Increases presence in the room.

elimination.verdict: That leaves D: reduces the number of separate entries into the room, which is the largest controllable cause of hospital sleep loss.

questions.stem: A patient on a medical unit reports he has not slept more than two hours at a stretch since admission. Observations are due at 0200 and 0600, his roommate's television is on until late, and the corridor light falls directly across his bed. Which action should the nurse take first?
questions.takeaway: Address what nursing controls first: clustering care, light, and noise. Medication is not the first answer to an environmental cause.
questions.strategy: Sort the causes by who can change them. Anything nursing controls comes before anything requiring an order.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Observation timing, television, corridor light.
All three are nursing.
One medicates, one normalizes.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A: fix what you control tonight.

options.text: Cluster the night-time care and address the light and noise
options.rationale: The causes described are environmental and within nursing control, so they are addressed before anything is requested from a prescriber.

options.text: Request an order for a sedative to help him sleep
options.rationale: Medicates around a problem that has an identified and modifiable cause.

options.text: Move him to a single room as the first step
options.rationale: May help and it depends on bed availability. The modifiable causes can be addressed tonight.

options.text: Reassure him that disrupted sleep is expected in hospital
options.rationale: Normalizes a problem that is slowing his recovery and can be changed.

questions.stem: A student asks the nurse how the body knows when to sleep and when to wake, given that patients on the unit sleep poorly regardless of how tired they are. The nurse explains the structure that governs the 24-hour cycle. Which structure is central to the regulation of the sleep-wake cycle?

options.text: The medulla oblongata
options.rationale: Controls autonomic functions including respiration and heart rate.

options.text: The cerebellum
options.rationale: Coordinates movement and balance.

options.text: The hypothalamus
options.rationale: Sleep regulation involves the hypothalamus, along with hypocretins for wakefulness and REM, prostaglandin, L-tryptophan, and growth factors.

options.text: The pituitary gland
options.rationale: Releases growth hormone during sleep and does not govern the circadian cycle.

questions.takeaway: The hypothalamus governs the 24-hour sleep-wake cycle, with hypocretins driving wakefulness and REM.
questions.strategy: Option D is the near-miss worth noting: the pituitary is involved in sleep through growth hormone, but it does not regulate the cycle.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Regulation of the sleep-wake cycle.
Movement and autonomic control.
Involved in sleep, not in regulating the cycle.

elimination.verdict: That leaves C: sleep regulation involves the hypothalamus, along with hypocretins for wakefulness and REM, prostaglandin, L-tryptophan, and growth factors.

questions.stem: An 80-year-old in long-term care reports poor sleep. She takes a diuretic and four other medications, has osteoarthritis with night-time pain, wears hearing aids she removes at bedtime, and gets up several times to void. Which factors contribute to sleep problems in older adults? Select all that apply.

options.text: Nocturia
options.rationale: Correct risk factor, and it fragments sleep through repeated waking.

options.text: Polypharmacy
options.rationale: Correct risk factor, and several drug classes affect sleep directly.

options.text: Pain
options.rationale: Pain both delays sleep onset and wakes the person repeatedly, and it is frequently under-treated at night.

options.text: Increased total sleep requirement with age
options.rationale: Total sleep requirement does not increase with age. Sleep becomes lighter and more fragmented.

options.text: Deeper slow-wave sleep with advancing age
options.rationale: Slow-wave sleep decreases with age rather than deepening.

options.text: Regular daytime physical activity
options.rationale: Daytime activity improves sleep rather than disrupting it.

questions.takeaway: Nocturia, polypharmacy, pain, comorbidities, and sensory impairment. Polypharmacy is the concurrent use of multiple medications, counting prescription, over-the-counter, and herbal products together.
questions.strategy: One option reverses the direction of an age-related change. That is the standard distractor pattern in lifespan items.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Factors contributing to sleep problems.
Sleep requirement decreases with age rather than increasing.

elimination.verdict: A, B and C are selected.

questions.concept: Polypharmacy is the concurrent use of multiple medications, counting prescription, over-the-counter, and herbal products together.

questions.stem: A nurse assesses sleep for a patient admitted three days ago who reports lying awake for a long time before sleep comes. She asks how long it usually takes him to fall asleep after getting into bed. Which component of the sleep assessment is this?

options.text: Sleep latency
options.rationale: The time from getting into bed to falling asleep, and it is an assessment component.

options.text: Perceived sleep quality
options.rationale: How rested the patient feels, which is asked separately.

options.text: Sleep efficiency
options.rationale: The proportion of time in bed actually spent asleep.

options.text: Nighttime awakenings
options.rationale: How often the patient wakes after falling asleep.

questions.takeaway: Assessment covers bedtime routine, sleep latency, nighttime awakenings, wake time, and perceived quality. Sleep latency is the time from getting into bed to falling asleep, and it is one of the sleep assessment components alongside awakenings, wake time, and perceived quality.
questions.strategy: Latency and awakenings point at different problems. Difficulty falling asleep suggests one pattern; repeated waking suggests another, such as nocturia or pain.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Time taken to fall asleep.
A ratio, not a duration.
Quality and frequency of waking.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A: the time from getting into bed to falling asleep, and it is an assessment component.

questions.concept: Sleep latency is the time from getting into bed to falling asleep, and it is one of the sleep assessment components alongside awakenings, wake time, and perceived quality.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease reports he cannot sleep in hospital. He explains that lying flat leaves him breathless, and he has been sitting upright in the chair for most of the night. Which factor most likely contributes to his difficulty sleeping?

options.text: Increased REM sleep in respiratory disease
options.rationale: Not a described feature.

options.text: Elevated melatonin production
options.rationale: Not a described feature of respiratory disease.

options.text: Reduced need for sleep with chronic illness
options.rationale: Illness increases the need for sleep while making it harder to get.

options.text: Positioning needs and breathlessness disrupt sleep
options.rationale: Breathlessness worsens lying flat, so the position that allows sleep and the position that allows breathing work against each other.

questions.takeaway: Illness increases the need for sleep and often makes it harder to get.
questions.strategy: Each disease group disrupts sleep by a specific mechanism. Respiratory is positioning and breathlessness; cardiac is nocturnal angina and apnea; gastrointestinal is nocturnal symptoms.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: COPD and difficulty sleeping.
Neither is described.
Reverses the relationship between illness and sleep need.

elimination.verdict: That leaves D: specified directly for respiratory disease including COPD and asthma.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old has slept about four hours a night for three weeks since starting a new job. His surgical wound from two months ago has not fully healed, he reports more pain from it than before, and he has had two upper respiratory infections. Which consequences result from inadequate sleep? Select all that apply.

options.text: Impaired immune function
options.rationale: And it links sleep to infection risk.

options.text: Impaired wound healing
options.rationale: Correct, alongside the growth hormone mechanism.

options.text: Reduced pain tolerance
options.rationale: And it explains why a poorly slept patient reports more pain from the same stimulus.

options.text: Improved concentration through increased alertness
options.rationale: Sleep deprivation impairs function, judgment, and mood rather than improving them.

options.text: Impaired judgment and mood
options.rationale: Judgment and mood decline with sleep loss, which matters clinically because a sleep-deprived patient makes poorer decisions about their own care.

questions.takeaway: Poor sleep impairs immunity, healing, pain tolerance, judgment, and mood.
questions.strategy: Reduced pain tolerance is the one worth carrying into practice. The patient who slept badly is not exaggerating the same wound the next morning.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Consequences of inadequate sleep.
States a benefit where it describes impairment.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, and E are selected.

questions.stem: A nurse teaches sleep hygiene to a 51-year-old who reports taking two hours to fall asleep most nights. She describes her evening routine and what she intends to change. Which patient statement indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "I will exercise during the day but not within an hour or two of bed."
options.rationale: Accurate. Daytime activity helps; activity close to sleep does not.

options.text: "I will stay in bed reading until I feel sleepy enough to drop off."
options.rationale: The bed is reserved for sleep only. Using it for other activities weakens the association between bed and sleep, which is the thing being rebuilt.

options.text: "I will stop the coffee after dinner and skip the nightcap."
options.rationale: Accurate. Caffeine and alcohol are both specified disruptors.

options.text: "I will keep the same bedtime and wake time, including at weekends."
options.rationale: Accurate. Weekend variation undoes the circadian consistency.

questions.takeaway: The bed is for sleep only. Consistent timing, no caffeine or alcohol late, screens off, daytime exercise.
questions.strategy: The wrong statement is the thing most people actually do, and it feels productive.

strategies: Negative polarity
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Find the mistaken habit.
Bed for sleep only.
Timing, substances, and exercise are correct.

elimination.verdict: A is the statement needing correction: reading in bed weakens the association.

questions.stem: A nurse reviews four patients on a medical unit, each with a different sleep complaint: one cannot fall asleep despite ample opportunity, one snores with witnessed pauses in breathing, one is simply not getting enough sleep in hospital, and one has been found walking at night. Match each description with the sleep disorder it BEST describes. Each term is used only once.

items.text: Difficulty falling asleep or staying asleep despite adequate opportunity
items.rationale: The most common complaint, and the opportunity for sleep is present while the sleep is not.

items.text: Repeated airway obstruction during sleep producing snoring, apneic episodes, and daytime sleepiness
items.rationale: Physical obstruction, and it is strongly associated with cardiovascular consequences.

items.text: Insufficient quantity or quality of sleep producing impaired function, judgment, and mood
items.rationale: It impairs immune function, wound healing, and pain tolerance, and it is common in hospitalized patients.

items.text: Undesirable physical events during sleep such as sleepwalking or night terrors
items.rationale: Behaviors occurring during sleep rather than a failure to obtain it.

questions.takeaway: Four specified disorders: insomnia, obstructive sleep apnea, sleep deprivation, and parasomnias. Obstructive sleep apnea is repeated airway obstruction during sleep, producing snoring, witnessed apneic episodes, and daytime sleepiness.
questions.strategy: Sort by whether the problem is getting to sleep, breathing during sleep, getting enough sleep, or doing something during sleep.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Airway obstruction is apnea.
Events during sleep are parasomnias.
Difficulty obtaining sleep versus insufficient sleep obtained.

questions.concept: Obstructive sleep apnea is repeated airway obstruction during sleep, producing snoring, witnessed apneic episodes, and daytime sleepiness.

questions.scenario: A 68-year-old on a medical unit reports he has not slept properly since admission four nights ago. He receives a diuretic at 2000, wakes three or four times to void, and reports the overhead light is on whenever staff enter. His pain score is 6 out of 10 at night. He is drowsy during the day, has been unsteady walking to the bathroom, and asks for a sleeping tablet.
questions.stem: Complete the diagram by selecting from the choices below.

options.text: Cluster nursing care and control light and noise during the night
options.rationale: Interruptions are the largest controllable cause of hospital sleep loss, and dimming lights supports melatonin release.

options.text: Discuss the timing of the diuretic and night-time pain control with the provider
options.rationale: Diuretic timing affects nocturia, and unrelieved pain is a cause of disrupted sleep. Both are treatable causes.

options.text: Request a benzodiazepine at bedtime
options.rationale: Short-term use only, with a specific risk of falls and confusion in older adults, and this patient is already unsteady.

options.text: Advise him to restrict all fluids after noon
options.rationale: Risks dehydration, which causes dizziness and falls, and it does not address the medication timing.

options.text: Reassure him that poor sleep in hospital is normal and expected
options.rationale: Common is not the same as acceptable, and it dismisses a problem with treatable causes.

options.text: Sleep deprivation from treatable environmental and physiological causes
options.rationale: Nocturia from diuretic timing, unrelieved pain, and light and noise are all identified and all modifiable.

options.text: Obstructive sleep apnea
options.rationale: Would require snoring with apneic episodes, and none is described.

options.text: A parasomnia
options.rationale: Undesirable events during sleep, which is not what he reports.

options.text: An expected age-related change requiring no action
options.rationale: Older adults sleep less, and a new problem with identifiable causes is still assessed.

options.text: Sleep quality, latency, and number of night-time awakenings
options.rationale: The specified assessment components, and they show whether the interventions are working.

options.text: Daytime drowsiness and steadiness when ambulating
options.rationale: Sleep deprivation impairs judgment and function, and he is already unsteady, which is a fall risk.

options.text: Serum sodium every four hours
options.rationale: Not indicated by anything described.

Diuretic timing, pain, light, and clustering.

questions.nursesNote: 2130: Patient admitted four days ago with community-acquired pneumonia. Reports he has not slept more than two hours at a stretch since admission. Receives furosemide at 2000 daily. Rates incisional-free chest discomfort 6/10 at night, last analgesia 1400. States staff switch on the overhead light at each entry. Wakes three to four times nightly to void. Observed dozing during physiotherapy this afternoon and unsteady walking to the bathroom, requiring a steadying hand. Requests "something to help me sleep." VS: T 37.1 C; HR 88; RR 18; BP 132/76; SpO2 94% on room air.

segments.text: Furosemide administered at 2000
segments.rationale: Diuretic timing drives nocturia. Moving the dose earlier is a change the team can make.

segments.text: Chest discomfort rated 6/10 at night, last analgesia 1400
segments.rationale: Unrelieved pain both delays sleep onset and wakes him, and it is treatable.

segments.text: Overhead light switched on at each entry
segments.rationale: Light suppresses melatonin, and dimming during evening hours is an intervention.

segments.text: Age 68
segments.rationale: Not modifiable. Older adults sleep less and more fragmented, which is expected rather than correctable.

segments.text: Staff enter separately for vital signs, medications, and blood draws
segments.rationale: Clustering care reduces interruptions, which is the largest controllable cause of hospital sleep loss.

segments.text: History of pneumonia requiring admission
segments.rationale: The reason he is here. It shapes the picture and is not itself a modifiable sleep cause.

steps.detail: Four causes are identified and all are modifiable.
Falls and confusion risk in an unsteady older adult.
Dismisses a treatable problem.

options.text: sleep deprivation from treatable environmental and physiological causes
options.rationale: Nocturia from diuretic timing, unrelieved pain, light, and interruptions are all identified and all modifiable.

options.text: obstructive sleep apnea

options.text: a parasomnia

options.rationale: Common is not the same as acceptable, and it dismisses a problem with treatable causes.

questions.stem: The nurse plans interventions for tonight. Which 2 actions should she take FIRST?
questions.takeaway: Remove the reason he wakes and treat the pain that keeps him awake. Both can happen before tonight.
questions.strategy: Exactly two are requested. Three wrong options manage the consequences of poor sleep rather than its causes. Some of the others may be appropriate later.

strategies: Priority key word

steps.detail: Nocturia and pain are the two acting tonight.
Risks dehydration and misses the timing issue.
Both add risk without addressing the cause.

elimination.verdict: A and B are selected.

options.text: Discuss moving the furosemide dose earlier with the provider
options.rationale: Removes the reason he wakes, and the timing change can be made before tonight.

options.text: Offer analgesia before he settles and reassess its effect
options.rationale: Unrelieved pain at 6 out of 10 will wake him regardless of any other change.

options.text: Restrict his fluids after noon
options.rationale: Risks dehydration, which causes dizziness and falls in older adults, and it does not address the medication timing.

options.text: Request a benzodiazepine at bedtime
options.rationale: Short-term use only, and it adds fall risk to a patient who is already unsteady.

options.text: Place a bed alarm and raise all four side rails
options.rationale: Four raised side rails are a restraint, and neither addresses why he is awake.

options.text: Document that he is requesting a sleep aid and reassess tomorrow
options.rationale: Records the request and changes nothing tonight.

questions.stem: For each proposed action, determine whether it is INDICATED or NOT INDICATED given this new information.
questions.takeaway: When a plan is working, you continue it and keep measuring. You do not add the intervention it made unnecessary.
questions.strategy: Improvement is the reason not to add sedation, not the reason it has become safe. One proposed action responds to improvement by adding the medication that was previously declined.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Voiding once, pain 2 out of 10, sleeping five hours, still unsteady.
The situation is improving and he remains a fall risk.
The measures are how you know it is still working.

rows.text: Cluster nursing care overnight and dim the lights
rows.rationale: Interruptions remain the largest controllable cause, and he still reports being woken by staff.

rows.text: Add a benzodiazepine now that other measures are in place
rows.rationale: He is sleeping longer and remains unsteady. Adding a sedating agent introduces fall risk to a situation that is improving.

rows.text: Continue scheduled night-time analgesia
rows.rationale: His pain fell from 6 to 2 out of 10 with the scheduled dose, which is why he is sleeping.

rows.text: Discontinue the assessment of his sleep now that it has improved

rows.text: Assess his steadiness before each ambulation
rows.rationale: Daytime drowsiness and unsteadiness are both fall risks and both are still present.
