questions.stem: A patient with type 1 diabetes receives rapid-acting insulin at 0730 in anticipation of breakfast. At 0745 the kitchen reports the trays are delayed by at least 40 minutes. His glucose before the dose was 148 mg/dL. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Obtain a carbohydrate source now, because rapid-acting insulin is already working
options.rationale: Rapid-acting insulin is given with food precisely because its onset is immediate, and a delayed tray creates a low.

options.text: Hold the next scheduled dose to compensate for the delayed meal
options.rationale: Addresses a future dose while the current one is still working.

options.text: Administer a second dose once the tray arrives
options.rationale: Compounds the problem with more insulin.

options.text: Wait for the tray to arrive and monitor him for symptoms meanwhile
options.rationale: The insulin is acting while he waits, and monitoring does not prevent the fall.

questions.takeaway: Rapid-acting insulin is given with food. A delayed tray after the dose is a hypoglycemic event waiting to happen.
questions.strategy: The timing relationship between insulin type and food is what these questions test, not the numbers themselves.

strategies: Priority key word

steps.detail: Dose given, food delayed.
Waiting does not stop the fall.
Future doses and additional insulin.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A: rapid-acting insulin is given with food precisely because its onset is immediate, and a delayed tray creates a low.

questions.stem: A nurse teaches foot care to a patient with a 15-year history of type 2 diabetes whose monofilament testing shows reduced sensation bilaterally. Which patient action requires correction?

options.text: Apply moisturizer to the tops and bottoms of your feet, and between your toes
options.rationale: Moisturizer goes on the tops and bottoms but never between the toes. Trapped moisture in a warm dark space grows fungus.

options.text: Buy new shoes at the end of the day when the feet are largest
options.rationale: Correct. Feet swell through the day, so shoes fitted in the morning are too tight by evening.

options.text: Inspect your feet and the soles daily for blisters, redness, or drainage
options.rationale: Correct. Daily inspection catches injury the patient cannot feel because of neuropathy.

options.text: Check the water temperature by hand before bathing the feet
options.rationale: Correct. Neuropathy means the patient may not feel a scald until the burn has happened.

questions.takeaway: Moisturize the tops and bottoms, never between the toes.
questions.strategy: In a spot-the-error item, three options are correct practice. Verify each against a rule you can name; the one you cannot justify is the answer.

strategies: Negative polarity

steps.detail: Intervenes means find the error. Three statements will be correct.
Daily inspection is standard teaching.
End-of-day shoe fitting accounts for swelling.
Water temperature checking addresses neuropathy.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A. Every foot-care rule traces to neuropathy or to poor circulation and infection risk; moisture between the toes belongs to the second.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old newly diagnosed with type 2 diabetes tells the nurse his uncle lost a foot to the disease and asks what he can do to avoid the same outcome. He works long hours on his feet and has never seen a podiatrist. Which teaching points does the nurse include? Select all that apply.

options.text: Inspect your feet daily
options.rationale: Neuropathy means injury is not felt, so it must be seen.

options.text: Attend regular eye examinations
options.rationale: Retinopathy can progress to irreversible blindness and is detectable before symptoms appear.

options.text: Keep blood pressure and lipid levels within target ranges
options.rationale: A stated goal of diabetes management, because macrovascular complications are driven by the same vascular damage.

options.text: Go barefoot indoors so the feet can breathe
options.rationale: Never barefoot. An unfelt injury on an insensate foot is how ulcers begin.

options.text: Trim toenails straight across
options.rationale: Reduces ingrown nails, and a podiatrist should do it if neuropathy or thick nails are present.

options.text: Use a heating pad on the feet in cold weather
options.rationale: Explicitly avoided. Neuropathy means the patient may not feel a burn.

options.text: Report any wound that is not healing
options.rationale: Impaired healing and immune response turn minor injuries into serious infections.

questions.takeaway: Every foot-care rule traces to one of two deficits: the patient cannot feel injury, or the injury will not heal.
questions.strategy: The two false options both involve exposing the foot to something it cannot feel. Once you see the pattern the item resolves quickly.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Prevention of complications in a new diagnosis.
Barefoot exposes an insensate foot to injury.
Heating pads risk burns the patient will not feel.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, E, and G remain, covering feet, eyes, vascular targets, and wound reporting.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old with type 1 diabetes is admitted with a glucose of 512 mg/dL, a pH of 7.19, and a bicarbonate of 14 mEq/L. The nurse suspects diabetic ketoacidosis. Which additional finding would confirm it?

options.text: Blood pressure of 98/56 with a pulse of 118
options.rationale: Reflects the dehydration that accompanies both ketoacidosis and hyperosmolar state.

options.text: A potassium of 5.4 mEq/L on admission
options.rationale: Common in ketoacidosis and it does not distinguish it. Potassium shifts out of cells in acidosis regardless of the cause.

options.text: Serum osmolality above 320 mOsm/kg with negative ketones
options.rationale: Describes hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state, which presents without significant ketones.

options.text: Serum ketones present with deep, rapid respirations
options.rationale: Ketones are what separate ketoacidosis from a hyperosmolar state, and Kussmaul respirations are the body blowing off carbon dioxide to compensate for the acidosis.

questions.takeaway: Ketones are the dividing line. DKA has them and hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state does not.
questions.strategy: Two options describe findings both conditions share. Look for the one that only fits ketoacidosis.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Ketones.
Negative ketones describes the hyperosmolar state.
Both occur in either condition.

elimination.verdict: That leaves D: ketones with Kussmaul respirations.

questions.concept: CUS escalates a concern with graded language: I am Concerned, I am Uncomfortable, this is a Safety issue. SBAR reports; CUS escalates when reporting has failed.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old with type 1 diabetes injects rapid-acting insulin into her thigh and then goes for a 30-minute walk. Her glucose has dropped sharply on three consecutive mornings. Which instruction does the nurse give?

options.text: Inject into the same thigh each day so absorption stays predictable
options.rationale: Repeated use of one site causes lipohypertrophy, which makes absorption less predictable, and the thigh is the problem here.

options.text: Use a site away from the exercising muscle, such as the abdomen
options.rationale: Blood flow to working muscle speeds absorption from that limb. Moving the site away from it removes the cause rather than the exercise.

options.text: Stop walking until the glucose stabilizes
options.rationale: Removes the exercise she benefits from when the injection site is what needs changing.

options.text: Switch the rapid-acting insulin to bedtime
options.rationale: Rapid-acting insulin is timed to meals. Moving it to bedtime creates an overnight low.

questions.takeaway: Exercise speeds absorption from the injected limb. Change the site, not the exercise.
questions.strategy: Two distractors remove something she should keep. Ask what actually caused the fast absorption.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Blood flow to the working thigh.
Rapid-acting insulin is timed to meals.
One removes exercise, one keeps the problem site.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B: inject away from the exercising muscle.

questions.scenario: A nurse cares for four patients with type 2 diabetes. One takes acarbose with each meal, one takes a sulfonylurea, one takes metformin alone, and one is on NPH insulin each morning at 0800. Each has asked how to manage a low blood glucose at home.
questions.stem: Which instructions does the nurse give? Select all that apply.

options.text: If the patient cannot safely swallow, use IV dextrose or glucagon rather than oral carbohydrate
options.rationale: Her deck states this directly: never give oral intake when swallowing is unsafe. Aspiration risk outweighs the speed of an oral dose.

options.text: Give 15 to 20 grams of fast-acting carbohydrate and recheck the glucose in 15 minutes
options.rationale: The rule of 15, and it applies to a conscious patient with a glucose under 70 who can swallow safely.

options.text: If the glucose is still low after 15 minutes, give another 15 grams and recheck again
options.rationale: Correct. One dose is frequently not enough, which is why the recheck is part of the treatment.

options.text: The patient on NPH at 0800 should expect the highest risk of a low in the early morning
options.rationale: NPH given at 0800 peaks a shift and a half later, so the risk window stretches from around noon to 2000.

options.text: The patient on metformin alone is at low risk of hypoglycemia
options.rationale: Metformin does not stimulate insulin release, so it rarely causes a low unless combined with an agent that does.

options.text: An unconscious patient should be given oral carbohydrate immediately
options.rationale: Never put anything in the mouth of a patient who cannot protect the airway. That patient needs intravenous dextrose or glucagon.

questions.takeaway: Rule of 15, glucose rather than table sugar on acarbose, and nothing by mouth if the patient cannot swallow safely. The rule of 15 treats hypoglycemia in a conscious patient who can swallow: give 15 to 20 grams of fast-acting carbohydrate, recheck in 15 minutes, repeat if still low.
questions.strategy: Two wrong options here reverse a real rule: the NPH peak window and the airway rule. Check the direction of each before selecting.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Four patients on different agents, each with a different risk profile.
NPH at 0800 peaks from about noon to 2000, not in the early morning.
Oral carbohydrate requires a patient who can protect the airway.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, and E are selected, covering the rule of 15, the acarbose exception, and the low risk with metformin alone.

questions.concept: The rule of 15 treats hypoglycemia in a conscious patient who can swallow: give 15 to 20 grams of fast-acting carbohydrate, recheck in 15 minutes, repeat if still low.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old with type 2 diabetes is brought in after four days of increasing confusion. Blood glucose is 640 mg/dL, serum ketones are negative, and the pH is normal. His mucous membranes are dry and his heart rate is 108. Which condition does the nurse suspect?

options.text: An expected postprandial rise
options.rationale: No meal produces a glucose of 640 in any patient.

options.text: Hypoglycemia, given the altered mental status on presentation
options.rationale: The glucose is 640 mg/dL.

options.text: Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state
options.rationale: Extreme hyperglycemia without significant ketones, occurring more often in type 2.

options.text: Diabetic ketoacidosis, given the markedly elevated blood glucose
options.rationale: DKA requires ketones and acidosis, and it occurs typically in type 1.

questions.takeaway: The dividing line between DKA and HHS is ketones, not the glucose number. Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state involves extreme hyperglycemia, glucose 600 or more, without significant ketones. DKA has ketones and acidosis. Ketones are the dividing line.
questions.strategy: Students sort by how high the sugar is and get it backwards, because HHS runs higher than DKA.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: No ketones, normal pH, type 2.
Ketones and acidosis are absent.
Glucose 640 is not low.
Not a postprandial value.

elimination.verdict: That leaves C: extreme hyperglycemia without significant ketones, occurring more often in type 2.

questions.concept: Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state involves extreme hyperglycemia, glucose 600 or more, without significant ketones. DKA has ketones and acidosis. Ketones are the dividing line.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old with a family history of type 2 diabetes is told his blood glucose is elevated. He asks whether he will need insulin like his brother, who has type 1. Which response is accurate?

options.text: Type 2 never requires insulin, only diet and oral medication
options.rationale: Some patients with type 2 do need insulin over time, and needing it does not mean poor control.

options.text: Type 2 means your pancreas still makes insulin, though your cells respond to it poorly
options.rationale: Type 2 is insulin resistance with insufficient or ineffective insulin. Type 1 is autoimmune destruction of beta cells, leaving little or none.

options.text: Type 2 becomes type 1 once the pancreas stops producing insulin
options.rationale: They are separate conditions with different causes. One does not convert into the other.

options.text: Type 2 is diagnosed at a younger age and progresses faster
options.rationale: Reverses the usual pattern. Type 1 often has a sudden onset at a younger age; type 2 is gradual.

questions.takeaway: Type 1 is autoimmune beta-cell destruction with little or no insulin. Type 2 is resistance with insulin present but insufficient.
questions.strategy: One distractor rules insulin out for type 2 entirely, which is the common misconception. Insulin use does not define the type.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Resistance against autoimmune destruction.
Type 2 may require insulin over time.
One claims conversion, one reverses the onset pattern.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B: insulin is present but the cells respond poorly.

questions.concept: The A1C reports average blood glucose over about three months, with a target under 7%. Diagnosis rests on a fasting blood glucose over 126 mg/dL on two occasions.

questions.scenario: A 74-year-old with type 2 diabetes is admitted after four days of increasing confusion. Blood glucose 618 mg/dL, serum ketones negative, serum pH 7.37, dry mucous membranes, poor skin turgor, heart rate 112, blood pressure 96/58.
questions.stem: For each nursing action, indicate whether it is indicated or not indicated for this patient.

rows.text: Establish intravenous access for fluid resuscitation
rows.rationale: Severe dehydration is the immediate threat in HHS, and fluid replacement is the priority.

rows.text: Monitor serum potassium during insulin administration
rows.rationale: Insulin drives potassium into cells, so the serum level can fall quickly and cause dysrhythmias.

rows.text: Administer sodium bicarbonate to correct acidosis
rows.rationale: There is no acidosis. The pH is 7.37 and ketones are negative.

rows.text: Perform frequent neurological assessment
rows.rationale: Altered mental status is the hallmark of HHS and the marker of whether treatment is working.

rows.text: Encourage independent ambulation to the bathroom
rows.rationale: A confused, hypotensive, dehydrated older adult is a fall risk and needs assistance.

rows.text: Monitor intake and output
rows.rationale: Osmotic diuresis is driving the fluid loss, so output guides replacement.

questions.takeaway: In HHS the priority is fluid, not insulin alone, and there is no acidosis to correct. Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state involves extreme hyperglycemia, glucose 600 or more, without significant ketones. DKA has ketones and acidosis. Ketones are the dividing line.
questions.strategy: Work matrix rows against the data given. Two rows here are wrong because the patient has no acidosis and is unsafe to mobilize alone.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Glucose over 600, no ketones, normal pH, and signs of volume depletion.
There is no acidosis to correct.
Confusion plus hypotension is a fall risk.

elimination.verdict: The four remaining rows are indicated: fluids, potassium monitoring, neurological checks, and intake and output.

questions.concept: Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state involves extreme hyperglycemia, glucose 600 or more, without significant ketones. DKA has ketones and acidosis. Ketones are the dividing line.

questions.stem: A nurse reviews four patients with type 1 diabetes who each had a hypoglycemic episode this week. She wants to identify the cause in each case so the pattern can be prevented rather than simply treated. Which situation is a recognized cause of hypoglycemia?

options.text: A patient who increased her activity without adjusting her insulin or intake
options.rationale: Increased activity without adjustment is a cause, alongside excess insulin, missed or delayed meals, inadequate carbohydrate intake, and alcohol without food.

options.text: A patient whose insulin was held because his glucose was 80
options.rationale: Holding insulin at a low-normal reading prevents a fall rather than causing one.

options.text: A patient who ate a larger breakfast than usual
options.rationale: More carbohydrate raises glucose rather than lowering it.

options.text: A patient who missed a scheduled dose of her prescribed insulin
options.rationale: Missing insulin causes hyperglycemia, and in type 1 it risks ketoacidosis.

questions.takeaway: Causes of hypoglycemia: excess insulin or diabetes medication, missed or delayed meals, inadequate carbohydrate, increased activity without adjustment, and alcohol without food.
questions.strategy: Work each option by asking whether it adds insulin effect or removes glucose. Only those two directions cause a low.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The question asks for a recognized cause of a low.
More carbohydrate raises glucose.
Missing insulin causes hyperglycemia.
Holding insulin at 80 prevents a fall.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A: increased activity without adjusting insulin or intake is one of the causes.

questions.stem: A patient newly diagnosed with type 2 diabetes asks the nurse why he has been passing so much urine and feeling constantly thirsty. His glucose is 348 mg/dL. Which explanation is accurate?

options.text: Insulin deficiency directly stimulates the bladder
options.rationale: Insulin has no direct action on the bladder.

options.text: High glucose damages the kidneys, causing them to leak fluid
options.rationale: Nephropathy develops over years. This symptom appears within days of a high glucose.

options.text: Glucose spills into the urine and draws water with it
options.rationale: Above the renal threshold, glucose passes into the urine and pulls water osmotically. The fluid loss is what drives the thirst.

options.text: Ketones irritate the urinary tract, increasing urgency
options.rationale: Ketones are not the mechanism, and type 2 diabetes does not usually produce them.

questions.takeaway: Osmotic diuresis: glucose above the renal threshold drags water into the urine, and the loss drives thirst.
questions.strategy: Trace the water. The polyuria comes first and the polydipsia follows it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Glucose in the filtrate holds it osmotically.
Neither ketones nor insulin act on the bladder.
Nephropathy takes years, not days.

elimination.verdict: That leaves C: glucose spills into the urine and draws water with it.

questions.stem: A 61-year-old with type 2 diabetes on a sulfonylurea becomes shaky, diaphoretic, and confused at 1500 after eating little at lunch. The glucose reads 58 mg/dL. He is alert, follows commands, and is swallowing safely. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Administer intramuscular glucagon from the emergency supply
options.rationale: Reserved for a patient who cannot swallow safely. This patient can take oral carbohydrate, which is faster and less invasive.

options.text: Start an intravenous dextrose infusion
options.rationale: Also reserved for unsafe swallowing, and it requires access this patient does not need.

options.text: Give 15 to 20 g of a fast-acting carbohydrate
options.rationale: The rule of 15. Give 15 to 20 grams of fast-acting carbohydrate, recheck in 15 minutes, and repeat if still low.

options.text: Recheck the glucose in 30 minutes and treat if it has fallen further
options.rationale: Delays treatment of a symptomatic low that can progress to seizures and loss of consciousness.

questions.takeaway: Conscious, glucose under 70, able to swallow: give 15 to 20 g of fast-acting carbohydrate and recheck in 15 minutes. The rule of 15 treats hypoglycemia in a conscious patient who can swallow: give 15 to 20 grams of fast-acting carbohydrate, recheck in 15 minutes, repeat if still low.
questions.strategy: The route is decided by swallowing, not by how low the number is. Check the stem for whether the patient can protect the airway.

strategies: Priority key word

steps.detail: Key word first, and the stem states the patient is alert and swallowing safely.
Glucagon is for the patient who cannot swallow.
Intravenous dextrose is for the same situation.
Waiting is not a treatment for symptomatic hypoglycemia.

elimination.verdict: That leaves C: 15 to 20 grams of fast-acting carbohydrate, rechecked in 15 minutes and repeated if still low.

questions.concept: The rule of 15 treats hypoglycemia in a conscious patient who can swallow: give 15 to 20 grams of fast-acting carbohydrate, recheck in 15 minutes, repeat if still low.

questions.stem: A parent brings a 9-year-old to the clinic reporting that she has started wetting the bed again after years of being dry, seems tired all the time, and is drinking constantly. She has lost 3 kg over the past month. Which findings support a possible new diagnosis of type 1 diabetes? Select all that apply.

options.text: New bedwetting after years of being dry at night
options.rationale: Osmotic diuresis producing enough urine to overwhelm a previously dry child is a classic presenting sign.

options.text: Excessive thirst
options.rationale: Polydipsia follows the fluid lost through osmotic diuresis.

options.text: Unusual fatigue and irritability
options.rationale: Glucose cannot enter cells without insulin, so it is unavailable as fuel.

options.text: Weight loss of 3 kg over a month
options.rationale: Fat and muscle are broken down for energy despite a normal or increased appetite.

options.text: Weight gain over the past month
options.rationale: Contradicts the history given and points away from type 1.

options.text: Dark velvety patches on the neck
options.rationale: Acanthosis nigricans reflects insulin resistance, which points to type 2.

questions.takeaway: Type 1 in a child: polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss despite eating, fatigue, and new bedwetting.
questions.strategy: Two distractors describe type 2 instead. Weight direction is the fastest discriminator.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 3 kg lost, not gained.
Contradicts the stated history.
Acanthosis nigricans points to type 2.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, and D are selected.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old is admitted in diabetic ketoacidosis with a glucose of 512 mg/dL and a pH of 7.18. The serum potassium is 5.1 mEq/L and an insulin infusion has just been started. The nurse reviews the orders before continuing. Which action is the priority?

options.text: Restrict all intravenous fluids until the serum potassium normalizes
options.rationale: Fluid resuscitation is a priority in DKA. Withholding it worsens the dehydration.

options.text: Monitor the serum potassium frequently during the insulin infusion
options.rationale: Insulin drives potassium into cells and correcting the acidosis reverses the shift, so the serum level can fall quickly and cause dysrhythmias.

options.text: Withhold all potassium replacement because the level is elevated
options.rationale: The level is misleading. Acidosis has pushed potassium out of cells while days of osmotic diuresis depleted the total body store.

options.text: Administer sodium bicarbonate to correct the acidosis more rapidly
options.rationale: Not a routine intervention, and correcting the pH quickly would accelerate the potassium shift the nurse is trying to control.

questions.takeaway: A normal or high potassium in DKA hides a real deficit that treatment is about to expose. Diabetic ketoacidosis involves hyperglycemia with ketones and acidosis, typically in type 1. Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state involves extreme hyperglycemia without significant ketones, typically in type 2. Ketones are the dividing line.
questions.strategy: When a stem gives a lab value that looks reassuring in a patient whose physiology is shifting, ask what the treatment will do to that value.

strategies: Priority key word

steps.detail: Key word priority. Insulin has just been started.
Treats the number as if it reflected total body potassium.
Not routine, and it accelerates the shift.
Fluids are central to DKA management.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B. Potassium replacement runs alongside the insulin, not after it.

questions.concept: Diabetic ketoacidosis involves hyperglycemia with ketones and acidosis, typically in type 1. Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state involves extreme hyperglycemia without significant ketones, typically in type 2. Ketones are the dividing line.

questions.stem: A 67-year-old with type 2 diabetes on a sulfonylurea tells the nurse he felt shaky and sweaty yesterday afternoon. He had skipped lunch because of an appointment and then walked to the pharmacy and back. Which factors most likely caused the episode?

options.text: The sulfonylurea alone, since it has no dependence on food intake
options.rationale: Names a real contributor and ignores the two circumstances that turned it into an episode.

options.text: Dehydration from the walk, which concentrated his medication
options.rationale: Not a mechanism of hypoglycemia. Fluid loss does not lower blood glucose.

options.text: An illness or infection he has not yet noticed
options.rationale: Illness and stress typically raise glucose rather than lower it.

options.text: A missed meal combined with increased activity while taking a medication that lowers glucose
options.rationale: Three of the named causes stacked in one afternoon: the sulfonylurea kept working, the carbohydrate never arrived, and the walk consumed more glucose.

questions.takeaway: Hypoglycemia causes: excess insulin or medication, missed or delayed meals, inadequate carbohydrate, increased activity, alcohol without food.
questions.strategy: Count how many causes are present. One option names a single factor; the key names the combination the stem actually describes.

strategies: Assessment before intervention

steps.detail: Sulfonylurea, no lunch, unplanned walk.
One factor of three.
Neither lowers glucose.

elimination.verdict: That leaves D: a missed meal plus activity on a glucose-lowering drug.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old with type 1 diabetes was found drowsy at her desk after skipping lunch and taking her usual rapid-acting insulin. The nurse assesses her and must distinguish a low glucose from a high one before treating. Which findings should the nurse recognize as signs of hypoglycemia? Select all that apply.

options.text: Diaphoresis
options.rationale: A sympathetic response to falling glucose and one of the earliest signs.

options.text: Shakiness
options.rationale: Also sympathetic, and often the first thing the patient notices.

options.text: Deep, rapid respirations with fruity breath
options.rationale: Kussmaul respirations and exhaled ketones belong to DKA, which is hyperglycemia.

options.text: Confusion
options.rationale: The brain depends on a continuous glucose supply, so cognition changes early.

options.text: Tachycardia
options.rationale: Part of the same sympathetic response.

options.text: Polyuria and polydipsia
options.rationale: Osmotic diuresis requires high glucose. These are hyperglycemic findings.

questions.takeaway: Hypoglycemia is sympathetic activation plus altered cognition. Hyperglycemia is fluid loss plus, in DKA, acidosis.
questions.strategy: Sorting findings by which state produces them prevents the most common error in diabetes items, which is treating one emergency as the other.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Signs of hypoglycemia specifically.
Kussmaul respirations and fruity breath are DKA findings.
The three Ps require hyperglycemia.

elimination.verdict: A, B, D, and E remain. Severe hypoglycemia progresses to seizures and loss of consciousness.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old with a fifteen-year history of type 2 diabetes reports tingling and numbness in both feet that has developed gradually over the past year. He mentions he no longer feels the water temperature clearly when he bathes. Which complication does the nurse recognize?

options.text: An expected change of aging
options.rationale: A specific bilateral sensory change in a patient with diabetes warrants assessment, not attribution to age.

options.text: An early sign of hypoglycemia
options.rationale: Hypoglycemia produces shakiness, diaphoresis, tachycardia, and confusion, not a chronic bilateral sensory loss.

options.text: A macrovascular complication
options.rationale: Macrovascular complications involve large vessels: coronary artery disease, myocardial infarction, and stroke.

options.text: A microvascular complication
options.rationale: Neuropathy is microvascular, alongside retinopathy and nephropathy. Small vessels supply the nerves, the eye, and the kidney.

questions.takeaway: Micro is small vessels: eyes, kidneys, nerves. Macro is large vessels: heart and brain.
questions.strategy: The prefix tells you which organs are involved. Sorting by vessel size answers most complication items without further recall.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Bilateral sensory change in the feet in long-standing diabetes.
Large-vessel disease affects the heart and brain.
A change from baseline is assessed, not attributed to aging.
Wrong symptom cluster and wrong time course.

elimination.verdict: That leaves D. Neuropathy plus poor circulation is why diabetic feet lose limbs.

questions.stem: Before discharge, a 24-year-old newly diagnosed with type 1 diabetes describes his plan to the nurse. He describes how he plans to manage his insulin, his glucose checks, and his feet at home. Which patient statement indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "If I am too unwell to eat, I should hold my insulin until I can manage a meal."
options.rationale: Stress hormones raise glucose during illness regardless of intake. Holding insulin in type 1 during illness is a direct route to ketoacidosis.

options.text: "Exercise speeds absorption from the limb I inject, so I should think about the site."
options.rationale: Accurate, which is why injecting the thigh before a walk is poor site choice.

options.text: "If my glucose is under 70 and I can swallow, I take 15 to 20 grams of fast-acting carbohydrate."
options.rationale: Accurate, and the glucose is rechecked in 15 minutes.

options.text: "I will inspect my feet every day and report any sore or change."
options.rationale: Accurate. Reduced sensation means injuries go unnoticed.

questions.takeaway: Insulin continues during illness in type 1. Reduced intake is managed, not by holding the insulin.
questions.strategy: The wrong statement is intuitive: no food, no insulin. It is the commonest route into ketoacidosis.

strategies: Negative polarity
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Find the dangerous belief.
No insulin means uncontrolled fat breakdown and ketones.
Rule of 15, exercise and site, and foot care are correct.

elimination.verdict: A is the statement needing correction: insulin continues during illness.

questions.scenario: A 19-year-old with type 1 diabetes presents with nausea and vomiting for one day. Glucose 412 mg/dL, serum ketones positive, pH 7.21, respirations 32 and deep, breath has a fruity odor.
questions.stem: Complete the diagram by selecting from the choices below.

options.text: Administer intravenous isotonic fluids
options.rationale: Dehydration from osmotic diuresis and vomiting is immediately life-threatening.

options.text: Administer a continuous intravenous insulin infusion
options.rationale: Insulin stops fat breakdown, which is what is generating the ketones and the acidosis.

options.text: Administer oxygen by non-rebreather mask
options.rationale: The deep rapid breathing is compensation for acidosis, not hypoxia. Oxygen does not treat it.

options.text: Encourage oral fluids only
options.rationale: The patient is vomiting and cannot replace the deficit orally.

options.text: Prepare for intubation to control the respiratory rate
options.rationale: Suppressing the compensation would worsen the acidosis.

options.text: Diabetic ketoacidosis
options.rationale: Type 1, rapid onset, ketones present, pH under 7.3, and Kussmaul respirations with fruity breath.

options.text: Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state
options.rationale: HHS has no significant ketones and a normal pH, and develops over days to weeks.

options.text: Hypoglycemia
options.rationale: The glucose is 412 mg/dL.

options.text: An expected postprandial rise in glucose
options.rationale: No meal produces this picture, and a postprandial rise does not generate ketones or acidosis.

options.text: Serum potassium
options.rationale: Insulin and correction of the acidosis both shift potassium into cells, so the serum level can fall fast.

options.text: Serum pH and anion gap
options.rationale: These show whether the ketone production is actually stopping.

options.text: Serum calcium
options.rationale: Not a monitoring priority in DKA.

options.text: Deep tendon reflexes
options.rationale: Not the parameter that tracks this patient's status.

options.text: Urine specific gravity
options.rationale: Volume status is followed through intake, output, and vital signs rather than this value.

questions.takeaway: DKA is treated with fluids, insulin, and potassium monitoring. The breathing pattern is compensation and is not treated directly. Diabetic ketoacidosis involves hyperglycemia with ketones and acidosis, typically in type 1. Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state involves extreme hyperglycemia without significant ketones, typically in type 2. Ketones are the dividing line.
questions.strategy: In a bow-tie, name the condition first. Once you have it, the actions and parameters follow from the pathophysiology rather than from recall.

strategies: Priority key word
Apply the ABCs

steps.detail: Ketones, pH under 7.3, and rapid onset in type 1 means DKA.
Kussmaul respirations are compensating; suppressing them worsens the pH.
The patient is vomiting.

elimination.verdict: Actions A and B, condition A, parameters A and B.

questions.concept: Diabetic ketoacidosis involves hyperglycemia with ketones and acidosis, typically in type 1. Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state involves extreme hyperglycemia without significant ketones, typically in type 2. Ketones are the dividing line.

questions.stem: Highlight the findings that require IMMEDIATE follow-up by the nurse.
questions.takeaway: Sudden confusion, fruity breath, tachycardia with a falling pressure, and polyuria together point at a hyperglycemic emergency.
questions.strategy: Separate background history from findings that have changed. Her hypertension and her prescription are context; the confusion and the fruity breath are new. Two findings describe her existing history rather than a change. Under plus and minus scoring a wrong highlight subtracts.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Three findings are stated to be new or recent.
Existing diagnoses and prescriptions are context.
Confusion, ketones, volume depletion, and polyuria form one picture.

elimination.verdict: Highlight s1, s2, s3, and s6.

questions.nursesNote: 0915: Patient presents to clinic accompanied by daughter. Last seen 11 months ago. History of type 2 diabetes mellitus diagnosed 9 years ago and hypertension. Takes metformin twice daily and lisinopril once daily. Daughter reports patient has been missing metformin doses for about three weeks since her supply ran out. Patient reports increased thirst and passing urine four to five times each night for the past two weeks, and unintentional weight loss of 7 lb (3.2 kg). Reports feeling increasingly tired and "not right" over the past two days. During the interview the patient is unsure of the month and believes she is at the hospital; daughter confirms this is new this morning. Skin dry with poor turgor. Breath has a fruity odor. VS: T 100.4 F (38.0 C); HR 112 beats/min; RR 26 breaths/min; BP 98/60 mm Hg; SpO2 97% on room air.

segments.text: New confusion about the month and her location
segments.rationale: A sudden change in mental status, confirmed as new by the daughter. In an older adult this is a red flag and here it accompanies signs of severe hyperglycemia.

segments.text: Fruity breath odor
segments.rationale: Exhaled ketones. In a patient with diabetes this indicates fat is being broken down for fuel and ketones are accumulating.

segments.text: Heart rate 112 beats/min with blood pressure 98/60 mm Hg
segments.rationale: Tachycardia with a low-normal pressure suggests volume depletion, which fits the polyuria, the dry skin, and the poor turgor.

segments.text: History of hypertension diagnosed before today
segments.rationale: Background history. It shapes her risk and is not a finding requiring action this morning.

segments.text: Takes metformin twice daily and lisinopril once daily
segments.rationale: The prescribed regimen. What matters is that she has not been taking it, which is a separate finding.

segments.text: Passing urine four to five times each night for two weeks
segments.rationale: Polyuria from osmotic diuresis, and it explains the dehydration and the weight loss.

segments.text: Accompanied by her daughter
segments.rationale: Useful for collateral history and not itself a clinical finding.

questions.caseTitle: Older adult with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes

questions.stem: Complete the sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.takeaway: The dividing line between DKA and HHS is ketones, not the glucose number. Diabetic ketoacidosis involves hyperglycemia with ketones and acidosis, typically in type 1. Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state involves extreme hyperglycemia without significant ketones, typically in type 2. Ketones are the dividing line.
questions.strategy: Type 2 diabetes points you toward HHS, and the fruity breath overrides it. Sort by the findings, not by the diagnosis on the chart. Her chart says type 2, which usually points away from this answer. One finding in the note overrides it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 462 mg/dL rules out a low.
Fruity breath means ketones.
HHS would have no significant ketones.

elimination.verdict: Blank 1 is A and blank 2 is A.

questions.scenario: A stat fingerstick glucose results at 462 mg/dL (25.6 mmol/L). The provider is notified and the patient is transferred to the emergency department.
questions.sentence: Based on the documented findings and the glucose result, the patient is most likely experiencing [[1]], because [[2]].

options.text: diabetic ketoacidosis
options.rationale: Fruity breath indicates ketones, and the picture developed over days in a patient who stopped her medication. Although DKA is typically type 1, it occurs in type 2 under enough physiological stress, and she has a fever suggesting infection.

options.text: hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state
options.rationale: HHS produces extreme hyperglycemia without significant ketones. The fruity breath tells you ketones are present.

options.text: a hypoglycemic episode
options.rationale: Her glucose is 462 mg/dL (25.6 mmol/L).

options.text: an acute stroke
options.rationale: Would not explain the polyuria, the weight loss, the fruity breath, or the fever.

options.text: ketones are present alongside marked hyperglycemia and dehydration
options.rationale: The presence of ketones is what separates this from HHS, and it is the finding that names the condition.

options.text: her glucose exceeds 600 mg/dL with no ketones
options.rationale: Neither figure matches. Her glucose is 462 and ketones are indicated by the breath odor.

options.text: her blood pressure has fallen below her usual range
options.rationale: A consequence of dehydration rather than the finding that identifies the condition.

questions.caseTitle: Older adult with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes
questions.concept: Diabetic ketoacidosis involves hyperglycemia with ketones and acidosis, typically in type 1. Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state involves extreme hyperglycemia without significant ketones, typically in type 2. Ketones are the dividing line.

questions.stem: The provider orders intravenous isotonic fluids, an intravenous insulin infusion with hourly glucose checks, potassium replacement per protocol, and continuous cardiac monitoring. Laboratory orders include a complete blood count, a complete metabolic panel, a venous blood gas, serum ketones, urinalysis, hemoglobin A1C, and a urine culture. Which 2 results will the nurse prioritize reviewing?
questions.takeaway: In DKA the two results that guide the next hour are potassium and pH. The A1C reports average blood glucose over about three months, with a target under 7%. Diagnosis rests on a fasting blood glucose over 126 mg/dL on two occasions.
questions.strategy: Ask of each result whether it changes what you do in the next hour. Three of these are useful later and none is urgent now. Several of the others are appropriate orders that will not guide care in the next hour.

strategies: Priority key word

steps.detail: Insulin is running and cardiac monitoring is in place.
Potassium and pH direct immediate management.
A1C, culture, hemoglobin, and urine glucose are all retrospective or slow.

elimination.verdict: A and B are selected.

options.text: Serum potassium
options.rationale: Insulin drives potassium into cells and correcting the acidosis reverses the shift, so the level can fall quickly and cause dysrhythmias. It is why cardiac monitoring was ordered.

options.text: Venous pH and blood gas
options.rationale: Confirms the acidosis and shows whether the ketone production is stopping, which is how the treatment is judged.

options.text: Hemoglobin A1C
options.rationale: Reports average control over about three months. Useful for the discharge plan and it changes nothing in the next hour.

options.text: Urine culture
options.rationale: The fever suggests infection and the result takes 24 to 48 hours, so it cannot guide immediate management.

options.text: Complete blood count hemoglobin
options.rationale: No bleeding is described, and the hemoglobin will not direct the acute treatment.

options.text: Urinalysis glucose
options.rationale: Adds nothing beyond the serum glucose already being measured hourly.

questions.caseTitle: Older adult with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes
questions.concept: The A1C reports average blood glucose over about three months, with a target under 7%. Diagnosis rests on a fasting blood glucose over 126 mg/dL on two occasions.

questions.stem: For each requested order, determine whether it is INDICATED or UNNECESSARY given this new information.
questions.takeaway: A falling potassium during insulin treatment is expected, anticipated, and replaced. It is not a reason to stop the insulin.
questions.strategy: Two orders here respond to the potassium by stopping or escalating treatment. Neither is correct: the shift is predictable and it is managed by replacing, not by withdrawing. One requested order responds to the potassium by withdrawing treatment. Consider whether the fall was expected.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Potassium 4.2 to 3.2, glucose trending down, urine output adequate.
The acidosis has not cleared.
No indication of kidney failure.

elimination.verdict: Four orders are indicated and two are unnecessary.

questions.scenario: Several hours into treatment the patient's mental status has improved and her glucose is trending down appropriately per protocol. Her potassium has fallen from 4.2 to 3.2 mEq/L (mmol/L) and urine output has been adequate. The nurse contacts the provider to discuss the plan.

rows.text: Add potassium to the intravenous fluids per protocol
rows.rationale: Her potassium has fallen from 4.2 to 3.2 mEq/L (mmol/L) while insulin is running, and urine output is adequate, so replacement is appropriate.

rows.text: Discontinue the insulin infusion immediately
rows.rationale: Glucose is trending down appropriately per protocol. Stopping the insulin would allow ketone production to resume before the acidosis has cleared.

rows.text: Continue hourly fingerstick glucose checks
rows.rationale: Ordered with the infusion and still required while the glucose is being titrated down.

rows.text: Prepare for emergent dialysis
rows.rationale: Nothing described indicates kidney failure. Urine output is adequate and the acidosis is metabolic from ketones, which insulin and fluids treat.

rows.text: Continue cardiac monitoring given the potassium trend
rows.rationale: A falling potassium is precisely why the monitoring was ordered, and dysrhythmias are the risk.

rows.text: Recheck the serum potassium after replacement
rows.rationale: The level is moving, so a single value does not tell you where it will settle.

questions.caseTitle: Older adult with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes
questions.concept: CUS escalates a concern with graded language: I am Concerned, I am Uncomfortable, this is a Safety issue. SBAR reports; CUS escalates when reporting has failed.

questions.stem: After transfer to the medical unit the nurse repositions the patient and notes a stage 1 pressure injury on the left heel. Which 2 actions should the nurse take at this time?
questions.takeaway: Stage 1 is intact skin with non-blanchable redness. Relieve the pressure and get specialist input.
questions.strategy: Four wrong options treat it as an open infected wound. Stage 1 has no break in the skin, and recognizing that eliminates all four at once. Four options describe care for an open or infected wound. Consider what stage 1 actually means.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Stage 1 means the skin is intact.
Culture, wet-to-dry, antibiotic, and alcohol all assume an open wound.
Pressure relief and specialist assessment.

elimination.verdict: A and B are selected.

options.text: Obtain a pressure-relieving device or heel protector
options.rationale: Stage 1 means the skin is intact with non-blanchable redness. Removing the pressure is what allows it to resolve and prevents progression.

options.text: Request a wound care consultation
options.rationale: Brings specialist assessment to a patient whose diabetes already impairs healing and circulation.

options.text: Clean the area gently with alcohol to disinfect it
options.rationale: Alcohol dries and damages intact skin, and there is no open wound to disinfect.

options.text: Obtain a wound culture of the area
options.rationale: The skin is intact at stage 1, so there is nothing to culture and no sign of infection described.

options.text: Apply a wet-to-dry dressing to the heel
options.rationale: A debriding dressing applied to intact skin, which would damage it.

options.text: Request an order for topical antibiotic ointment
options.rationale: No break in the skin and no infection, so an antibiotic treats nothing.

questions.caseTitle: Older adult with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes

questions.stem: For each finding today, determine whether it reflects IMPROVEMENT, NO CHANGE, or DECLINE compared with the emergency visit, or whether it is a NEW FINDING not previously assessed.
questions.takeaway: Compare each finding against its own baseline. A finding never measured before is new information, not a change.
questions.strategy: Glucose 210 is still abnormal and it is improved. Improvement is a direction, not an arrival at normal. One finding is neither improved nor declined. It was not previously assessed, so consider it carefully.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Four values and one mental status were recorded at the emergency visit.
Each row has a corresponding baseline except one.
Her feet were never assessed, so numbness has no comparison.

elimination.verdict: Five findings are improved and one is a new finding.

questions.nursesNote: 1400: Patient returns to clinic one week after discharge for follow-up, accompanied by daughter. Reports taking metformin twice daily since discharge and has a 90-day supply. Reports thirst and night-time urination have resolved. States she has noticed numbness in both feet over the past few days, which she has not mentioned before. VS: T 98.4 F (36.9 C); HR 84 beats/min; RR 16 breaths/min; BP 128/78 mm Hg; SpO2 98% on room air. Fingerstick glucose 210 mg/dL (11.7 mmol/L). Oriented to person, place, and time.
questions.baseline: Emergency visit: HR 112 beats/min, BP 98/60 mm Hg, blood glucose 462 mg/dL (25.6 mmol/L), confused to date and place.

rows.text: Blood pressure 128/78 mm Hg
rows.rationale: Up from 98/60, which reflects restored volume after the fluid resuscitation.

rows.text: Heart rate 84 beats/min
rows.rationale: Down from 112. The compensatory tachycardia has resolved with rehydration.

rows.text: Fingerstick glucose 210 mg/dL (11.7 mmol/L)
rows.rationale: Down from 462. Still above target, and the direction is the comparison being asked for.

rows.text: Oriented to person, place, and time
rows.rationale: She was confused to date and place at the emergency visit.

rows.text: New report of numbness in both feet
rows.rationale: Her feet were not assessed at the emergency visit, so there is no baseline to compare against. It is new information requiring assessment for peripheral neuropathy, not a change in a previous measure.

rows.text: Reports taking metformin twice daily since discharge
rows.rationale: She had missed doses for three weeks before the admission, which contributed to the crisis.

skills.title: Administering Nonparenteral Medications
skills.subtitle: Oral, enteral tube, topical, ophthalmic, otic, nasal, and inhaled routes

questions.stem: A 74-year-old being discharged on six medications explains his plan to the nurse, including an enteric-coated tablet, a topical ointment, and eye drops. He lives alone and will manage the regimen himself. Which patient statement indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "If a tablet is hard to swallow I will crush it and mix it with applesauce."
options.rationale: An enteric-coated tablet is never crushed or split, because the coating protects the stomach lining from the medication. A different form is requested from the prescriber or pharmacist instead.

options.text: "Temporary blurring after my eye drops is expected rather than a reaction."
options.rationale: Accurate. Temporary burning or blurring may follow ophthalmic medication.

options.text: "I will clean the skin before applying the next dose of my ointment."
options.rationale: Accurate. New medication is never applied over a previous application.

options.text: "I will keep the head of my bed raised for an hour after my tube feed medication."
options.rationale: Accurate. A minimum of 30 degrees for one hour reduces aspiration risk.

questions.takeaway: Never crush or split an enteric-coated tablet. Change the form, not the technique.
questions.strategy: The wrong statement is what a patient with swallowing difficulty would reasonably do. It destroys the coating that protects the stomach.

strategies: Negative polarity
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Find the unsafe practice.
Enteric coating cannot be broken.
Topical, tube feed positioning, and eye drops are correct.

elimination.verdict: A is the statement needing correction: request a different form rather than crushing.

questions.stem: A nurse is working with assistive personnel and reviews which parts of medication administration may be assigned and what the AP must be told. Which statements are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: Administering oral medications cannot be delegated to assistive personnel
options.rationale: The skill itself stays with the nurse.

options.text: Administering medications through an enteral feeding tube cannot be delegated
options.rationale: And the aspiration risk is why.

options.text: Assistive personnel may give oral medications if the nurse observes
options.rationale: Observation does not change scope. Administration remains with the nurse.

options.text: The AP reports coughing, choking, gagging, or drooling of liquid to the nurse immediately
options.rationale: The AP is told what to watch for and what to report, which is what makes the instruction complete.

options.text: Assistive personnel may crush tablets if the nurse has checked they are crushable
options.rationale: Preparing a medication is part of administration and remains with the nurse.

options.text: Ophthalmic and otic medications may be delegated if the AP has been shown the technique
options.rationale: Neither may be delegated. Being shown a technique does not change the scope.

questions.takeaway: The administration itself stays with the nurse. What is delegated is observation, positioning, and reporting. The administration of oral, enteral, ophthalmic, otic, nasal, and inhaled medications cannot be delegated to assistive personnel. Some agencies permit specially trained AP to apply certain topical agents, so agency policy is checked.
questions.strategy: Topical is the single exception where agency policy may allow trained AP, and being shown a technique never expands scope on its own.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Separate the skill from the support

options.text: Respond immediately to the identified need
options.rationale: Acute distress interrupts the assessment. The presenting problem is assessed and addressed first.

options.text: Obtain vital signs
options.rationale: This is part of the response to acute distress.

options.text: Notify the health care provider
options.rationale: Correct.

options.text: Complete the remaining systems before addressing the distress
options.rationale: Acute distress interrupts the assessment. The presenting problem comes first.

questions.takeaway: Acute distress: respond immediately, obtain vital signs, notify the provider. Unable to give information: family caregivers and the record. questions.stem: A nursing instructor reviews assessment technique with a student after observing her examine two patients on a medical unit. She asks the student to describe the order she used and why. Which student statement indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "Every other system runs inspection, palpation, percussion, auscultation."
options.rationale: Accurate, and the abdomen is the single exception.

options.text: "Stridor is the one adventitious sound that stops the assessment."
options.rationale: Accurate. It indicates a narrowed or partially blocked upper airway and is often an emergency.

options.text: "I palpate the abdomen first so I know where the tenderness is before I listen."
options.rationale: The abdominal assessment begins with inspection and follows with auscultation, because palpation and percussion alter the frequency and character of bowel sounds.

options.text: "Crackles are not cleared by coughing, which separates them from larger airway sounds."
options.rationale: Accurate. They arise from sudden reinflation of alveoli.

questions.takeaway: Abdomen: inspect, auscultate, then palpate and percuss. Touching first changes what you were about to hear.

skills.title: Infection Prevention and Control
skills.subtitle: Chain of infection, hand hygiene, medical and surgical asepsis, and health care-associated infections

questions.stem: A student sets up a sterile field for a dressing change on a wound with a temperature of 38.4 C, then reaches across the field to retrieve gauze from the far side. Nothing visibly touched the drape. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Consider the field contaminated and set up a new one
options.rationale: Reaching over a sterile field is a common error. Contamination has occurred whether or not anything was touched.

options.text: Continue, since nothing visibly touched the field
options.rationale: Contamination is not judged by what is visible.

options.text: Cover the field with a second sterile drape and proceed
options.rationale: Adding a drape over a contaminated field does not restore sterility.

options.text: Remove only the item nearest where she reached
options.rationale: The field is treated as a whole rather than as separate zones.

questions.takeaway: Common sterile technique errors: reaching over the sterile field, talking or coughing over it, and dropping items below waist level.
questions.strategy: Sterility is not a judgment call. Once a rule is broken the field is contaminated regardless of whether anything was seen to touch it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Reaching over the field.
Visibility is not the test.
The field is whole, and a drape does not restore it.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A: start again.

questions.concept: Common sterile technique errors: reaching over the sterile field, talking or coughing over it, and dropping items below waist level.

questions.stem: A quality committee reviews the unit's health care-associated infection data for the past quarter, which shows a rise in central line and urinary catheter infections. The committee is identifying contributing factors before proposing changes. Which factors contribute to these infections? Select all that apply.

options.text: Invasive procedures
options.rationale: They bypass the body's normal barriers and create a portal of entry.

options.text: Antibiotic administration
options.rationale: Disrupts normal flora and selects for resistant organisms, which is why it appears as a cause rather than only a treatment.

options.text: Multidrug-resistant organisms
options.rationale: Correct.

options.text: Breaks in infection prevention and control activities
options.rationale: The category that covers missed hand hygiene, broken technique, and inadequate cleaning.

options.text: Community-acquired infections present on admission
options.rationale: By definition not health care-associated, since they were not acquired during care.

questions.takeaway: HAIs arise from invasive procedures, antibiotic administration, multidrug-resistant organisms, and breaks in infection prevention. Health care-associated infections occur as a result of invasive procedures, antibiotic administration, multidrug-resistant organisms, and breaks in infection prevention and control activities.
questions.strategy: Antibiotics appearing as a cause is the counterintuitive one. They disrupt normal flora, which is one of the body's own defenses.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Acquired during health care.
Present on admission means it was not acquired here.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, and D are selected.

questions.concept: Health care-associated infections occur as a result of invasive procedures, antibiotic administration, multidrug-resistant organisms, and breaks in infection prevention and control activities.

questions.stem: A patient's wound swab grows MRSA. He is afebrile, the wound is clean and granulating, his white cell count is normal, and he has no systemic symptoms. Which term describes his status?

options.text: An infectious disease requiring immediate antibiotic therapy
options.rationale: Treatment decisions rest on clinical evidence of disease rather than on the culture alone.

options.text: Infection, because MRSA has been identified
options.rationale: Infection requires the organism to produce a host response and clinical signs.

options.text: A health care-associated infection
options.rationale: Would require an infection acquired during care, and no infection is present.

options.text: Colonization, because the organism is present without producing disease
options.rationale: Organisms are present and multiplying without a host response or clinical signs. Contact precautions still apply.

questions.takeaway: Colonization is the organism present without a host response. Infection produces signs and a response. Colonization is the presence and multiplication of organisms without a host response or clinical signs. Infection produces a host response and clinical evidence of disease.
questions.strategy: The practical consequence is that precautions and treatment separate. A colonized patient still needs contact precautions and does not necessarily need antibiotics.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Organism present, no host response, no clinical signs.
Both require evidence of disease.
No infection has occurred.

elimination.verdict: That leaves D: colonization.

questions.concept: Colonization is the presence and multiplication of organisms without a host response or clinical signs. Infection produces a host response and clinical evidence of disease.

questions.stem: A patient on a surgical unit develops a wound infection. The nurse plans interventions and is asked which links in the chain of infection each one breaks. Which are links in the chain of infection? Select all that apply.

options.text: Reservoir
options.rationale: Where the organism lives and multiplies.

options.text: Portal of exit
options.rationale: How the organism leaves the reservoir.

options.text: Susceptible host
options.rationale: The person in whom the organism can establish itself.

options.text: Incubation period
options.rationale: The interval between exposure and symptoms. It describes the course of an infection rather than a link in the chain.

options.text: Virulence
options.rationale: How readily an organism causes disease. A property of the agent rather than a separate link.

options.text: Antibody titer
options.rationale: A laboratory measure of immune response, not a link in the chain.

questions.takeaway: Six links: infectious agent, reservoir, portal of exit, mode of transmission, portal of entry, susceptible host.
questions.strategy: Three distractors describe properties of an organism or a lab value. A link is a stage in how infection travels from one place to the next.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A stage in the journey from source to host.
An interval and a property of the organism.
A laboratory measure of the host response.

elimination.verdict: A, B, and C are selected.

questions.concept: The chain of infection has six links: infectious agent, reservoir, portal of exit, mode of transmission, portal of entry, and susceptible host. Nursing interventions work by breaking a link.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old receiving chemotherapy has a white cell count of 0.8. He is afebrile with no identified source of infection. Which type of precaution does the nurse anticipate?

options.text: Protective isolation
options.rationale: Also called reverse isolation. The direction of protection reverses: the patient is protected from the environment.

options.text: Droplet precautions
options.rationale: Also directed at protecting others from a patient with a transmissible organism.

options.text: Contact precautions
options.rationale: Protects others from the patient, and he is not the source.

options.text: Standard precautions only
options.rationale: Severe immunocompromise calls for more than the baseline.

questions.takeaway: Protective or reverse isolation reverses the direction, protecting an immunocompromised patient from organisms in the environment. Every other precaution protects others from the patient. Transmission-based precautions protect others from the patient.
questions.strategy: Ask which direction the protection runs. That question sorts protective isolation from every other category in one step.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The patient, from organisms around him.
Protects others from the patient, and he is not the source.
Also directed at protecting others from a patient with a transmissible organism.
Severe immunocompromise calls for more than the baseline.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A: also called reverse isolation.

questions.concept: Transmission-based precautions protect others from the patient. Protective or reverse isolation reverses the direction, protecting an immunocompromised patient from organisms in the environment.

questions.stem: Infection control practice is discussed at a staff meeting after an audit found variation in hand hygiene practice on a unit caring for several patients with C. difficile. Which statement by a staff nurse indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "Hand hygiene is the single most effective intervention for reducing health care-associated infections."
options.rationale: Accurate, which is why it sits at the top of standard precautions.

options.text: "Standard precautions apply to every patient, not only those with a known infection."
options.rationale: Accurate, and transmission-based precautions are added on top.

options.text: "Alcohol-based rub is fine after C. difficile care as long as my hands are not visibly soiled."
options.rationale: C. difficile forms spores that alcohol does not kill. Soap and water is used for visibly soiled hands and for C. difficile and norovirus.

options.text: "If I reach across a sterile field, it is contaminated even if nothing touched it."
options.rationale: Accurate. Contamination is not judged by what is visible.

questions.takeaway: Alcohol does not kill spores. Soap and water for C. difficile, norovirus, and visibly soiled hands.

strategies: Negative polarity
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Find the incorrect practice.
Spore-forming organisms need soap and water.
Hand hygiene, standard precautions, and the sterile field are correct.

elimination.verdict: A is the statement needing correction: spores survive alcohol.

questions.stem: A nurse reviews with a student what standard precautions require on every patient, every shift, regardless of whether a diagnosis has been confirmed. The unit has several admissions with results still pending. Which elements are included? Select all that apply.

options.text: Hand hygiene
options.rationale: The foundation, and the single most effective intervention for reducing health care-associated infections.

options.text: PPE selected according to the anticipated exposure
options.rationale: The task determines the PPE, not the diagnosis.

options.text: Safe injection practices
options.rationale: Correct.

options.text: Respiratory hygiene and cough etiquette
options.rationale: Including ensuring patients cover mouth and nose, use tissues, and dispose of them in a waste receptacle.

options.text: An N95 respirator for every patient encounter
options.rationale: Respirator use belongs to airborne precautions rather than to routine care.

questions.takeaway: Standard precautions apply to all patients and include hand hygiene, PPE based on anticipated exposure, safe injection practices, and respiratory hygiene and cough etiquette. Hand hygiene is the single most effective intervention for reducing health care-associated infections.

steps.detail: Hands, PPE, injections, respiratory hygiene.
An N95 is for airborne precautions.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, and D are selected.

questions.concept: Standard precautions apply to all patients and include hand hygiene, PPE based on anticipated exposure, safe injection practices, and respiratory hygiene and cough etiquette. Hand hygiene is the single most effective intervention for reducing health care-associated infections.

questions.stem: A nurse finishes caring for a patient with Clostridioides difficile. Her hands are not visibly soiled and an alcohol-based hand rub is mounted outside the room. Which action is correct?

options.text: Use alcohol-based rub followed by gloves for the next patient
options.rationale: Gloves do not compensate for spores remaining on the hands.

options.text: Wash with soap and water, because alcohol does not kill spores
options.rationale: C. difficile forms spores that alcohol-based rub does not destroy. Soap and water physically remove them through friction and rinsing.

options.text: Use the alcohol-based hand rub, since the hands are not visibly soiled
options.rationale: Visible soiling is one indication for soap and water. Spore-forming organisms are another, and this patient has one.

options.text: No hand hygiene is required if gloves were worn throughout
options.rationale: Hand hygiene is performed after glove removal every time.

questions.takeaway: Soap and water is used for visibly soiled hands and for C. difficile, and norovirus. difficile and norovirus, because alcohol does not kill spores. Alcohol-based hand rub is preferred for most situations because it is faster and less irritating. Technique requires a minimum of 20 seconds of friction covering all surfaces including nails and between fingers.

Alcohol does not kill spores.

questions.stem: A nurse performs hand hygiene, dons clean gloves, and cleans a bedside commode between two patients. No invasive procedure is involved. Which type of asepsis is she practicing?

options.text: Protective isolation
options.rationale: A precaution category for immunocompromised patients.

options.text: Terminal cleaning
options.rationale: The discharge clean of a room rather than a technique used during care.

options.text: Medical asepsis
options.rationale: Clean technique, which reduces the number and spread of organisms through hand hygiene, gloving, and cleaning.

options.text: Surgical asepsis
options.rationale: Sterile technique, which eliminates all organisms and is used for invasive procedures.

questions.takeaway: Medical asepsis is clean technique and reduces organisms. Surgical asepsis is sterile technique and eliminates them. Medical asepsis is clean technique and reduces the number and spread of organisms through hand hygiene, gloving, and cleaning. Surgical asepsis is sterile technique and eliminates all organisms, and it is used for invasive procedures.
questions.strategy: The distinction is the goal, not the effort. Reducing organisms is enough for most care; eliminating them is required whenever a body cavity or the bloodstream is entered.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
Global or umbrella option

steps.detail: Hand hygiene, clean gloves, cleaning equipment.
Sterile technique, which eliminates all organisms and is used for invasive procedures.
A precaution category for immunocompromised patients.
The discharge clean of a room rather than a technique used during care.

elimination.verdict: That leaves C: clean technique, which reduces the number and spread of organisms through hand hygiene, gloving, and cleaning.

questions.stem: A nurse sets up a sterile field for an invasive procedure at the bedside. The overbed table has been cleared and dried, and she has opened the sterile pack in the center of it. Which principles apply? Select all that apply.

options.text: Only sterile items may touch other sterile items
options.rationale: Sterile-to-sterile is the governing rule, and any contact with a non-sterile surface contaminates.

options.text: The outer one-inch border of the field is considered contaminated
options.rationale: Which is why items are placed toward the center rather than near the edge.

options.text: Reach across the field only when retrieving sterile items
options.rationale: Reaching over a sterile field contaminates it regardless of what is being retrieved.

options.text: Never turn your back on the sterile field
options.rationale: A field you cannot see cannot be confirmed sterile.

options.text: Items held below waist level remain sterile if they were opened on the field
options.rationale: Anything below waist level is out of view and considered contaminated.

options.text: Consider a damp area sterile if the drape beneath is intact
options.rationale: Moisture means contamination. Fluid wicks organisms through the drape.

questions.takeaway: Sterile to sterile, one-inch border contaminated, moisture contaminates, never turn your back, nothing below waist level. Sterile field principles: keep sterile to sterile, never turn your back on the field, the outer one-inch border is contaminated, and moisture means contamination. Keep bedside surfaces clutter-free, clean, and dry.
